public_statements.boeing:
The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it has stayed there for a long time now. The 737 and 787 lines are running stable. That's the base a lot of people built by doing it the right way every day, and we're not going to give it back.

The 737 MAX is coming toward the end of its production life, and its rate will come down over the next several years. We'll bring it down the way we brought it up: in steps, on the data, keeping the line and our suppliers stable. Some customers will wait longer than they'd like. I don't take that lightly, but I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable. We're keeping our people. As the 737 steps down, skilled people will move to the 787 in Charleston and across the company, and we'll keep our experienced narrowbody team together. We keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston.

On a new airplane, I'll be straight with you. We haven't launched one, and I'm not going to pretend that waiting is free. But how we decide hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. We're ready financially, and the technology is there. The business case isn't there yet. I'm not going to launch an airplane to meet a date, and I'm not going to launch one that doesn't pay. We're keeping the work going on the airplane and on how we'd build it, so we're prepared when the case is there. When we launch, the airplane will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability ahead of everything else. There'll be headroom in the schedule, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. You'll get a date from me when we launch, not before.

We'll keep working with the rest of the industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since 2037. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, paced by our customers' demand and the maturity of our production system, and never at the expense of safety or quality. It flies with two engine sources, CFM and Pratt & Whitney. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, remains a condition of that ramp, and we are extending our long-range, rate-gated signals to our suppliers for the years ahead, sized to our own needs. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. On widebodies, the A350 family continues to serve our customers and we keep improving it step by step. Any further step will be taken only once its engine is mature and its durability is proven, and we will speak of it in windows, not dates. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting and training, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build the next generation of Airbus aircraft.
public_statements.cfm:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's new single-aisle, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. We'll support that ramp on the signals Airbus gives us, jointly with Safran, and spares won't crowd out new engines. LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It's in every new -1A engine and going into the fleet through the shops. We'll report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say. It's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and a new engine comes when an airframer and the returns are both there.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
public_statements.pratt_whitney:
I'll start where we always start, with the fleet. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and our customers carried that. We own it, and we have not forgotten it. So we control what we can control.

GTF2 has been in service on Airbus's next-generation single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We judge it the way our customers do, on time on wing. We will report that record as the fleet measures it, and not before. Any later-block feature enters the fleet only when it is proven and instrumented. We will not compress testing to meet anyone's rate.

Supply is where we have let customers down before. So we are adding castings and forgings capacity in steps, with our suppliers, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material.

For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared, GTF2 is available today on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit, on the same terms.

Rolls-Royce has made its commitment public, and we respect it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We share risk and investment with partners, never our core technology.

We keep investing in geared technology for the next cycle. It is technology, and we have no product or date to announce.

We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
public_statements.rolls_royce: So. Our commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney stands, as we said it would. When we commit something, we honor it. It is on standard terms, terms that credit the technology we bring. No payment, no concession. No solo narrowbody programme. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through our partners will be in place before we take any share of the fleet. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
public_statements.embraer:
Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

On a new airplane I will give you the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies so that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. A launch needs a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. We have done the work again this year, and the numbers do not prove the return. The investment has to prove its return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. Any large investment will be made with partners, with the funding defined at the time of approval. I will not say conservative, but I would say, realistic.

On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

On trade, Embraer is about engineering. We focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic.

We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost. As we proudly say in Embraer, We Live for the Challenge.

boeing.detail: This is production capacity for 787 rates in the teens, not a development program [BX-1317, B-2336]. It is funded inside the debt lines and the board does not price it. Pope finds the added 787 demand fits: about 117 a year by 2060 (9.75 a month). Charleston also takes skilled people transferred off the 737 line as it steps down.

boeing.move: Next-narrowbody engine requirement: a stable, multi-source engine supply (restated)
boeing.detail: We tell CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce again that Boeing's next narrowbody will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability first [BX-1298]. There is no launch, no date and no engine selection this round. At launch we will request code 7, the only code that names all three makers. This serves Control's engine enabler at no grid cost (Board recommendation 5).

boeing.move: Zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace, with the industry
boeing.detail: We keep working with industry associations for a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts. It is good for every company in the industry [B-2290]. No grid effect.

airbus.move: Long-range, rate-gated supply signals extended to 2050 (NGSA engine sets only)
airbus.detail:
We extend the signals to CFM and P&W to cover the NGSA ramp to 2050. The A320neo LEAP-1A and GTF tail ends by 2047.
- Sized to our own needs only: on the delivery path about 41-45 CFM and 54-59 P&W sets a month, gated on rate, with ceilings at capacity (Wagner).
- No payment, advance or take-or-pay, and nothing reserved against other customers.
- Announced in general terms only, with no volumes and no internal plan targets [A-0159, A-0243, A-0360, AX-0005].

airbus.move: NGSA engine line: code 7 final, neutral on how the makers organise
airbus.detail:
NGSA flies CFM and P&W GTF2, so the dual source is met. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. We neither invite nor discourage the Rolls-Royce / P&W Joint Venture.
- On Wagner's plain reading, fitting was settled at EIS, so NGSA keeps CFM plus P&W's engine either way. That is two sources, and the Joint Venture counts as one.
- Whether Rolls-Royce would then count as a third maker in the market is a ruling for the game master.
- No payment, advance or take-or-pay to induce any engine launch. Anything above EUR 300m would be its own Board item, and none is proposed. No confidential information is exchanged [A-0243, A-0360, AX-0054].

airbus.move: Secure our own materials and work packages
airbus.detail: Titanium through Aubert & Duval, additive manufacturing, the raw-materials watchlist, and the Spirit work packages, fully integrated. All of it serves our own ramp only [AX-0060, AX-0061, AX-0062, AX-0063].

airbus.move: Recruiting and training for the NGSA ramp and the next generation
airbus.detail: Our own hiring, apprenticeships and training, in Europe and across our global footprint. It targets no rival's staff [A-0485, A-0366].

airbus.move: Zero-for-zero trade advocacy in an industry coalition
airbus.detail: With industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing and Embraer included as allies on trade. It stays strictly to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information [AX-0088, AX-0046].

cfm.move: RISE kept whole as technology with Safran
cfm.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme. There is no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214], and it is never cancelled for cost [CX-0398]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. No entry date, and no ground-test or flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice: Safran is a full partner in RISE.

LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It is in every new -1A engine and goes into the fleet at shop visits [CX-0225, CX-0209]. We report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it, and we claim nothing before then (Ali's wording; the -1B fleet outcome is not in his record) [CX-0210, CX-0009]. OE engines come first, and spares never crowd them out [CX-0529]. This is joint practice with Safran. Facts only, no promise dates [CX-0436].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 on offer, on standard terms, to any fps or new narrowbody that selects P&W, sole or shared
pratt_whitney.detail: GTF2 has been ready since 2036 and is available on standard terms to any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared (codes 2, 6, 7). This answers Boeing's stated call for more than one engine source with durability first. For Embraer, GTF2 or the GTF family at the GTF Advantage standard, at Embraer's choice. Both are installations, not developments. We claim no selection beyond NGSA's code 7, and we say nothing about any airframer's dates or rates [PX-0109, P-0746, PX-0062]. No discount, concession or free upgrade [PX-0055]. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: NGSA and A320neo GTF tail: rate-gated supply agreements continue on standard terms
pratt_whitney.detail: We continue to sign against Airbus's rate-gated signals on standard terms. Volumes stay inside our castings and forgings plan, with no take-or-pay, no volume promise beyond that plan, no discount and no free upgrade. We announce no volumes, no NGSA share and no Airbus date or rate. The ramp is balanced jointly with Airbus, and the fleet keeps first call on material [PX-0099, PX-0110, PX-0055]. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: Respectful answer to Rolls-Royce's standing Joint Venture commitment
pratt_whitney.detail: We have no Joint Venture to announce and are opening no terms. We share risk and investment with partners, never our core technology [P-1233]. We respect Rolls-Royce's commitment and keep the relationship professional. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: GTF Hot Section kit continues at shop visit, on standard terms
pratt_whitney.detail: Upgrades are sold, not given [PX-0100]. We give no time-on-wing figure until measured fleet data supports one, per Mitchill's ground-4 advice and Eddy's ground-1 standing condition [PX-0088, PX-0106]. No grid effect.

pratt_whitney.move: Next-generation geared technology kept funded as technology only
pratt_whitney.detail: This is a reallocation inside the existing self-funded R&D envelope of about $6B a year. There is no new bill and no stretch. We name no product, no date, no dollar figure and no performance claim. Mitchill cleared it on ground 4 and on envelope fit. Eddy ranks it last when engineering work collides. Scope and figure go to the Finance Committee at the next annual GTF2 NPV review, as a dated follow-up ranked by payback. 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] and 'an and, not an or' [PX-0109] are RTX-wide statements, applied to engines here by inference. No grid effect.

rolls_royce.move: Standing Joint Venture commitment with Pratt & Whitney, restated on standard terms
rolls_royce.detail: The 2035 `jv_with_pw: commit` stands. It is for an airframe that has chosen both makers. The terms credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. That asks for value; it is not a concession. There is no payment to P&W or to any airframer, no launch-style pricing and no free upgrades. The terms are unchanged, so no new joint CEO-CFO sign-off is needed. No dates, and nothing on any airframer's fleet or on when our share would start.

rolls_royce.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
rolls_royce.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work continues inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing and durability. No new programme, no new bill, no dates.

embraer.move: Deliver the plan and keep building cash to support a potential next move
embraer.detail: We keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan in the harvest season. Productivity comes before new capacity. Commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it, and we keep supply-chain headroom [EX-0053, EX-0080, EX-0077, EX-0078, EX-0087]. We keep the cash and the low net debt ($0.7B) to support a potential next move. The board does not price this.

embraer.move: Keep technology readiness funded for the next product cycle
Trade: argue on data, not politics
embraer.detail: We keep working with both governments for zero-for-zero in aerospace. Our case is more than 40% US content and US jobs: tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and a limited ability to invest in the future [EX-0098, EX-0100, EX-0101, EX-0124]. The 10% share cut is already in the brief. It is no reason for this decision either way. On this grid it is worth about $0.01B.

boeing.move: 737 MAX phase-out: step down with demand, keeping the line stable
boeing.detail: Pope's plan. Rate-downs follow deliveries, not the capacity curve: about 50.7 a month in 2045, 42.3 in 2046 and 39-40 in 2047-49. Each step is no larger than 5 a month, at least 6 months apart (the up-ladder rule B-2351 applied to rate-downs, inference). Lines consolidate: about 2 Renton lines in 2047-50, 1 from 2053, and none from 2056 if Everett North runs at 15. We accept waiting customers from 2053 rather than an unstable line [BX-1274, B-1031]. The KPI gate stays on every step.

boeing.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot through the phase-out, with buffers
boeing.detail: This covers sole-source MAX parts and the suppliers Boeing kept above rate [BX-1243, B-2330]. Their fixed cost per shipset rises as volume falls 37% by 2050 and 69% by 2055. Doctrine's order: embedded staff, buffers, requalified second sources, funding, and acquisition only as a last resort [B-0073, B-2043, B-2285, B-2174, B-2195]. We name no supplier problem in public.

boeing.move: Long-range, rate-gated LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability cover through 2060
boeing.detail: OE and spares cover for a 737 tail that falls from 1,368 engines (2044) to 856 (2050), 428 (2055) and 0 (2060), with spares for a fleet that flies long after. Joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our tail and our competitor's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We make no -1B durability claim before CFM reports the fleet data.

boeing.move: Retain the trained workforce through the phase-out
boeing.detail: Transfer people as the line steps down to the Charleston 787 expansion and to defence, and keep the experienced narrowbody core on Everett North and the last Renton line. Keep the fps engineering and production-system team intact so a 2050 launch could be staffed, and hire at launch, as in 2022 [B-1941, B-0729]. Pope's correction is logged: on deliveries, output is down 11% in 2045 and 26% in 2046, so the workforce hit comes earlier than the capacity line shows. The production gap opens in 2055-60.

boeing.move: fps definition, production system and the 2050 package (no launch, no date)
boeing.detail: The work continues: definition, the production system, the 10-year Solo ramp, Renton under Pope's wind-down condition, and code 7. For 2050 we bring Malave's split and his test of what a launch would need. A 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.6B in PV and needs more than $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B (more than $1.60B to come within ε). No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

boeing.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine file current (no commitment)
boeing.detail: Pope's findings are restated: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 17 years ahead of a 2050 EIS; strain is $0; Charleston fits; there is no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; watch item: it starts on GE alone. A 2050 version would be worth about $0.45B before rival moves, so this hold is probably final. It is re-tested in 2050 only if the brief shows more than +$1B and no A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3).

airbus.move: NGSA ramp report to the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review
airbus.detail:
Wagner reports safety, quality and the ramp at the 2045-50 rates.
- Deliveries are 1,137 (2045), 1,180 (2047) and 1,250 (2050), against capacity of 1,328, 1,429 and 1,489. The lines run at 83-86% of capacity.
- The extra lines from 2045 are paced to demand, not to the calendar.
- The A320 tail (26 aircraft in 2045, none from 2047) ends on running lines, with no design change.
- Nothing compresses testing. A quality or safety escape is acted on at once [AX-0015, AX-0056, A-0303].

airbus.move: GTF2 fleet watch at the product-safety review
airbus.detail: GTF2 carries about 57% of NGSA (Wagner's inference from the bulletin's engine shares), from a maker that says its earlier GTF fleet 'was not where it needed to be'. Wagner reports GTF2 time on wing as P&W makes it public, and the state of the CFM fallback. A GTF2 durability event calls the contingent CFM framework. NGSA's ramp re-times; it is never accelerated to make up the gap [AX-0054, A-0218].

Triggered only by a GTF2 event that leaves NGSA on CFM alone. It is re-sized from 99 sets a month by 2044 to about 95 / 98 / 104 a month (2045 / 2047 / 2050) on deliveries, up to 124 at capacity (Wagner). It covers our own needs only and claims no capacity Boeing uses. CFM's total load falls as the MAX winds down.

airbus.move: A350 Re-engine: hold, recorded for the Board
airbus.detail:
Recorded for the Board at its request.
- Holding forgoes +0.89 in S1, S2, S4, S5, S8 and S9 and +0.90 in S3 (+0.68 on my weights, +0.58 at equal weights). The plan's floor stays at +9.00 rather than +9.89.
- It avoids -0.50 in S6 and S7, the $5B ($1.0B a year over 2045-49) and an unpriced engine-slip exposure: no widebody engine on the record can be proven by a 2050 EIS. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2051 at the earliest, or 2056 if Rolls-Royce waits.
- It is most likely a forgo for good. 2050 is the last decision round, a 2055 EIS is not priced, and rule 3 closes the option after a 787 Re-engine (Toepfer).
- The 2050 re-test applies only if no 787 Re-engine is on the record and a widebody engine with a date that can be proven before EIS is public. Otherwise the A350 stays at Do Nothing, with continuous improvement and competition on price, as the A330 did [A-0003, A-0090, A-0091].
- No programme is timed to reopen any other lever.

airbus.move: CFO's 2045 cash and returns report to the Audit Committee; returns proposal to the Board

cfm.move: Support NGSA with the LEAP family on Airbus's rate-gated signals, jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record. We answer Airbus's long-range, rate-gated supply signals on standard terms, with no launch-era pricing, concession or free upgrade. We quote no volume or rate that Airbus has not stated, and we do not repeat Airbus's own ceiling in our statement (Ghai's advice). Narrowbody price and capacity are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166, CX-0160]. The LEAP load falls from 2,191 engines (2045) to 1,926 (2050). OE comes first and spares never crowd it out [CX-0529]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586].

cfm.move: Engine talks with Boeing and Embraer, jointly with Safran
cfm.detail: We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. A LEAP derivative is on offer for the fps and for Embraer's next jet, on standard terms. Narrowbody price and capacity are joint with Safran [CX-0184]. Boeing wants more than one engine source with durability first, so we come with time-on-wing facts we can back on test or field data, and no price. A new CFM engine comes only when an airframer and the returns are both there. Talks stay private. No comment on US-Brazil trade.

cfm.move: Answer the market with win rates, not reactions
cfm.detail: We make no public comment on any rival or any Joint Venture, and no price cut in response [CX-0580, CX-0609, CX-0625]. We compete on LEAP durability, time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran. That's the scoreboard [CX-0218]. Ghai keeps his Joint Venture sizing (-$1.7B to -$3.9B; 2050 share about 49.9-50.1%) on the internal watch list and re-books if a commitment from the other partner appears on the record. No board effect.

cfm.move: Measure supplier output before any future stack (lean before capital)
cfm.detail: Ali reports that output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages is not measured in his record [CX-0613]. We measure it, at supplier level, against OE plus shop-visit spares, before any future programme stack. We fix flow before we add capital [CX-0540, CX-0633]. No capital commitment and no board effect.

cfm.move: Hot-and-harsh core testing inside the RISE envelope
cfm.detail: Compact-core HPT durability testing in dust continues inside the existing joint RISE budget, and its results feed LEAP upgrades [CX-0222, CX-0216]. It builds the turn-on, turn-off test basis Ali says we lack [CX-0009]. No Ducted launch, no date and no new bill.

pratt_whitney.move: Castings and forgings plan to the 2052 peak and through the decline (Eddy owns it, released through Mitchill's gate)
pratt_whitney.detail: Order tranche 1 now: +88 engines over 2044's 1,361, to the 1,449 level by 2049. Order tranche 2 by about 2049, before the 2050 round: +148 to the 1,597 peak (2052). Forging takes 2 to 2.5 years to add [P-0079]. No new fixed plant. Everything above the 1,361 built in 2044 comes from supplier and partner capacity, in tranches against Airbus's rate signals. Mitchill's sustainable band (about 1,400 to 1,450, held only over 2049-54) caps any fixed-plant proposal brought later through his gate. Use the 2045-47 plateau (1,299 to 1,355) for fleet lift. Do not shed suppliers after 2052 until a Boeing fps is resolved either way. Pre-qualify suppliers for an Embraer line (about 192 engines a year at full rate), with no capital until a launch is on the record. Allocation is daily, reported weekly to the ExCo, and the fleet keeps first call [PX-0123, PX-0099, PX-0110].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 fleet durability record and CMC block status to the Governance and Public Policy Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: Eddy brings the measured GTF2 record on NGSA since 2037: time on wing, unscheduled removals, life-limited parts against full life, the severe-environment fleet, and the Hot Section kit's measured time on wing. Neither the brief nor his evidence carries it, and the absence of a reported problem is not proof [PX-0112]. The CMC hot-section block deferred in 2035 is treated as still waiting and out of the fleet. It enters only as a later block, instrumented and proven at no less than the Advantage endurance multiple [P-1214, P-1215, P-0779]. No testing is compressed for any airframer's rate.

pratt_whitney.move: Annual GTF2 NPV review through the Finance Committee
pratt_whitney.detail: Hold against Do Nothing: +6.10 (engine +8.10, R&D -2.00). About +2.32 of PV was earned to 2044 and +5.72 is still ahead. Against a buyback, about +6.10 (a buyback is about 0 NPV, inference). The commit's item value is -6.69 / -6.46 / -6.52 against hold/hold, -6.58 weighted on the decision's predictions (Mitchill's weights) and -6.60 on the framing weights; it is all share, no cash. The baseline tracks the 2035 hold row: 1,054 (2041) and 1,361 (2044). Engine value gaps are +3.8 (2045), +4.7 (2050) and +5.8 (2052). Management's 2045 figures, including debt against pre-ASR, are a dated follow-up. None are in our files, and none is invented.

Fleet engineering is ring-fenced with first call. When work collides, the order is: fleet, then an installation with a date on the record (Embraer or fps), then the CMC block, then technology-only geared work. The stretch case is an Embraer 2049 EIS plus an fps on the 7-year ramp to 2052. Eddy reports headcount against it when either launch goes on the record [PX-0123, PX-0129].

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture revisit conditions for the 2050 round
pratt_whitney.detail: A `jv_with_rr: commit` comes back only on a 2050 grid that meets all of these: the commit's weighted item value against hold is at least 0; no plausible column is below -$2B; Rolls-Royce is still committed, or a live airframe not yet in service carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7; the Joint Venture engine is ready by that EIS; and the terms keep P&W's gear and core out (Eddy's terms: P&W owns the gear and core modules and their data, holds the type certificate and continued airworthiness, and licenses IP for the Joint Venture product only). The test case is a new code-1 or code-4 airframe on the public record.

rolls_royce.move: Narrowbody support plan, named at formation and in place before our share starts (Watson)
rolls_royce.detail:
If P&W commits this round, the plan goes into the Joint Venture agreement at formation:
(1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA, which has supported the fleet since 2037, is the base from day one.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model are named at formation and take work only once each is qualified.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, funded inside our $4B share.
(4) Narrowbody castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
(5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators is named at formation.
(6) Our V2500 operator relationships.
Before our share starts, we review GTF2's fleet time on wing and size the spares pool to it. We will not accept terms that leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one. Watson reports the plan through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. Milestones stay private.

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan insertion rule for the Joint Venture engine
rolls_royce.detail: The core definition is the folded GTF2, a proven engine. UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme. Nothing that would reopen the folded engine's test programme goes in, and nothing changes the core definition before it is proven. The business case counts on none of it. This is Watson's condition.

rolls_royce.move: 2050 review of the standing commitment (last round)
rolls_royce.detail:
If the Joint Venture has not formed by 2050, we re-read the withdraw item on the 2050 grid, column by column. This is McCabe's test and the Board's recommendation 7.
- Keep the commitment if the formation column is at least 0 against the withdraw and its off-grid worst case is no worse than the $4B bill.
- Withdraw if the formation column is below 0 (an orphan, or too little market left to 2056 to earn back the bill), or if no live airframe can use the engine in time.
- If the item is exactly 0 everywhere, the commitment stands.
At the same review we take Watson's flag on the A350 franchise: the risk of an A350 Re-engine after 2050 (S5).

rolls_royce.move: Widebody: Do Nothing on programmes; time on wing inside base R&D
rolls_royce.detail: Widebody share is 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, above the 50% line. No Re-engine is on the record. Trent XWB, Trent 7000 and Trent 1000 time on wing and durability stay in base R&D, which is not a programme and carries no strain. We re-test the Trent 1000 upgrade only if the commitment is withdrawn on our tests. We re-test UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, priced with the $5B strain if the Joint Venture has formed.

rolls_royce.move: Pricing discipline on every engine campaign
rolls_royce.detail: No concessions to buy a narrowbody selection or to induce P&W. Every new contract goes through the Investment Committee, with win-win terms and value paid for [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097]. Any aggressive term needs joint CEO-CFO sign-off, and none is proposed.

The capital order stays: balance sheet first, then the dividend (30-40%), then investment and extra distributions. No equity, no new borrowing and no levering up for buybacks.
If the Joint Venture forms, our $4B share is funded from free cash flow and redeployed inside a broadly flat R&D envelope. That is £0.49bn a year over six years at 1.36 $/£, or £2.94bn if booked at formation. Base UltraFan maturation is the natural source (McCabe's advice).

embraer.move: Continue the Team Korea / KAI talks on a funding solution
embraer.detail:
I follow the talks personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined before any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034].

On this brief's terms, a launch reaches zero in S1 only if our own share falls to about 29%. That means partners near 71%, about $2.6B more than the $4.5B the brief shows. It reaches the Board's -2 yp in S3 only at about 43%, about $1.2B more. It clears the inherited 2x leverage line only at about 9.5%. No credit until a brief shows the money.

No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control and no military technology moves, so the state's consent is not needed (golden share; Board recommendation 8).

embraer.move: Carry the 2045 numbers into the 2050 package
embraer.detail:
Santana carries forward:
- $0.27B of operating profit in PV, against $0.50B for our 55% of the bill and $0.05B of debt penalty (a $0.59B rise in 2049, counted once). That gives -0.28 $B in S1.
- Net debt from $0.7B to $6.2B: 56% of EV, about 7.5x against the inherited 2x.
- The cash call of $1.375B a year against the ~$2B floor.
- The partner shares that would close the gap.
- His rough 2050 readings for S1: -0.17 by pure discount, -0.23 with the line to 2060, -0.12 at full rate to 2073. All are below zero, and the pure-discount figure is likely optimistic.

Meijer recounts the window at a 2054 entry into service from the 2050 bulletin, with the H3 check, and says plainly if it is shut. Any fps launched this round shuts it.

2050 is the last round, so a launch then is a one-way door too. The 2050 grid decides.

other_moves.move: Continue the Charleston 787 capacity expansion
other_moves.detail: This is production capacity for 787 rates in the teens, not a development program [BX-1317, B-2336]. It is funded inside the debt lines and the board does not price it. Pope finds the added 787 demand fits: about 117 a year by 2060 (9.75 a month). Charleston also takes skilled people transferred off the 737 line as it steps down.

other_moves.move: Next-narrowbody engine requirement: a stable, multi-source engine supply (restated)
other_moves.detail: We tell CFM, P&W and Rolls-Royce again that Boeing's next narrowbody will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability first [BX-1298]. There is no launch, no date and no engine selection this round. At launch we will request code 7, the only code that names all three makers. This serves Control's engine enabler at no grid cost (Board recommendation 5).

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace, with the industry
other_moves.detail: We keep working with industry associations for a tariff-free regime for aircraft and parts. It is good for every company in the industry [B-2290]. No grid effect.

other_moves.move: 737 MAX phase-out: step down with demand, keeping the line stable
other_moves.detail: Pope's plan. Rate-downs follow deliveries, not the capacity curve: about 50.7 a month in 2045, 42.3 in 2046 and 39-40 in 2047-49. Each step is no larger than 5 a month, at least 6 months apart (the up-ladder rule B-2351 applied to rate-downs, inference). Lines consolidate: about 2 Renton lines in 2047-50, 1 from 2053, and none from 2056 if Everett North runs at 15. We accept waiting customers from 2053 rather than an unstable line [BX-1274, B-1031]. The KPI gate stays on every step.

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot through the phase-out, with buffers
other_moves.detail: This covers sole-source MAX parts and the suppliers Boeing kept above rate [BX-1243, B-2330]. Their fixed cost per shipset rises as volume falls 37% by 2050 and 69% by 2055. Doctrine's order: embedded staff, buffers, requalified second sources, funding, and acquisition only as a last resort [B-0073, B-2043, B-2285, B-2174, B-2195]. We name no supplier problem in public.

other_moves.move: Long-range, rate-gated LEAP-1B OE, spares and durability cover through 2060
other_moves.detail: OE and spares cover for a 737 tail that falls from 1,368 engines (2044) to 856 (2050), 428 (2055) and 0 (2060), with spares for a fleet that flies long after. Joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our tail and our competitor's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We make no -1B durability claim before CFM reports the fleet data.

other_moves.move: Retain the trained workforce through the phase-out
other_moves.detail: Transfer people as the line steps down to the Charleston 787 expansion and to defence, and keep the experienced narrowbody core on Everett North and the last Renton line. Keep the fps engineering and production-system team intact so a 2050 launch could be staffed, and hire at launch, as in 2022 [B-1941, B-0729]. Pope's correction is logged: on deliveries, output is down 11% in 2045 and 26% in 2046, so the workforce hit comes earlier than the capacity line shows. The production gap opens in 2055-60.

other_moves.move: fps definition, production system and the 2050 package (no launch, no date)
other_moves.detail: The work continues: definition, the production system, the 10-year Solo ramp, Renton under Pope's wind-down condition, and code 7. For 2050 we bring Malave's split and his test of what a launch would need. A 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.6B in PV and needs more than $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B (more than $1.60B to come within ε). No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine file current (no commitment)
other_moves.detail: Pope's findings are restated: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 17 years ahead of a 2050 EIS; strain is $0; Charleston fits; there is no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; watch item: it starts on GE alone. A 2050 version would be worth about $0.45B before rival moves, so this hold is probably final. It is re-tested in 2050 only if the brief shows more than +$1B and no A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3).

boeing.public_statement:
The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it has stayed there for a long time now. The 737 and 787 lines are running stable. That's the base a lot of people built by doing it the right way every day, and we're not going to give it back.

The 737 MAX is coming toward the end of its production life, and its rate will come down over the next several years. We'll bring it down the way we brought it up: in steps, on the data, keeping the line and our suppliers stable. Some customers will wait longer than they'd like. I don't take that lightly, but I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable. We're keeping our people. As the 737 steps down, skilled people will move to the 787 in Charleston and across the company, and we'll keep our experienced narrowbody team together. We keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston.

On a new airplane, I'll be straight with you. We haven't launched one, and I'm not going to pretend that waiting is free. But how we decide hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. We're ready financially, and the technology is there. The business case isn't there yet. I'm not going to launch an airplane to meet a date, and I'm not going to launch one that doesn't pay. We're keeping the work going on the airplane and on how we'd build it, so we're prepared when the case is there. When we launch, the airplane will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability ahead of everything else. There'll be headroom in the schedule, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. You'll get a date from me when we launch, not before.

We'll keep working with the rest of the industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every field, for the third time. fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site), rate_737 hold (the only value on offer) and re787 hold. Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.

HOW THE TEAM RULE APPLIES
1. Malave's binding veto (the buffer test) strikes every fps form. In S3 the best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -2.91 against a limit of -2.29, so it fails by $0.62B. The 10-year rows run from -2.91 to -3.57, the 7-year from -4.30 to -4.77 and via Embraer from -7.00 to -7.48. I have no override and I want none, because I agree with him on the merits. S1 minus S3 is only $0.05-0.08B, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip. In S1, before any Delay Tactics, the best fps row is already $2.56B below Do Nothing.
2. The KPI veto (Pope's seat) has no object this round. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. hold is the only rate value.
3. The 787 Re-engine is my call. Its item value is +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 / +0.74, inside ε in every column, so on my own test it is a tie [BX-1239]. Four things break the tie for Do Nothing:
- doing less, better [BX-1239];
- the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548];
- Malave's meet-and-beat: Do Nothing has the higher worst column, -0.62 against -1.43;
- company doctrine, which launches no Re-engine below ε (profile §6, §11.4). Doctrine, not my record, drove this last ground.
The Board would also veto the Re-engine on its business case (+0.74 against the +$1B it requires), and its only alternative is hold. So a launch would revert to hold anyway, and I would have brought the Board a case I know fails.

WHAT THE RE-ENGINE HOLD COSTS
It costs $0.74B in S1. On expected value it costs 0.74 - 1.55p, where p is the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine. At the 25-35% I assign to S2, that is about $0.20-0.35B. Holding now is probably final: a 2050 Re-engine would be worth about $0.45B before rival moves (Malave confirms), and H3 bars it for good once an A350 Re-engine is on the record. I log the $0.74B as the Board's business-case threshold, not a management premium.

THE fps, ON MY OWN TESTS
- Market leg: fails by at least $3.06B on its own and $2.56B on the cheapest row.
- Debt before the next airplane: passes on cash. Every 10-year row keeps a $0.0B stress peak, and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes. But a launch that is fundable is not a launch worth funding.
- H8: at $2.56-3.06B or more against Do Nothing, it is above the $2B cap and buys no scored objective. No fps launched now enters service before 2052, so preference share stays at 31% in 2045 and 26% in 2050 in every row, and the 2050 engine count stays at 1.
- Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].

THE LONG-CYCLE COST OF A THIRD HOLD, PLAINLY
The hold costs $0 on the grid this round, because every fps row is below Do Nothing. What it uses up is the option.
- 2050 is the last decision year, so the earliest EIS is 2057 (7-year ramp) or 2060 (10-year), the year the MAX line reaches zero.
- MAX capacity is 428 (2050), 214 (2055) and 0 (2060). Delivered share is 22.2%, 12.7% and 0%; preference share is 26%, 21% and 16%.
- By the lead rule (inference), the long-run split from a 2050 launch is about 30/70 or 27/73, against 35/65 or 32/68 from a launch now.
- The -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid. The brand, the jobs and the last-US-airliner-maker identity are not priced.
- Malave's arithmetic for 2050: a 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.6B in PV (bill $1.98B, penalty $0.62B). It needs more than $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B, about three times what today's launch earns. A straight five-year shift lands it near -1.9: inside his buffer, but outside the Board's +$1B case and its $1B downside limit.
So, plainly: unless the 2050 brief shows a materially different market, this board has Boeing leave the narrowbody market in 2060. I don't like it, and I'm not going to dress it up. But I'm not going to launch an airplane that loses $3B to meet a date, and I'm not going to trade a hard rule for share. My first priority, after culture, stability and development execution, is to build a new future for Boeing [BX-1245], and on this grid the airplane that would do it does not pay.
Pope's workforce test fails, unpriced: there is a 2057-60 gap with no successor line, and it is recorded. Her plan for it is in the other moves.

CORRECTIONS AND CHECKS
- I take Pope's correction. On deliveries, output against 2044 is down 11% in 2045 and 26% in 2046. My frame used capacity (6% and 13%).
- I take Malave's correction. The cheapest fps row is the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine: $2.56B below Do Nothing and $3.30B below the grid's best in S1.
- My 2035 predictions of observed delivered share all held: 40.7% (2039), 40.0% (2040) and 32.7% (2044).

THE CASE FOR THE BOARD (its grid, all four columns)
- Submitted row = default row = Do Nothing: -0.29 / -0.62 / -0.29 / -0.46.
- For reference, the Re-engine row: +0.45 / -1.43 / +0.45 / +0.28.
- For reference, the best fps row: -2.85 / -4.73 / -2.91 / -3.14.
- Expected column: S1.
- Buffer test: S3 is -0.29 against a limit of -2.29, a pass.
- H3: not engaged. H4: no overlap. H5: nothing launched. H6: moot. H8: $0 management premium.

memo_weighing.cfo: Malave is my independent check on program estimates [BX-1316], and his buffer test is the go/no-go. It binds, and it strikes every fps form. I checked his numbers against the brief and they agree on every row. His split of the -3.06 is what the Board asked for: bill $3.27B in PV, discounted penalty $1.02B, gains about $1.23B, so the fps still trails by $2.04B without the penalty. His 2050 test of what a launch would need is the most useful thing in either memo, and it goes into the 2050 package. I took his correction on the cheapest fps row. His meet-and-beat tie-break (the higher worst column) reaches the same Re-engine hold I reach on doing less, better, and he confirms the 48% breakeven and the $0.45B for a 2050 Re-engine. His seat is thin: his record is one call (Low), so I weigh his views beyond the buffer test as advice. Here the advice is arithmetic I can check against the brief, so I gave it full weight. I discount his closing line ('we're bullish on our outlook'). It is not a test, and I would not say it in a round where we hold for a third time.
memo_weighing.ops: Pope's seat runs on operations doctrine with Very low airplane evidence, and she says so. I weigh her results as doctrine applied by inference, but they are careful and tied to the brief's numbers. I took her KPI result: nothing is live, the gate is open, and her veto has no object. I took her phase-out plan: step down with demand, no step larger than 5 a month, line consolidation, and waiting customers accepted from 2053. I took her supplier and LEAP-1B cover plan and her correction on delivered output. Her Re-engine finding is that it is operations-ready (GEnx upgrade 17 years ahead, strain $0, Charleston fits) and that readiness does not decide it: value does. I agree. For the launch round I took her ramp and Renton results: operations can deliver the 10-year ramp predictably, and the phase-out frees two Renton lines by 2053, so her wind-down condition costs little. She fails via Embraer on IP: invest, do not partner. Her workforce test fails, unpriced, and I record it plainly rather than buy my way past it, which H8 would not allow.

boeing.expected_scenario: S1: rivals hold. Confidence on Airbus is Low, and all four columns are plausible, as the Board says. S2, a same-round A350 Re-engine, is more plausible than in earlier rounds: NGSA has been in service since 2037, so Airbus's 'one major development at a time' no longer rules it out. I put it at about 25-35%. S3, Delay Tactics, cannot act on any fps-hold row, so S3 equals S1 for Do Nothing. On S4, Embraer says 'the numbers today do not prove the return', so I put a launch at about 15-20%.
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: fps: hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.45 in S1 (+0.74 against Do Nothing's -0.29). I do not take it. It is inside ε in every column (+0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 / +0.74), so it is a tie. Doing less, better [BX-1239], the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548], Malave's higher-worst-column test (-0.62 against -1.43) and company doctrine (no Re-engine below ε) all break the tie for Do Nothing. The Board would veto it on the business case (+0.74 against +$1B). Chosen plan: Do Nothing, -0.29 in S1.
boeing.premium_reason:
Management doctrine plus objective premium: $0.
- The Re-engine: the $0.74B gap in S1 between the grid's best plan (fps hold + 787 Re-engine, +0.45) and Do Nothing (-0.29) is logged as the Board's business-case threshold, as the Board asked. It is not a management premium. My own tie-break within ε and Malave's reach the same hold independently. If it were counted as a doctrine premium, it would be $0.74B, inside the $2B cap. On expected value at a 25-35% chance of S2, the gap is about $0.20-0.35B.
- Holding the fps costs $0: every fps row is below Do Nothing. The cheapest is $2.56B below in S1 (10-year at Renton with the Re-engine), above the cap, and it buys no scored objective.
- The rate order costs $0: hold is the only value.
- The engine enabler: no premium can buy a scored leg, since every row shows 1 source in 2050.
- What would break the number: a same-round A350 Re-engine turns the Re-engine's +0.74 into -0.81. A slip of our own would deepen any fps row.
boeing.objective_note:
Control's objectives on Do Nothing (Malave's tracker, brief §2):
- Repair the balance sheet: met. Net debt reaches the historical level ($0) in 2029.
- Keep it repaired: met. $0.0B at end-2035, 2040, 2045 and 2050.
- Stress case: met. Back to $0 in 2030 and held, peak $0.0B. Base free cash flow is $13.8B a year, the stress case about $9.2B.
- Defend incumbency: not met. Preference share is 31.0% in 2045 and 26.0% in 2050, the worst year.
- Hold the 50/50 split: not met (52.6% in 2040 only, 31.0% in 2045, 26.0% in 2050).

No fps launched now enters service before 2052, so no plan on this grid can buy a share objective or a scored enabler leg at any premium. The public multi-source requirement, the LEAP-1B supply and durability work, and code 7 at launch (CFM + GTF2, 2 sources at a 2055 EIS, 3 if Rolls-Royce launches when selected) serve the enabler at no grid cost. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source.

We will compute any missing piece from the brief and note it; a missing piece is not a veto ground by itself.

Hold the 787 Re-engine. The test that binds has changed. It now clears our downside limit (worst -0.81, in S2), but it no longer clears the business case: +0.74 in S1, S3 and S4 against the +$1B we require. A gain inside ε is a tie, not a well-founded launch. If you hold it, log the $0.74B as the Board's business-case threshold, not a management premium. If you want it re-tested in 2050, ask Pope to restate her GEnx engine-path and Charleston strain findings. A 2050 launch would enter service in 2055 and be discounted further, so we expect this hold to be final. We will not re-test once an A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3).

Hold the fps this round: the market leg is not there. The best item value is -3.06, against +$1.00 required. It has improved from -4.41 (2030) and -4.77 (2035), but it is still $4.06B short. Set out plainly in the rationale what a third hold means. 2050 is the last decision year in the game, so the earliest EIS is 2057 or 2060, and the MAX line reaches zero in 2060. Under Do Nothing, delivered share falls to 22.2% (2050), 12.7% (2055) and 0% (2060), and the -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid. At our horizon we grant no extra downside, and even a $2B allowance would not carry -3.06. Ask Malave to split the fps loss into debt penalty and operating shortfall, so the 2050 package shows what would make the case clear. Keep the fps definition, production-system and workforce-retention work going, with no date.

When the fps does come, we prefer the 10-year ramp. It beats the 7-year by $1.15-1.45B in every column, more than ε, and has the higher worst column. Weigh Renton (+0.16 to +0.20 in every column), subject to Pope's condition that each MAX line comes down only after the fps is certified and has shown rate. Request code 7. Publish no fps date before launch, set a conservative EIS at launch, and take on no development at a fixed price.

Report the engine enabler plainly. Every plan on this grid shows one source on our narrowbody in 2050, still one if P&W and Rolls-Royce launch, because no fps launched in 2045 enters service before 2052. Rolls-Royce is not fitted to NGSA, so there cannot be three makers in the market in 2045 or 2050. No premium can buy a scored leg this round, so none is payable. Keep the public multi-source requirement and the LEAP-1B supply and durability work, which serve the enabler at no grid cost. Ask for code 7 at launch, the only code that names all three makers. Note Rolls-Royce's standing Joint Venture commitment: a Joint Venture engine counts as one source.

Keep debt first, and keep all three debt lines met to 2050, the stress case included. On this grid the plans that break the stress line are the 7-year fps at new sites, the 7-year fps with the Re-engine (at Renton in S2 and S4) and every fps via Embraer. The tracker's practice of sending surplus cash to the owners is a scoring convention, not a decision of this Board. Any return of cash to owners remains reserved to us and is not part of this package.

Keep the public statement measured: no fps date, no reference to Airbus, no blame on the FAA or suppliers. Keep fps_site at new sites while the fps is held. Log every premium (H8) with its reason. Answer each recommendation in board_response; all seven from 2035 were answered.

frame.question:
It is 2045. NGSA has been in service since 2037. We have launched nothing, and the 737 MAX began to phase out last year: 641 aircraft this year, 428 in 2050, none from 2060. After this round only one decision is left, in 2050.

So the question is whether anything clears the bar this round: an fps (and if so, in which form), or the 787 Re-engine. If nothing does, we hold for a third time. I want the cost of that on the record in plain words. On this board, unless the 2050 case clears, the MAX line runs out in 2060 with nothing behind it. "I think that we're turning it. I don't think it's turned" was 2025. The ship has turned, but we have not built the next airplane.

My four questions:
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Is any quality, FAA or supply-chain problem live, and does the MAX phase-out itself put the line or the supply base at risk? [BX-1271]
(2) Are the market, the technology and our balance sheet all ready? [BX-1296, BX-1305]
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I want Malave's risk-case column, S3 (Delay Tactics). [BX-1319]
(4) Is each plan doing less, better, against Do Nothing in the same column? [BX-1239]
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (2045)
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM and P&W engines. Rolls-Royce was not ready by NGSA's EIS, so it is never fitted to NGSA. Airbus is on the Alt plan and adds lines from 2045.
- P&W GTF2 has been ready since 2036, and the GEnx upgrade since 2033.
- Rolls-Royce committed to a Joint Venture with P&W in 2035 and says it will run "no solo narrowbody programme". P&W has "no Joint Venture to announce", so no Joint Venture has formed.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the record. Embraer has "no decision to announce".
- Our 2030 and 2035 orders were Do Nothing on every field.
- Check on my 2035 predictions: no A350 Re-engine and no Embraer launch, both correct. I said Rolls-Royce would not commit to the Joint Venture unless P&W committed first. It committed on its own, so I was wrong there.

WHERE DO NOTHING LEAVES US
- Score by column: -0.29 (S1, rivals hold), -0.62 (S2, A350 Re-engine), -0.29 (S3, risk case: Delay Tactics), -0.46 (S4, Embraer narrowbody).
- Components: narrowbody profit -3.64, politics -0.12, supply and demand +3.47.
- The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects.
- The MAX phase-out is under way. Capacity is 684 (2044), 641 (2045), 556 (2047), 428 (2050), 299 (2053), 214 (2055) and 0 (2060).
- Preference share is 31% in 2045, 26% in 2050, 21% in 2055 and 16% in 2060. Delivered share is 31.3%, 22.2%, 12.7% and 0%.
- Waiting customers: 97 in 2045, cleared by 2047. They return from 2053 (51; 62 in 2055; 96 in 2060) as capacity falls below what customers want.
- On this board, Do Nothing means Boeing leaves the narrowbody market in 2060.

BALANCE SHEET (tracker, brief section 2)
- Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (since 2030 in the stress case) and holds to 2050, with a stress peak of $0.0B. All three debt lines are met.
- Free cash flow is $13.8B a year in the base case and about $9.2B in the stress case.
- Missed objectives: incumbency and the 50/50 split (worst year 26.0%), and the engine enabler (CFM alone on the MAX, two makers in the market).

ITEM VALUE AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4)
The grid's ΔPV already nets each plan's discounted debt penalty, so I do not subtract it again.
- **787 Re-engine alone:** +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 / +0.74.
  - It is the grid's best plan in S1, S3 and S4, but it is inside ε in every column.
  - It beats Do Nothing on expected value only if the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine is below about 48%, and it never beats it by more than ε.
  - It was worth +2.01 in 2035; ten years of waiting took most of the value.
- **fps 10-year at Renton, the best fps on its own:** -3.06 / -3.06 / -3.12 / -3.17. At new sites it is -3.22 to -3.33. Renton is worth +0.16 in every column.
- **fps 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, the best fps row:** -2.56 / -4.11 / -2.62 / -2.68.
  - Overlap is 2048-50, 2 years ($1.2B undiscounted), which H4 allows.
  - On top of the fps, the Re-engine adds +0.50 / -1.05 / +0.50 / +0.49.
- **fps 7-year:** -4.21 to -4.58 on its own. The 10-year ramp beats it by $1.15-1.45B in every column. At new sites it breaks the stress line ($0.5-0.7B). With the Re-engine it overlaps 5 years, which H4 bars, and its stress peak is $1.7-2.7B.
- **fps via Embraer:** -6.80 to -7.19 on its own, $3.63-4.10B behind the 10-year Solo. It breaks the stress line in every column ($0.9-5.3B).
- **Trend in the best fps item:** -4.41 (2030), -4.77 (2035), -3.06 (2045). My inference: it improved because discounting shrinks the bill and the penalty, and because the MAX phase-out leaves empty slots for an fps to fill. The market did not arrive.
- **My rough split of the -3.06 (Malave to confirm):** the bill is about $3.3B in PV (60.32 x 0.98 x 0.055 at EIS 2055) and the discounted penalty about $1.0B. Without the penalty the fps would still trail Do Nothing by about $2.0B.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS, AS I READ THE BRIEF
(1) KPIs: no problem is reported. Pope to confirm, and to say whether the phase-out strains the line or the suppliers.
(2) Readiness:
- Balance sheet: ready.
- Technology: ready (GTF2, the GEnx upgrade, and CFM always available).
- Market: fails for the fps by at least $3.06B. For the Re-engine the market leg is a tie.
(3) Certification slip: every fps fails Malave's buffer in S3. The best fps row is -2.91 against a limit of -2.29. S1 minus S3 is only $0.05-0.08B on the fps rows, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip. The Re-engine passes S3 at +0.45. Its real risk column is S2: -0.81, inside the $2B buffer.
(4) Doing less, better: no plan beats Do Nothing by more than ε in any column. The Re-engine is a tie, so the plan with less to execute wins. Do Nothing also has the higher worst column: -0.62 against -1.43.

BOARD RISKS (its guidance; it does not bind me)
- It would veto the 787 Re-engine on the business case (+0.74 against the +$1B it requires). Its alternative is hold.
- It would veto every fps form: the business case, the downside limit and rating first (S3 against -2.29) all fail, and at new sites the 7-year also breaks a debt line. Via Embraer also runs behind the Solo launch. Its alternative is hold.
- It approves Do Nothing.
- It wants:
  - the long-cycle trade of a third hold stated plainly;
  - Malave's split of the fps loss into debt penalty and operating shortfall;
  - Pope's plan for the phase-out and for retaining the workforce;
  - Pope's GEnx and Charleston findings restated;
  - code 7 at any launch;
  - the $0.74B logged as its business-case threshold.

LONG CYCLE OF A THIRD HOLD
- 2050 is the last decision round, so the earliest EIS becomes 2057 (7-year ramp) or 2060 (10-year), the year the MAX reaches zero.
- By the lead rule (my inference), the long-run split from a 2050 launch is about 30/70 or 27/73, against 35/65 or 32/68 from a launch now.
- Discount factors from 2026: 0.091 (2050), 0.075 (2052), 0.055 (2055), 0.045 (2057), 0.034 (2060).
- A Re-engine launched in 2050 (EIS 2055) would be worth about $0.45B before any rival move (0.74/1.105^5). Holding it now is probably final, and once an A350 Re-engine is on the record, H3 bars it for good.
- The -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid.
levers_in_play: fps form and ramp: hold, launch_10yr (EIS 2055), launch_7yr (EIS 2052) or launch_via_embraer (EIS 2055). fps_site is new_site (the default) or renton. Renton is worth +0.16 to +0.20 in every column and avoids about $3.0B of new-site capex, but it counts only at launch, and the Board asks us to keep new_site while the fps is held.
737 rate: hold is the only value on offer. The Rate Increase was a 2030-only order. The KPI gate now governs the phase-out of the line rather than a rate step.

787 Re-engine: hold or launch. Development 2045-50, EIS 2050, $5B booked at EIS, $0.6B of undiscounted debt penalty. Worth +0.74 in S1, S3 and S4 and -0.81 in S2: inside ε everywhere. The engine path (GEnx upgrade, ready since 2033) is on the record. A Re-engine now would leave any 2050 fps free of overlap.

Engine code: JSON null while the fps is held; 1-7 at launch. At a 2055 EIS, codes 6 and 7 give CFM + GTF2 (2 sources), and code 7 gives 3 if Rolls-Royce launches when selected. Rolls-Royce says it will run no solo narrowbody programme and stands committed to a Joint Venture that P&W has not joined. A Joint Venture engine counts as one source. No code is barred against NGSA's code 7. No plan reaches the enabler in a scored year: every row shows 1 source in 2050.
Cancel: not available, since nothing is launched. H5 would bar it anyway.

red_lines: H1 (no fps in Round 1) and H3's first half (no 787 Re-engine in Round 1) were Round-1 rules, which I lifted for 2030 on the evidence [B-2326, BX-1305, BX-0550]. They do not reach this round. My own red line, no new airplane before debt repair and finished developments [BX-1247, B-2326], is met: the 777X and MAX 7/10 are done, and net debt has been $0 since 2029.

H3, second half: no 787 Re-engine once Airbus has launched the A350 Re-engine. None is on the record, so the rule is in force but not engaged. A same-round A350 Re-engine is the S2 risk, not a breach. If one appears this round, H3 bars any 2050 Re-engine.

H4: at most 2 years of overlap between a Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine. A 2045 Re-engine (2045-50) with a 10-year fps (2048-55) overlaps 2 years, which is legal. With a 7-year fps (2045-52) it overlaps 5 years, which is barred.

H6: no Rate Increase as a reply to Airbus or under a live problem. No rate order is on offer, so it is moot.

H8: gaps within ε ($1B) are ties that doctrine decides. Doctrine plus objective premium is at most $2B, and every premium is logged. Anything held for the Board's threshold is logged as the Board's, not as a management premium. Every fps costs at least $3.06B against Do Nothing and $3.80B against the grid's best, so no fps can be bought as a premium.
H2 cannot bind and H7 has no trigger. My FAA-process gate [BX-1309] passes, since the brief reports no certification trouble.

My own red line: no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. No re-engined 787 is built at rate before certification, and each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps is certified and has shown rate.
My own red line: no rate request without stable KPIs [BX-1259, BX-1322].

My own red line: no plan that breaks a debt line, the stress case included. This is my inference from debt first [BX-1305, B-2327]. On this grid it strikes the 7-year at new sites, every 7-year row with the Re-engine and every fps via Embraer.
My own red line: no fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304]. The board does not price it; it goes in statements.
My own red line: no blame on the FAA [BX-1323]. No supplier problem is attributed to Airbus before exposure (company doctrine). Nothing is timed to Airbus [B-2313].

Confirm.

fps:

787 Re-engine:

Cash:
