- If Pope reports a live problem in the MAX phase-out, that strengthens the hold. It does not change it.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, my test on the grid's own numbers, with the risk case as the baseline.

Buffer test, S3 no lower than -2.29: Do Nothing passes at -0.29 and the Re-engine row at +0.45. Every fps fails. The best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -2.91, $0.62B outside. The 7-year runs -4.30 to -4.77, via Embraer -7.00 to -7.48. Delay Tactics move these rows only $0.05-0.08B, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip. My veto on every fps form binds under the team rule.

Your split is right. Of the 10-year at Renton's -3.06, about $1.0B is discounted debt penalty and $3.3B the bill in PV, against roughly $1.2B of gains. Without the penalty it still trails by about $2.0B.

The Re-engine is a tie this time: +0.74 in three columns, -0.81 in S2. Within a tie I take the higher worst column, and that is Do Nothing at -0.62, against -1.43. So I recommend hold on every field, with $0 of management premium and the $0.74B logged as the Board's threshold.

On 2050, plainly: a 10-year fps would cost about $2.6B in PV and need $3.6B of gains to clear +$1B, three times what today's launch earns. I don't see 2050 clearing ε. Shift today's gains five years and it lands near -1.9: inside my buffer, outside the Board's limit.

Every debt line holds, barring a launch that breaks one, and we're bullish on our outlook.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery (record: BX-1331, applied to airplanes by inference)
tests.threshold: Can each plan's EIS be delivered as stated? Read the risk-case column S3 (Delay Tactics) against S1 and say how much of each plan's value depends on the nominal date. Where S3 does not test a plan's own date, read its worst column.
tests.numbers: S3 minus S1 by plan: Do Nothing 0.00; 787 Re-engine 0.00 (+0.45 in both); fps 10-year -0.06 (new sites and Renton), -0.05 / -0.06 with the Re-engine; 7-year -0.07 / -0.08; via Embraer -0.05 / -0.06. At most 2.1% of any fps row (0.06 of -2.85) depends on the fps date, so every fps fails on its bill, not on its date. S3 does not test the Re-engine's own date. Its worst column is S2 (row -1.43, item -0.81), which is a rival-timing risk, not a delivery risk. The grid does not price our own slip. Doctrine prior for a major derivative: +2 years central (range +1 to +4). My sensitivity is about $0.07B of item value per year of slip (0.74 x (1 - 1/1.105)), $0.13B at +2 years and $0.24B at +4 (inference). Clean-sheet prior: +3 years central (range +2 to +5), so a 10-year EIS of 2055 becomes 2058, when the MAX builds 86 a year. The MAX phase-out under Do Nothing is predictable (next tests). Basis: my record for the delivery-first rule; doctrine for the slip priors.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase: my binding veto's test (doctrine; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5, at least 6 months apart, KPI-gated. Never a reply to Airbus (H6). No plan may rely on FAA leniency.
tests.numbers: Confirmed: the brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects, so the gate is open. rate_737 hold is the only value on offer (the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order), so my veto has no object and H6 is moot. The brief carries no measured KPI data. I confirm that no problem is reported, not a six-KPI result [B-2283, B-2274]. No certification trouble is reported, and no plan on the grid relies on FAA leniency: certification timing stays ceded to the FAA [B-2241], and the FAA holds the rate lever [B-2236]. Does the phase-out itself make a problem live? No. It is the game's assumption, the same in every plan and in the status quo, and the brief reports no supplier distress. It is a watch item (next two tests), not a veto ground.

tests.name: MAX phase-out: line and supply-base stability (doctrine plus inference; CEO ask 2; the Board's ask)
tests.threshold: Run the line down predictably. Step the rate down with demand, in steps no larger than the up-ladder's 5 a month and at least 6 months apart (the up-ladder rule B-2351 applied to rate-downs, inference). Curtail with a little more demand than airplanes at the end [B-1031]. Accept waiting customers rather than an unstable line [BX-1274].
tests.numbers:
Capacity falls in a straight line, 42.75 aircraft a year (3.6 a month each year): 684 (2044), 641 (2045), 556 (2047), 428 (2050), 299 (2053), 214 (2055), 0 (2060). Deliveries run below capacity in 2045-49 (idle slots 33, 90, 74, 41 and 1), so the line steps down with demand, not with the capacity curve: 57 a month (2044), 50.7 (2045), 42.3 (2046), 39-40 (2047-49), 35.7 (2050), 24.9 (2053), 17.8 (2055). The sharpest stretch is now: 684 to 508 over 2044-46, -14.7 a month. That is three steps of 5, which fit at 6-month spacing. From 2050 the line falls by less than one step of 5 a year.
- Correction to the CEO's figures: on deliveries, output against 2044 is down 11% in 2045 and 26% in 2046 (capacity: 6% and 13%). The workforce hit comes earlier than the capacity line shows.
- Waiting customers: 97 (2045), cleared by 2047; back from 2053 (51), 62 (2055), 96 (2060). Confirmed: we accept unhappy customers rather than an unstable line [BX-1274]. Boeing has curtailed lines this way before [B-1031, B-2245].
- Line consolidation (inference): Everett North runs at 10 a month and Renton's three lines at about 15.7 each. The MAX needs about 2 Renton lines in 2047-50, 1 from 2053, and none from 2056 if Everett North runs to 15.

tests.name: Supplier readiness, a hard gate, and engines through the phase-out (doctrine; CEO ask 4)
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate [B-2308]. Keep fragile suppliers hot and funded [BX-1243, B-2330], with buffers [B-2043]. An engine is real when its launch is in the event log [B-0524].
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no live supply problem. Volume falls for every MAX-only supplier. Our LEAP-1B call: 1,368 engines (2044), 1,216 (2045), 1,016 (2046), 856 (2050), 428 (2055), 0 (2060). CFM's share of narrowbody engines fell from 75.8% (2026-34) to 64.1% (2044) as GTF2 flies on NGSA, so our -1B tail shrinks inside a CFM book that is moving to NGSA.
- Which suppliers turn fragile (inference): sole-source MAX parts (LEAP-1B, and the fuselage, in-house since Spirit [B-2195]), plus the suppliers Boeing kept above rate because they needed support [B-2330, BX-1243]. Their fixed cost per shipset rises as volume falls 37% by 2050 and 69% by 2055.
- Keep them hot and funded, in doctrine's order: embedded staff [B-0073, B-2097], buffers [B-2043], requalified second sources [B-2285], funding [B-2174, B-2264], and acquisition only as a last resort [B-2195].
- LEAP-1B: rate-gated OE and spares cover through 2060, with spares for a fleet that flies long after. CFM says publicly that spares never crowd out OE engines and that it will report -1B durability when the fleet data is in, so we make no claim before then.
- Joint capacity planning with CFM on our tail, our spares and Airbus's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325].
None of this adds a second MAX source. The enabler stays at 1 source and 2 makers in every row.

tests.name: Two-front strain and engineering capacity (doctrine; H4; one major development at a time)
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine overlap at most 2 years. Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps counted from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine from EIS-5 to EIS.
tests.numbers:
Recommended plan (Do Nothing): no development, overlap 0, strain $0.
- Re-engine alone (2045-50): overlap 0, $0.
- 10-year fps (2048-55) with the Re-engine: overlap 2048-50, 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted, which H4 allows. On top of the 10-year fps, the Re-engine adds +0.50 / -1.05 / +0.50 / +0.49.
- 7-year fps (2045-52) with the Re-engine: 5 years, $3.0B, an H4 breach.
- Charleston is production capacity for rates in the teens, not a development [BX-1317, B-2336].
- A Re-engine launched now would leave any 2050 fps free of overlap (a 2050 fps counts from 2050 on the 7-year ramp, from 2053 on the 10-year).

tests.name: 787 Re-engine readiness for a 2045 launch and a 2050 EIS, restated (doctrine; CEO ask 5; the Board's ask)
tests.threshold: An engine path on the record and ready by EIS, durability first [BX-1298]. Engineering capacity free. No production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]. Suppliers ready. Charleston capacity for the added demand.
tests.numbers:
- Engine path: met. The GEnx upgrade was launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2033 (bulletin): 17 years ahead of a 2050 EIS. CFM/GE calls it ready for 787 customers. The observed widebody engine share moved from 42.0% to 44.8% CFM/GE in 2042, so the upgrade has market time before our EIS (inference). My durability-first condition is met.
- Engineering: one development, strain $0.
- Concurrency: we can hold to it. No re-engined 787 is built at rate before certification, and Charleston keeps building today's 787 until then [BX-1263, B-2228].
- Charleston: +1 pp a year of a 170-aircraft market from 2050 takes the 787 from 100 to about 117 a year (9.75 a month) by 2060 and about 132 (11 a month) by 2069. That fits inside rates in the teens (inference).
- Suppliers: no live problem.
- Watch item: it starts on GE alone. Rolls-Royce has no widebody upgrade on the record, and the 787 flies both makers today [B-0940]; Rolls-Royce had 55.2% of widebody engines in 2044.
- Slip: about $0.07B of value a year.
Value: +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 / +0.74, inside epsilon in every column, so readiness does not decide it. Company doctrine launches no Re-engine below epsilon (profile §6, §11.4). H3: no A350 Re-engine is on the record, so the rule is in force but not engaged. A 2050 launch (EIS 2055) would be worth about $0.45B before rival moves. This finding stands for that re-test.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year, with engine readiness by EIS (inference, BX-1331; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Which ramp can operations deliver predictably with the engines, workforce and suppliers in the brief? State each ramp's strain, EIS, worst column and engine margin. Each named engine must be ready by EIS with a durability margin [BX-1298, B-2304].
tests.numbers:
- 10-year: EIS 2055. Strain $0 alone, $1.2B with the Re-engine. Worst column -3.68 (Renton) / -3.84 (new sites). Every debt line met.
- 7-year: EIS 2052. Strain $3.0B with the Re-engine (barred). Worst column -4.85 / -5.04. At new sites it breaks the stress line ($0.5-0.7B).
- The 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.15-1.45B in every column.
Engine margin under code 7:
- P&W GTF2, ready 2036: 19 years to a 2055 EIS (16 to 2052). It has flown on NGSA since 2037, so it is the most proven new engine, and P&W enters service only once durability is proven.
- UltraFan NB, if selected now: ready 2052, so 3 years to 2055 and 0 to 2052, with no narrowbody fleet time (never fitted to NGSA). Rolls-Royce rules out a solo programme, so I expect no launch on selection.
- The Joint Venture is unformed because P&W has not committed. If it formed now, its engine would be ready in 2051 and count as one source.
- CFM: always available, as a LEAP derivative with the durability hardware now in the -1A fleet, or a new engine committed with a committed airframer. -1B durability data is still pending.
Code 7 at a 2055 EIS gives CFM + GTF2 (2 sources; 3 if Rolls-Royce launches when selected), none in a scored year: every row shows 1 source in 2050. A +3-year clean-sheet slip fits inside the 10-year margins; the 7-year leaves UltraFan none. Operations can deliver the 10-year ramp predictably. The fps is held on value, so this result is for the launch round.

tests.name: Renton wind-down against a falling MAX line (doctrine; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: No production-certification concurrency [BX-1263, B-2228]. Each Renton MAX line comes down only after the fps is certified and has shown rate. Predictable delivery through the handover.
tests.numbers:
The fps is held, so Renton has no grid effect this round. Keep new_site (the Board's ask). At launch, Renton is worth +0.16 to +0.17 on the 10-year ramp and +0.18 to +0.20 on the 7-year in every column, and avoids about $3.0B of new-site capex (in full if chosen at least 3 years before EIS).
The phase-out now does much of the wind-down for us (inference). Renton carries 47 of our 57 a month on three lines (about 15.7 each); Everett North carries 10, and up to 15 on the Renton plan. The MAX needs about 2 Renton lines in 2047-50, 1 from 2053 and none from 2056. A 2055 10-year EIS (2058 at the +3-year slip) lands on two freed Renton lines, while the MAX builds 214 a year (86 at 2058), which Everett North alone nearly carries. My condition costs little on this timetable and leaves no delivery gap. A 2052 7-year EIS lands while the MAX still needs one or two Renton lines (342 a year).

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer (record: BX-1330, BX-1333, applied by inference; CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: fps Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds what Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: The bill is $100B against $60.32B for the 10-year Solo (+$39.68B), with the same EIS (2055) and no strain or capacity relief on the board. On its own it runs $3.91B behind the 10-year Solo in S1-S3 and $3.63B in S4; with the Re-engine, $4.09-4.10B and $3.81B. The S4 narrowing ($0.28B) is the one thing the partner brings: it blocks Embraer's own narrowbody. Unpriced: Embraer's engineering talent [B-1420], set against the 2020 exit and the arbitration [B-2131]. It breaks the stress-case debt line in every column ($1.8-3.1B on its own; $0.9-5.3B with the Re-engine). Korean-supplier watch item, kept: Korean industry builds structures for Boeing today and Embraer is talking to partners in Korea (bulletin), so an Embraer-Korea programme would draw on the same suppliers (inference). The Solo fps and the 787 Re-engine build on our own IP: invest, do not partner.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand: Rate Increase (one remark, BX-1329; inference)
tests.threshold: Back the Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column, and only where demand is visible.
tests.numbers: rate_737 hold is the only value; the Rate Increase was a 2030-only order. Demand is visible again from 2053 (51 waiting; 62 in 2055; 96 in 2060). But the rules phase the MAX out whatever Boeing orders, so no board lever adds MAX capacity. The only capacity that answers that demand is a successor line, the fps. On the widebody, Charleston is capacity that follows visible 787 demand [BX-1317, B-2336]; the board does not price it.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion (record: BX-1327, BX-1332, BX-1326, applied by inference)
tests.threshold: For each option, when the bill lands and what it does to cash, as a number. Every debt line met, the stress case included.
tests.numbers:
- Do Nothing: no bill. Free cash flow is $13.79B a year ($9.19B in the stress case). Net debt has been $0 since 2029 (2030 in the stress case); stress peak $0.0B.
- 787 Re-engine: $5B over 2045-50, about $1.0B a year (7% of base and 11% of stress free cash flow), booked at EIS in 2050. Stress peak $0.0B. Undiscounted debt penalty $0.6B.
- fps 10-year: $60.32B over 2045-54 (governments carry 2%). About $3.0B in 2045 and $8.4B at the year-7 peak (2051): 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow. At the tracker's 79%, stress free cash flow stays about $2.5B positive in the peak year (inference). Every line met, at either site, with or without the Re-engine. Penalty $19.1B.
- fps 7-year: $65.00B over 2045-51, $9.3B a year on average, above stress free cash flow. It breaks the stress line at new sites ($0.5-0.7B); with the Re-engine it breaks it at new sites ($2.5-2.7B) and at Renton in S2 and S4 ($1.7-1.9B). Penalty $22.0B.
- Via Embraer: $100B, about $10B a year with a $14B peak year, above base free cash flow. It breaks the stress line in every row ($0.9-5.3B). Penalty $52.5B.
Recommended package (Do Nothing): pass. The CEO's cash timing for each move is confirmed.

tests.name: Share objectives an fps could buy (rules arithmetic, inference; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: Incumbency: preference share at least 40% in 2045 and 2050. The 50/50 split: at least 50% in 2045 and 2050 (2040 is played).
tests.numbers: Your reading is confirmed. NGSA has been in service since 2037. No fps launched now enters service before 2052, so preference share in 2045 and 2050 stays at 31% and 26% in every row. Long-run split from a launch now: 35/65 (7-year, 15 years behind) or 32/68 (10-year, 18 years behind). From a 2050 launch: 30/70 (EIS 2057, 20 behind) or 27/73 (EIS 2060, 23 behind). Starting from about 24% (2052) or 21% (2055), Boeing gains 1 pp a year and reaches the split around 2063 or 2066 (inference). Delay Tactics take 5 pp for 5 years from EIS. No share objective can be bought this round at any premium.

tests.name: Trained workforce through the MAX phase-out (the operating seat's judgement, dashboard_game.md §3; inference; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: A successor line ready as the MAX phases out, so that the trained workforce and the suppliers keep their work. State the gap in aircraft a year.
tests.numbers:
The board does not price this. Output against 2044, on deliveries: -11% (2045), -26% (2046), -37% (2050), -50% (2052), -69% (2055), -81% (2057), -100% (2060). On a third hold the earliest fps EIS is 2057 (7-year ramp from 2050) or 2060 (10-year), when the MAX builds 128 or 0 a year. At the +3-year clean-sheet slip that becomes 2060 or 2063: a gap of 0 to 3 years with no narrowbody output.
Plan (doctrine and inference):
(1) Keep the fps definition and production-system team intact, with no date, so that a 2050 launch can be staffed for engineering.
(2) Transfer people as the line steps down: to Charleston's 787 expansion (rates in the teens [BX-1317, B-2336]) and to defence. This reverses the 2011-13 move that took about 8,000 of 9,000 defence staff into Commercial Airplanes [B-0729].
(3) Retain the experienced narrowbody core on the last lines, Everett North and the last Renton line.
(4) Hire at launch, as Boeing did in 2022 with 10,000 engineers [B-1941].
What a 2050 launch takes: in 2050 the MAX still builds 428 (63% of 2044), so the production workforce is still largely in place. The gap opens in 2055-60. This finding is advice, not a premium ground: the cheapest fps is $3.06B below Do Nothing, above the $2B cap in H8, and the Board grants no extra downside.

vetoes.plan: rate_737: increase
vetoes.ground: KPI doctrine veto not invoked. No Rate Increase is on offer this round (it was a 2030-only order). The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. My veto has no object. If a later brief reported a live problem, it would bind against any rate step.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr together with re787: launch (same round)
vetoes.ground: Hard-rule flag H4, not my veto. The overlap is 5 years (fps 2045-52 against Re-engine 2045-50), with $3.0B of undiscounted strain, beyond the 2-year cap. The stress-case debt line breaks at new sites ($2.5-2.7B) and at Renton in S2 and S4 ($1.7-1.9B). The rule binds the CEO.

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_7yr (any site)
vetoes.ground: Advice: operations cannot deliver it predictably. UltraFan NB would have 0 years of margin to a 2052 EIS, and the MAX still needs one or two Renton lines then. The 7-year runs $1.15-1.45B behind the 10-year ramp in every column, and at new sites it breaks the stress-case debt line ($0.5-0.7B).

vetoes.plan: fps: launch_via_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice: it fails invest-or-partner on IP. The bill is $100B against $60.32B, with the same EIS and no strain or capacity relief. It runs $3.63-4.10B behind the 10-year Solo in every column and breaks the stress-case debt line in every column ($0.9-5.3B).

vetoes.plan: re787: launch
vetoes.ground: Advice, not a veto: the Re-engine is operations-ready (GEnx upgrade 17 years ahead of EIS, strain $0, Charleston fits). I recommend hold because its value is inside epsilon (+0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 / +0.74) and company doctrine launches no Re-engine below epsilon, not on any readiness ground. If the CEO launches it, my conditions are: (1) no re-engined 787 built at rate before certification; (2) a conservative public EIS, with the slip range published at launch (about $0.07B of value a year); (3) under H5, re-baseline once and never cancel, even if Airbus re-engines the A350 in the same round.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Any of the following would change my orders. (1) A brief that reports a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. I would hold every development until it clears, and my KPI veto would bind against any rate step (none is on offer). (2) A durability problem on the GEnx upgrade, or a withdrawn engine path: no Re-engine on readiness grounds. (3) An A350 Re-engine on the record: no 787 Re-engine, ever (H3). (4) A corrected grid that shows the Re-engine above +$1B in the expected column and no worse than -$1B in any column: I would recommend launching it, since operations is ready. If the CEO breaks the tie for the Re-engine on this grid, I have no operations ground against it. (5) An fps row that beats Do Nothing by more than epsilon and passes Malave's buffer: then the 10-year Solo with code 7, at Renton under my wind-down condition, with no date before launch and the slip range published at launch. (6) A partner that brings capital, capacity or IP Boeing lacks, so that via Embraer beats the Solo by more than epsilon in every column. (7) A supplier exit signal in the MAX tail, or -1B durability data that shows a problem: that triggers the supplier doctrine (embed, buffer, requalify, fund, acquire), and if the brief reports it as live, it gates any rate step.
ops.memo:
My record is thin. My KPI, supplier, strain and workforce results are Boeing's operations doctrine; the delivery, IP and cash tests are my 2022 BGS rules, applied by inference.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and no rate order is open, so my veto is idle. The phase-out is predictable: capacity falls 43 aircraft a year, 3.6 a month, less than one step of 5. The sharp stretch is now: deliveries fall from 684 in 2044 to 508 in 2046, about 15 a month, so we step down with demand, in steps of 5. We accept waiting customers from 2053 rather than an unstable line.

Second, suppliers. Our LEAP-1B call falls from 1,368 engines in 2044 to 856 in 2050 and 428 in 2055. Keep fragile suppliers funded, with buffers, and lock OE and spares cover to 2060.

Third, the 787 Re-engine is operations-ready: the GEnx upgrade is 17 years ahead of a 2050 EIS, strain is $0 and Charleston fits. At +$0.74B it is inside epsilon, so doctrine holds it.

Fourth, the fps. The 10-year Solo is the ramp we can deliver, and the phase-out frees two Renton lines by 2053. But it trails Do Nothing by $3.06B. Via Embraer adds $39.7B of bill and no IP.

And finally, the workforce. Deliveries are down 26% by 2046. A 2050 launch can be staffed for engineering; production faces a 2057-60 gap with no successor line. Record it.

other_moves.move: Zero-for-zero tariffs in civil aerospace, with the industry

Joint capacity planning with CFM so it can support our tail and our competitor's lines [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We make no -1B durability claim before CFM reports the fleet data.

other_moves.move: Retain the trained workforce through the phase-out

Keep the fps engineering and production-system team intact so a 2050 launch could be staffed, and hire at launch, as in 2022 [B-1941, B-0729]. Pope's correction is logged: on deliveries, output is down 11% in 2045 and 26% in 2046, so the workforce hit comes earlier than the capacity line shows. The production gap opens in 2055-60.

For 2050 we bring Malave's split and his test of what a launch would need. A 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.6B in PV and needs more than $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B (more than $1.60B to come within ε). No fixed-price development [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine file current (no commitment)
other_moves.detail: Pope's findings are restated: the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, 17 years ahead of a 2050 EIS; strain is $0; Charleston fits; there is no production-certification concurrency [BX-1263]; watch item: it starts on GE alone. A 2050 version would be worth about $0.45B before rival moves, so this hold is probably final. It is re-tested in 2050 only if the brief shows more than +$1B and no A350 Re-engine is on the record (H3).

decision.public_statement:
The balance sheet is where it belongs, and it has stayed there for a long time now. The 737 and 787 lines are running stable. That's the base a lot of people built by doing it the right way every day, and we're not going to give it back.

The 737 MAX is coming toward the end of its production life, and its rate will come down over the next several years. We'll bring it down the way we brought it up: in steps, on the data, keeping the line and our suppliers stable. Some customers will wait longer than they'd like. I don't take that lightly, but I'd much rather have a customer waiting than a production system that goes unstable. We're keeping our people. As the 737 steps down, skilled people will move to the 787 in Charleston and across the company, and we'll keep our experienced narrowbody team together. We keep adding 787 capacity in Charleston.

On a new airplane, I'll be straight with you. We haven't launched one, and I'm not going to pretend that waiting is free. But how we decide hasn't changed. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, and all three have to be there. We're ready financially, and the technology is there. The business case isn't there yet. I'm not going to launch an airplane to meet a date, and I'm not going to launch one that doesn't pay. We're keeping the work going on the airplane and on how we'd build it, so we're prepared when the case is there. When we launch, the airplane will be planned around a stable supply of parts, engines first, with more than one engine source and durability ahead of everything else. There'll be headroom in the schedule, and we won't take on development at a fixed price. You'll get a date from me when we launch, not before.

We'll keep working with the rest of the industry for a tariff-free environment in aerospace. That's good for everybody in this business.

It is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing on every field, for the third time. fps hold (engine code null, fps_site new_site), rate_737 hold (the only value on offer) and re787 hold. Every order is the default, so no item goes to the Board.

HOW THE TEAM RULE APPLIES
1. Malave's binding veto (the buffer test) strikes every fps form. In S3 the best fps row, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, is -2.91 against a limit of -2.29, so it fails by $0.62B. The 10-year rows run from -2.91 to -3.57, the 7-year from -4.30 to -4.77 and via Embraer from -7.00 to -7.48. I have no override and I want none, because I agree with him on the merits. S1 minus S3 is only $0.05-0.08B, so the fps fails on its base case, not on the slip. In S1, before any Delay Tactics, the best fps row is already $2.56B below Do Nothing.
2. The KPI veto (Pope's seat) has no object this round. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and the board has no injects. hold is the only rate value.
3. The 787 Re-engine is my call. Its item value is +0.74 / -0.81 / +0.74 / +0.74, inside ε in every column, so on my own test it is a tie [BX-1239]. Four things break the tie for Do Nothing:
- doing less, better [BX-1239];
- the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548];
- Malave's meet-and-beat: Do Nothing has the higher worst column, -0.62 against -1.43;
- company doctrine, which launches no Re-engine below ε (profile §6, §11.4). Doctrine, not my record, drove this last ground.
The Board would also veto the Re-engine on its business case (+0.74 against the +$1B it requires), and its only alternative is hold. So a launch would revert to hold anyway, and I would have brought the Board a case I know fails.

WHAT THE RE-ENGINE HOLD COSTS
It costs $0.74B in S1. On expected value it costs 0.74 - 1.55p, where p is the chance of a same-round A350 Re-engine. At the 25-35% I assign to S2, that is about $0.20-0.35B. Holding now is probably final: a 2050 Re-engine would be worth about $0.45B before rival moves (Malave confirms), and H3 bars it for good once an A350 Re-engine is on the record. I log the $0.74B as the Board's business-case threshold, not a management premium.

THE fps, ON MY OWN TESTS
- Market leg: fails by at least $3.06B on its own and $2.56B on the cheapest row.
- Debt before the next airplane: passes on cash. Every 10-year row keeps a $0.0B stress peak, and Malave's 'Fundable when the 777X turns' test passes. But a launch that is fundable is not a launch worth funding.
- H8: at $2.56-3.06B or more against Do Nothing, it is above the $2B cap and buys no scored objective. No fps launched now enters service before 2052, so preference share stays at 31% in 2045 and 26% in 2050 in every row, and the 2050 engine count stays at 1.
- Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313].

THE LONG-CYCLE COST OF A THIRD HOLD, PLAINLY
The hold costs $0 on the grid this round, because every fps row is below Do Nothing. What it uses up is the option.
- 2050 is the last decision year, so the earliest EIS is 2057 (7-year ramp) or 2060 (10-year), the year the MAX line reaches zero.
- MAX capacity is 428 (2050), 214 (2055) and 0 (2060). Delivered share is 22.2%, 12.7% and 0%; preference share is 26%, 21% and 16%.
- By the lead rule (inference), the long-run split from a 2050 launch is about 30/70 or 27/73, against 35/65 or 32/68 from a launch now.
- The -0.12 political cost of leaving the narrowbody market is already in the grid. The brand, the jobs and the last-US-airliner-maker identity are not priced.
- Malave's arithmetic for 2050: a 10-year fps entering service in 2060 costs about $2.6B in PV (bill $1.98B, penalty $0.62B). It needs more than $3.60B of gains to clear +$1B, about three times what today's launch earns. A straight five-year shift lands it near -1.9: inside his buffer, but outside the Board's +$1B case and its $1B downside limit.
So, plainly: unless the 2050 brief shows a materially different market, this board has Boeing leave the narrowbody market in 2060. I don't like it, and I'm not going to dress it up. But I'm not going to launch an airplane that loses $3B to meet a date, and I'm not going to trade a hard rule for share. My first priority, after culture, stability and development execution, is to build a new future for Boeing [BX-1245], and on this grid the airplane that would do it does not pay.
Pope's workforce test fails, unpriced: there is a 2057-60 gap with no successor line, and it is recorded. Her plan for it is in the other moves.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since 2037. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, paced by our customers' demand and the maturity of our production system, and never at the expense of safety or quality. It flies with two engine sources, CFM and Pratt & Whitney. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, remains a condition of that ramp, and we are extending our long-range, rate-gated signals to our suppliers for the years ahead, sized to our own needs. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. On widebodies, the A350 family continues to serve our customers and we keep improving it step by step. Any further step will be taken only once its engine is mature and its durability is proven, and we will speak of it in windows, not dates. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting and training, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build the next generation of Airbus aircraft.
airbus.rationale:
DECISION, ROUND 3 (2045): HOLD
Every field stays at its default: ngsa hold, no engine code (7 has been final since EIS), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. That means no Board items and no override.

MY ORDER OF QUESTIONS
1. The five pillars. Both live rows pass. Every Delay Tactics row is struck.
2. The ramp. NGSA runs at 83-86% of capacity and demand sets our deliveries. Wagner reports no crunch and no event.
3. The next decades. The A350 Re-engine is the derivative path, but no widebody engine on the record can be proven by a 2050 EIS.
4. Can I take it to the Board? A hold is never vetoed. The Re-engine does not meet the Board's second condition ('Toepfer passes it').

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP

1. Deletions (red lines and the pillars, never traded for PV)
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move on A scores -11.46 in S1, S6 and S8, and its best is +0.14 (S4).
  - Rule 5 fails on row A, because nothing of ours is in development.
  - Bottleneck and both also fail the pillars, and both counts as two moves.
  - The Board vetoes all three.
  - The team's stricter condition cannot be met, because NGSA has been in service since 2037. I do not set it aside.
- There is no cancel option this round.

2. Tests
- Row A (the default) survives.
  - Toepfer passes it on cash ($0), robustness (worst S8 and S9, +9.00), liquidity and Board items (none).
  - Wagner passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch and the pillars.
- Row B (A350 Re-engine 2045, EIS 2050) does not survive.
  - Toepfer passes it on cash: $1.0B a year, 19% of the $5.2B line, no overlap, $0 strain.
  - He also passes it on row robustness and on the Board's $2B downside test.
  - He fails it on the $1B launch condition. The item scores +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50 / +0.89 / +0.89, so no column reaches $1B. This is a binding soft veto.
  - Wagner holds no operating veto. He passes capacity, absorption, line readiness, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.
  - Wagner records one exposure: Rolls-Royce has launched no UltraFan widebody, so the engine would be ready in 2051 at the earliest, or 2056 if Rolls-Royce waits. That is a slip of 1 to 6 years or more, which the grid does not price. In S6 and S7 it would leave us worse than -0.50.
- I judge Toepfer's flag sound, not mistaken.
  - He calls the clause his own reading, but profile §6 states it as a Re-engine launch condition: 'whatif shows at least $1B over Do Nothing, including strain'. My framing cited it.
  - Where the team rule and the profile differ, the profile governs.

3. Choice
- Row A is the only survivor.
- It is also the company default, within $1B of the best grid plan in my expected column. In S1 the gap is $0.89B.
- Every tie-break favours hold:
  - No early EIS: B's priced 2050 EIS is earlier than any engine on the record can be proven.
  - Less concurrency: none in A, against a widebody development during the NGSA ramp in B.
  - Later capex start: none in A, against $1.0B a year from 2045 in B.
  - Fewer Board items: 0 against 1.

4. Override
None is possible. The Re-engine's margin over the best passing option is +0.89 in S1 and +0.90 at best, below the $1B bar. The Board would also veto it on governance. The override budget stays unused.

5. Why I do not use the band the other way
The Board's horizon favours this window, and I take that seriously. In my framing I named what would move me:
- clean passes from both colleagues;
- an engine path that can be proven by 2050, or an honest re-time;
- confirmation from Thomas that returns stay fundable.
Thomas confirmed fundability and that holding is most likely a forgo for good. The other two conditions failed:
- Thomas did not pass the item.
- Lars named no engine path that can be proven by 2050.
Launching now would mean committing to a date we already know is ahead of the engine. My rule is to re-time, never accelerate, and my risk appetite on technology and EIS is Low [AX-0006, AX-0020]. On expected value alone the item would be positive: it turns negative only if S6 and S7 together carry more than 64%, and on my weights they carry 15%. So I hold on the $1B condition and on the engine, not on the downside.

6. What holding forgoes and avoids (the Board's ask)
- It forgoes +0.89 in seven columns (+0.90 in S3), which is +0.68 on my weights and +0.58 at equal weights. The plan's floor stays at +9.00 instead of +9.89.
- It avoids -0.50 in S6 and S7, the $5B bill and the unpriced slip exposure.
- It is most likely a forgo for good. 2050 is the last decision round, a 2055 EIS is not priced, and rule 3 closes the option after a 787 Re-engine.

7. Engines
- Code 7 is final, with CFM + GTF2: 2 sources and 2 makers in every cell.
- The Joint Venture: on Wagner's plain reading, NGSA keeps two sources whether or not it forms. Whether Rolls-Royce would count as a third maker is a ruling for the game master.
- The line stays neutral, with no inducement.

8. Supply
There is no crunch. On deliveries, CFM needs about 41-45 sets a month (under 51) and P&W about 54-59 (near its 2044 level). CFM's total load falls as the MAX winds down. The signals are extended to 2050 and the CFM framework is re-sized, both to our own needs only.

9. Board-gate lines
There are no Board items. For the record:
- rea350 hold: pillars pass; Toepfer passes; Wagner passes; ΔPV 0 against the default.
- The Re-engine, considered and not brought: pillars pass; Toepfer fails (soft veto on the $1B condition, passes on cash); Wagner passes, with the engine exposure recorded; grid +0.89 in seven columns and -0.50 in S6 and S7.

10. Round 2 check
I expected an fps (S2), and Boeing held (S1). This round I name S1. The choice of row does not depend on the column, because A is the only survivor in every column.

For the Re-engine, Wagner should set out production readiness and the engine.

- He should confirm A350 line readiness and engineering capacity alongside the NGSA ramp.

Our 2050-54 gains (up to 1.5 pp a year) would stand, so on the rules' logic the item would sit between -0.50 and +0.89 (inference). The brief gives neither the sign nor the size, and I give no number. A later 787 Re-engine cannot enter service first, so no cancel case arises.

tests.name: What holding forgoes: deferral or forgo (ask 4)
tests.threshold: State only what the brief supports, with no estimate it does not give
tests.numbers: On the grid, holding forgoes +0.89 to +0.90 in seven columns and avoids -0.50 in S6 and S7. It is most likely a forgo for good, for four reasons. (a) 2050 is the last decision round (rules.md). (b) A 2050 launch enters service in 2055, and the brief does not price it. (c) Each year later is another year's discount at 8%: five years is a factor of 0.68 (arithmetic, not a value). (d) Rule 3 closes it in S6 and S7, and in 2050 a sealed same-year 787 Re-engine could meet it again. It stays open only where Boeing holds the 787 again, and then only to a later EIS that is not priced. The profile's own Re-engine window (2033-35, last in T4 2035-37) has passed. I give no number.

tests.name: Overlap and one launch per round (rule 6)
tests.threshold: At most one new launch per round; NGSA / A350 Re-engine overlap of 2 years or less unless the grid shows at least $1B more
tests.numbers: Row B has one new launch (the Re-engine), 0 years of overlap with NGSA development (2030-36) and $0 strain. Row A has no launch.

tests.name: Liquidity, net cash, rating and returns through 2049 (ask 5; this year's cash report to the Audit Committee)
tests.threshold: Net cash positive through 2049; payout within 30-50%; any buyback inside an AGM authority of up to 10% of capital; no equity raise; rating anchored on positive net cash (inference)
tests.numbers: The board reports no FCF, net cash or rating, so these are static FY2025 bounds (inference). FCF is $5.2B a year. The dividend, scaled from EUR 2,527m at 48%, is $1.74B at 30%, $2.32B at 40% and $2.90B at 50%. Share-plan buybacks are about $1.0B (EUR 916m). The 2026 programme of EUR 5bn over three years is about $1.83B a year. Entering 2045, net cash is about $11.8B on the most conservative path (the $2.1B end-2036 trough from my 2035 memo, then +$1.21B a year over 2037-44 at a 50% payout plus share-plan buybacks), against $13.4B in FY2025. Annual change in 2045-49, hold / Re-engine: 40% + share plans +1.88 / +0.88; 50% + share plans +1.30 / +0.30; 40% + EUR 5bn programme +1.05 / +0.05; 50% + EUR 5bn programme +0.47 / -0.53. End-2049 net cash: about $21B for hold at 40% + share plans, about $16B for the Re-engine at 40% + share plans, and about $9.1B in the worst case tested (Re-engine, 50%, EUR 5bn programme). It stays positive in every path. On the brief's profit path ($17.1-18.9B operating profit), FCF and the dividend both scale up and the fixed $1.0B weighs less. Rating: A+ (S&P) and A1 (Moody's) as of 2026. The record holds no rating thresholds, and with net cash positive in every tested path nothing here strains the rating. Proposal: a 40% payout; buybacks to cover share plans inside an 18-month AGM authority of up to 10% of capital; a larger programme only on reported FCF and a Board re-test, and with the Re-engine only at a payout of 40% or less. No equity raise. Launch aid is priced as our own money. In a shock, the dividend goes first.

tests.name: Fine exposure: any Delay Tactics move this round (rule 4; ask 6)
tests.threshold: Red line: no move before an fps is on the public record. A naked move draws the $48.32B fine
tests.numbers: No fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine, booked at the 2045 order year (later than the 2041 snapshot). That is 9.3 years of FCF and 3.6 times FY2025 net cash. One move on A: -11.46 / -0.10 / -0.10 / +0.14 / -0.10 / -11.46 / -0.10 / -11.46 / -0.11. Its best is +0.14 (S4), $0.86B short of $1B. On B, one move scores -11.47 to +0.14. B plus one move shows +1.03 against A in S4 only because it adds the Re-engine's +0.89 to the move's +0.14. Red line, struck; no override.

tests.name: Second move: delay_tactics both (rule 4)
tests.threshold: Red line: never a second move; both counts as two
tests.numbers: Both moves on A score -11.72 (S1, S6, S8) to -0.07 (S4). That is $0.19-0.26B worse than one move in every column, because the second $1B buys nothing. The Board vetoes both in every round.

tests.name: Poaching (rule 5)
tests.threshold: Poaching only while NGSA or an A350 Re-engine is in development
tests.numbers: Row A has nothing in development from 2045 (NGSA in service since 2037), so poaching on A breaks rule 5. On B the Re-engine would be in development in 2045-49, which meets rule 5 on paper, but rule 4 still strikes the move. No programme should be timed to reopen this lever.

tests.name: Delay Tactics cash (spend only)
tests.threshold: Spread each $1B move evenly from the order year to fps EIS and add it to that year's spend
tests.numbers: Naked (S1, S6, S8): $1.0B lands in 2045, making 2045 spend $1.0B on A or $2.0B on B. In the fps 10-yr columns (EIS 2055) it is $0.10B a year over 2045-54; in S4 (EIS 2052), $0.14B a year. All are under $5.2B. Both moves double the add ($2.0B on A and $3.0B on B in 2045, naked). It is the fine, not the spend, that fails (fine-exposure test above).

tests.name: Cancel (rule 7 and the Re-engine cancel discipline)
tests.threshold: Never cancel NGSA. Cancel an A350 Re-engine only if the 787 Re-engine enters service first and the remaining spend loses at least $1B. Write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years
tests.numbers: There is no cancel option this round: NGSA has been in service since 2037, and an airframe can be cancelled only before EIS. For a 2045 Re-engine the cancel case cannot arise. A 787 Re-engine launched in 2045 enters service in 2050, the same year as ours, and any later one enters later. If it were cancelled anyway, the write-off would be $5B x years elapsed / 5, $1.0B per year elapsed. That is a reported charge, shown even where it is adjusted out of EBIT Adjusted.

tests.name: Capex timing (tie-break within $1B; ask 8)
tests.threshold: Between options within $1B, prefer the later capex start
tests.numbers: The rows are within $1B in every column (largest gap 0.90). Hold starts no capex, while the Re-engine starts $1.0B a year in 2045. The tie-break favours hold.

tests.name: Board items and engine inducement (asks 7 and 8)
tests.threshold: Every order above EUR 300m is a Board item; within $1B, prefer fewer
tests.numbers: Row A has 0 Board items. Row B has 1: rea350 launch, $5B, a Qualified Majority item above EUR 800m. No engine inducement is proposed, and any payment, advance or take-or-pay above EUR 300m would be its own item. Both tie-breaks favour hold. What cuts the other way in the cash picture: this is the cheapest window the game has offered (19% of the line and $0 strain, against $6.67B a year in the 2030 and 2035 rounds), so cash gives no reason to wait; and B's row floor is $0.89B higher. Neither reaches $1B.

tests.name: Five pillars and integrity (Audit Committee defensibility)
tests.threshold: No order whose integrity or compliance I could not defend to the Audit Committee
tests.numbers: Row A and row B: no flag. Neither has a covert move, an inducement or a confidential exchange, and neither discloses internal plan targets. Any bottleneck move beyond a first claim on scarce capacity, and both, would be integrity flags, and they are struck above.

vetoes.plan: Row B: NGSA hold (A320 Alt plan) + A350 Re-engine launched in 2045 (EIS 2050)
vetoes.ground: Failed added-move robustness test (soft veto). The item scores +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50 / +0.89 / +0.89 against hold. No column reaches the company's $1B condition for an added move, so no weighting can, and it turns negative in S6 and S7, which the Board counts plausible. Its grid margin over the best passing option (row A, hold) is +0.89 in S1 (the CEO's expected column), +0.90 at best and +0.68 on his weights, all below the $1B override bar, so no override is available under the team rule. Peak cash is not the objection: $1.0B a year against $5.2B, with $0 strain, passes. The added-move clause is the drafter's reading of profile §6 and is not in teams.md; I state it so that the Board can weigh it. On my tests I do not pass the Re-engine, so the Board's condition 'Toepfer passes it' is met on cash and not on robustness.

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching or both), on row A or row B
vetoes.ground: Company red lines; no override possible. Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (one move on A: -11.46 in S1, S6 and S8; best +0.14 in S4). 'both' is a second move. Rule 5: poaching on row A has nothing in development. A bottleneck move beyond a first claim on capacity is also a five-pillars integrity flag that I could not defend to the Audit Committee.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: Any of three things. (1) A passing plan shows at least $1B over row A in the CEO's named expected column. No column on this grid does: the Re-engine's best is +0.90. (2) The Board decides that, with peak cash passing, its own downside test (a gain in the named expected column and no loss above $2B) governs this item instead of the $1B added-move clause, which is the drafter's reading of profile §6 and not in teams.md. I would then withdraw the soft veto. The Re-engine would pass all my tests, and the choice inside the band would be Faury's, although my tie-breaks (later capex, fewer Board items) still favour hold. (3) Facts that would harden hold rather than change it: a supply crunch or an unproven widebody engine (Wagner's calls), a 787 Re-engine on the record (rule 3), or a cash shock that would put the dividend first. No grid margin moves me on Delay Tactics, which are red lines this round.
cfo.memo:
CFO test memo, round 3 (2045).

Fundability. Hold: no programme cash. The A350 Re-engine takes $5B / 5 = $1.0B a year over 2045-49: 19% of the $5.2B line (EUR 4,753m at an assumed $1.10), $4.2B of headroom, no NGSA overlap, $0 strain. Cash: pass, no soft veto, no re-base needed.

Value. The item gains +0.89 to +0.90 in seven columns and loses -0.50 in S6 and S7, where a same-year 787 Re-engine cancels the share gain. No column reaches $1B, so no weighting can. The company's test for an added move asks at least $1B over the same plan without it; one that misses it and turns negative in a plausible column fails. Fail: a soft veto, binding. Margin over hold, the best passing option: +0.89 in S1, below the $1B override bar. The Board's $2B downside test passes.

Holding forgoes +0.89 in seven columns and avoids -0.50 in two. 2050 is the last round, a 2055 EIS is unpriced, and rule 3 closes it after a 787 Re-engine: most likely a forgo for good.

Flexibility. On a static FY2025 base, a 40% payout plus share-plan buybacks keeps net cash rising with the Re-engine (+$0.88B a year) and without (+$1.88B). A EUR 5bn three-year buyback is neutral with it at 40%, and draws $0.53B a year at 50%. No equity raise.

Strikes. Any Delay Tactics move is naked: -11.46 in S1, S6, S8.

Orders: all defaults; no engine code (7 is final; I defer to Wagner). No Board items.

tests.name: Ask 1: NGSA ramp safety and quality, 2045-50 (report for the Board's twice-yearly product-safety review), both rows
tests.threshold: No order whose execution or public explanation contradicts safety or quality (five pillars, binding, no override). Nothing may compress testing.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no inject and no safety, quality or supply event. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and GTF2 was ready in 2036, proven before EIS on P&W's own record. Demand now sets our deliveries: 1,137 (2045), 1,180 (2047) and 1,250 (2050), against capacity of 1,328, 1,429 and 1,489. That leaves 191, 249 and 239 aircraft of headroom (14.4%, 17.4%, 16.1%), so the lines run at 83-86% of capacity. Nothing pushes rate, and nothing compresses testing. The A320 tail is 26 slots in 2045 and none from 2047. On the board, NGSA fills first, so those slots are not called on (inference). The tail ends on running lines with no design change. On the extra lines from 2045 (5 a month more each year, up to 20), the brief's demand does not call on all of them. Pace them to demand, not to the calendar (inference). The Re-engine row adds no narrowbody line work.

tests.name: Ask 1: A320 ramp shield, both rows
tests.threshold: No new programme spend that competes with the open A320 ramp commitment. Passes unless the brief reports a ramp problem (no override).
tests.numbers: The end-2027 commitment (rate 70-75, then 75) is 18 years behind us. The brief reports no ramp problem. NGSA deliveries are limited by demand, not capacity. The Re-engine is widebody work at about $1.0B a year in cash, and on the board it takes no A320 or NGSA line capacity.

tests.name: Ask 2: supply-crunch re-test, CFM and P&W engine sets a month, 2045 / 2047 / 2050
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a supply crunch, no new concurrency, and the A350 Re-engine waits (doctrine row 12; no override). No plan may ask an engine maker for more than it supplies today without a rate signal behind it.
tests.numbers:
The brief reports no crunch, so doctrine row 12 is not triggered. Engine shares exclude COMAC. From the bulletin's NB engine shares, GTF2's share of NGSA is 57.0% (2041), 57.2% (2042) and 57.1% (2044), an inference from the arithmetic, so the split is about 43/57 rather than equal.
- On deliveries (94.8 / 98.3 / 104.2 aircraft a month): CFM 40.7 / 42.3 / 44.8 sets a month (47.4 / 49.2 / 52.1 on an equal split); P&W 54.0 / 56.1 / 59.4.
- On capacity (110.7 / 119.1 / 124.1 a month): CFM 46.7-54.2 / 51.2-59.5 / 53.4-62.0 (board split to equal split); P&W 61.8 / 67.9 / 70.7 at 57%. The A320 tail adds at most about 2 a month in 2045 (1.3 LEAP-1A, 0.9 GTF).
- Against the 51 I cited for 2037-45: on deliveries CFM stays below it every year. Only at full capacity does it reach 53 (board split) or 54-62 (the Board's equal-split arithmetic).
- LEAP-1B on the MAX at Boeing's capacity: 53.4 / 46.3 / 35.7 a month. CFM's total is 94.2 / 88.6 / 80.5 on deliveries, and at most 109.0 / 105.9 / 97.7 at capacity on an equal split. That compares with 106.3 in 2034 and 101.2 in 2044, so CFM's load falls as the MAX winds down.
- P&W stays near its 2044 level (56.7 a month) on deliveries, 2.7 more by 2050. It would reach 62-71 only if we built to capacity, which the brief's demand does not call for. That is my watch item.
- The Re-engine adds no narrowbody engine demand.

tests.name: Ask 3: rate-gated signals and the contingent CFM framework, 2045-50
tests.threshold: Sized to our own needs only. No payment, advance or take-or-pay. Nothing reserved against other customers (five pillars; not a bottleneck move).
tests.numbers: Both remain sized to our own needs. One update is needed: extend the signals to 2050, covering NGSA sets only, since the A320neo LEAP-1A/GTF tail ends by 2047. On the delivery path that is CFM about 41-45 and P&W about 54-59 sets a month. They are gated on rate, with ceilings at capacity of CFM 53 and P&W 71. The contingent CFM framework is triggered only by a GTF2 event, with NGSA on CFM alone. Re-size it from 99 by 2044 to about 95 / 98 / 104 sets a month (2045 / 2047 / 2050) on deliveries, up to 124 at capacity. CFM's total would then be about 148 / 145 / 140 a month with the MAX, falling as the MAX falls. Announce in general terms only, with no volumes and no internal plan targets. Anything above EUR 300m paid to a maker is its own Board item, and none is proposed.

tests.name: Ask 4: Joint Venture reading (P&W commits this round, the Joint Venture forms, GTF2 folds in)
tests.threshold: No public line or order that can cost NGSA its second source (supply first). This is a recommendation, not a veto ground. How the makers organise is their decision.
tests.numbers:
If P&W commits, the Joint Venture forms in 2045. The rules date its engine 6 years later (2051), 'or earlier if a partner folds in a solo programme that is further along'. GTF2 has been ready since 2036, so the plain reading (inference) dates the joint engine at once.

Fitting was settled at EIS: a maker is fitted only if its engine is ready by the airframe's EIS, and GTF2 was ready in 2036, before 2037. So NGSA keeps CFM plus P&W's engine, whether it is called GTF2 or the Joint Venture engine. That is 2 sources, since the Joint Venture counts as one. Rolls-Royce was not ready by 2037 and stays dropped from NGSA.

Only one reading puts the second source at risk: that the fold turns the in-service GTF2 into a joint engine not ready until 2051. That would leave CFM alone in 2045-51, at 95-104 of our sets a month (about 140-148 in CFM's total). The rules do not support it: a fold writes off spend; it does not unfit an engine in service (inference).

Third maker: the share rule gives P&W and Rolls-Royce equal NB shares under a Joint Venture. On that reading, Rolls-Royce would hold NB engine share through the joint engine in 2050. Whether the GM counts it as a third maker is a ruling; the brief's grid (2 / 2 in every cell) does not price a Joint Venture.

Watch item: a change of organisation on our highest-volume engine (57% of NGSA) during the ramp. Our line stays neutral: no invitation, no discouragement, no inducement, no confidential exchange.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA engine code (dual-source enabler)
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker. This is a recommendation, not a veto ground.
tests.numbers: Code 7 has been final since EIS 2037, and there is no code order this round (ngsa_engine_code: None). CFM plus P&W GTF2 are fitted: 2 sources in 2040, 2045 and 2050, so the dual-source enabler is met. Three makers is not reachable: 2 / 2 in every grid cell, brackets included, because no live airframe not yet in service can trigger launch_if_selected. No PV is traded for it, and no inducement is proposed.

tests.name: Ask 5: engineering capacity, A350 Re-engine launched 2045 (EIS 2050); rule 6
tests.threshold: NGSA / A350 development overlap of 2 years or less ($1.2B strain) unless the grid shows at least $1B more. At most one new launch per round (rule 6, red line).
tests.numbers:
NGSA development ran 2030-36 (EIS 2037). The Re-engine would develop over 2045-49 (EIS 2050). Overlap is 0 years and strain is $0 ($3B x 0/5). It is the only launch, so rule 6 passes. Rule 3 is not triggered: no 787 Re-engine is on the record.

The shared development teams are free: NGSA development ended 9 years ago. That is the evidence my file names as moving me toward a Re-engine.

Watch item, not a fail: NGSA production engineering still carries the ramp to 1,489 a year and the extra lines, and talent binds both. The grid prices no strain.

Item value against hold: +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50 / +0.89 / +0.89.

tests.name: Ask 5: A350F and Spirit absorption, A350 Re-engine 2045
tests.threshold: No A350 Re-engine while the A350F and the Spirit A350 work packages are being absorbed. Round 2 (2035) at the earliest.
tests.numbers: The A350F has been in its industrial phase since 2025, and the Spirit A350 packages were acquired in 2025. Our 2045 public record calls them fully integrated, so absorption has had 20 years. 2045 comes after my earliest date, not before it.

tests.name: Ask 5: production readiness, A350 Re-engine (the line)
tests.threshold: A derivative launches only on a production system that is ready for it. Soft veto if failed.
tests.numbers: It is a derivative on a running line. The A350 builds 70 a year on the board (41.2% of 170, about 6 a month), as the A330neo did on the A330 line. There is no new line and no new wing. I hold no production-readiness soft veto.

tests.name: Ask 5: A350 Re-engine engine maturity (durability proven before EIS)
tests.threshold: The Re-engine's engine has its durability proven before EIS. If not, EIS re-times later, never earlier, and the exposure is recorded honestly. Company doctrine answers this with a re-time, not a veto.
tests.numbers:
This passes the launch only with the re-time condition. The priced 2050 date itself does not pass.

Engine assumption: the A350 flies Rolls-Royce Trent XWB only. The A330neo precedent is a Rolls-Royce re-engine (Trent 7000), and the profile's default Re-engine engine is Rolls-Royce UltraFan. Rolls-Royce has launched no UltraFan widebody and gives no dates ('Widebody is our core').
- If it launched UltraFan WB this round (orders are sealed, so we cannot know), it would be ready in 2051. That is one year after a 2050 EIS, and before any time on wing.
- If it waits to see our launch and orders it in 2050, it is ready in 2056.
- The record holds no other widebody engine for the A350. The GEnx upgrade (ready 2033) is a 787 engine.

So no proven new engine on any public path can meet the priced 2050 EIS. The honest exposure is a slip of 1 to 6 years or more, which the grid does not price. Direction only:
- A slip delays the +0.89 share gain.
- In S6 and S7, a 787 Re-engine entering service in 2050 would be first. Our gains would never start, and the A350 margin would be 6.47% rather than 10.76%: worse than the grid's -0.50.

Conditions for a launch: an engine-maturity gate at the product-safety review, and a window, not a date, in public. Any payment, advance or take-or-pay above EUR 300m to bring a widebody engine to market is its own Board item; none is proposed.

tests.name: Ask 5: A350 Re-engine on the no-override tests (safety, quality, ramp shield, supply crunch); doctrine triggers
tests.threshold: Explicit pass or fail. The Board accepts no override. Supply crunch: no concurrency. Demand-shock round: no Re-engine launch.
tests.numbers: Safety: pass on the condition that nothing enters service before its durability is proven (engine gate above). Quality: pass. It is a running line, and the brief reports no event. Ramp shield: pass. The Re-engine takes no A320 or NGSA capacity, and the NGSA lines run at 83-86% of capacity. Supply crunch: pass. None is reported, and widebody engines are a separate supply from LEAP and GTF2. Demand-shock trigger: not triggered. Demand is 1,847 (2045) and 1,933 (2050), and the brief reports no shock. In 2035 I said a 2045 launch passes my tests unless rule 3 applies or there is a supply crunch. That still holds. The engine is an exposure I record, not a fail.

tests.name: Delay Tactics, any row (rules 4 and 5, five pillars)
tests.threshold: Only after an fps is on the public record and before its EIS. At most one move ('both' is two). Bottleneck only as a first claim on scarce capacity for our own ramp. Poaching only while a programme of ours is in development.
tests.numbers:
No fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine (rule 4).
- One move on A, against A: -11.46 / -0.10 / -0.10 / +0.14 / -0.10 / -11.46 / -0.10 / -11.46 / -0.11.
- Both moves on A: -11.72 (S1, S6, S8) to -0.07 (S4).
- One move on B, against B: -11.47 to +0.14.

On the hold row, rule 5 also fails: NGSA is in service and nothing of ours is in development. Bottleneck and both also breach the five pillars. NGSA has been in service since 2037, so the team's stricter condition (who enters service first) cannot be met.

tests.name: Ask 7: five pillars on the orders, the other moves and the public line
tests.threshold: No covert move, no inducement, no confidential exchange with any engine maker, nothing on engines coordinated or shared with Boeing.
tests.numbers: With delay_tactics: none, there is no covert move. The rate-gated signals and the contingent CFM framework cover our own needs only, with no payment, advance or take-or-pay. The engine line stays neutral. Recruiting is our own and untargeted. Trade advocacy with Boeing stays to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information. The public line must lead with the pillars, give windows, not dates, for any Re-engine (an EIS 2050 date cannot be met with a proven engine on the record), and never mention Delay Tactics.

tests.name: Ask 6: production, quality or supply events not in the bulletin
tests.threshold: Report any event the bulletin does not show.
tests.numbers: My record holds none, and the brief reports none. Watch items only: GTF2 carries about 57% of NGSA, on a maker that says its earlier GTF fleet 'was not where it needed to be'. CFM's LEAP-1B durability data is still pending, though that is Boeing's engine, not ours.

tests.name: NGSA gates and engine maturity slip (NGSA)
tests.threshold: Rule 1: no NGSA EIS before 2035. On an engine slip, re-time; never cancel.
tests.numbers: NGSA has been in service since 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. The brief offers no cancel option.

tests.name: Boeing Rate Increase
tests.threshold: No reaction: we keep our own disciplined ramp.
tests.numbers: None is on the record. Boeing's MAX capacity falls under the phase-out: 641 (2045), 556 (2047), 428 (2050).

vetoes.plan: Any Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching or both, on hold or on the Re-engine)
vetoes.ground: Company red line, rule 4: no fps is on the public record, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move against A is -11.46 in S1, S6 and S8, with a best of +0.14 (S4). Both moves are -11.72 to -0.07. On the hold row, rule 5 also fails, because nothing of ours is in development. Bottleneck and both also breach the five pillars. Not overridable.

vetoes.plan: Row B: NGSA hold (Alt) + A350 Re-engine launched 2045 (EIS 2050)
vetoes.ground: No operating veto. This is an exposure recorded for the Board, not a red-line flag. It passes engineering capacity (0 years of overlap, $0 strain), A350F and Spirit absorption, production readiness of the line, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch. Recorded exposure: no widebody engine on record can be proven by 2050. UltraFan WB would be ready in 2051 if launched this round, or 2056 if launched in 2050. Under doctrine, EIS re-times later, which the grid does not price. Item value against hold: +0.89 in seven columns, -0.50 in S6 and S7. I lean hold on the engine. The choice inside the $1B band is Guillaume's.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Toward launching the Re-engine:
(1) A widebody engine for the A350 goes on the public record with a date that can be proven before EIS. Examples: Rolls-Royce launches UltraFan WB (ready 2051), or puts a Trent XWB derivative on record. The re-time would then be about one year, which can go to the Board as a window.
(2) The GM rules that the board's Re-engine flies an engine already proven.
In either case I would support Guillaume's launch inside the band, with the engine-maturity gate at the product-safety review.

Toward a fail:
(3) A 787 Re-engine on the record closes it (rule 3).
(4) A reported supply crunch (LEAP, GTF2, castings and forgings, titanium) or a quality escape on the NGSA ramp: no new concurrency, and the Re-engine waits.
(5) A GTF2 fleet durability event. NGSA would then lean on CFM at about 95-104 of our sets a month (about 140-148 in CFM's total with the MAX), and the contingent framework is called.
(6) Any payment, advance or take-or-pay to bring a widebody engine to market without its own Board item, or anything that compresses testing.

On the Joint Venture: if the GM rules that a fold unfits GTF2 from NGSA, I would fail any public welcome, as in 2035.

Nothing on this board moves me on Delay Tactics while no fps is public.
ops.memo:
Operating test, 2045. My tests come from my role. Nothing on record is in my own words, so confidence is Very low.

NGSA ramp: pass on safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch. There is no inject. Demand sets our deliveries now: 1,137, 1,180 and 1,250 against capacity of 1,328, 1,429 and 1,489. The lines run at 83-86% of capacity, so nothing pushes rate or compresses testing.

Engines: no crunch. The bulletin puts GTF2 at about 57% of NGSA. On deliveries we need 41-45 CFM sets a month, under my 51, and 54-59 from P&W, about its 2044 level. As the MAX winds down, CFM's total load falls from 101 to about 81 sets a month. Extend the rate-gated signals to 2050 and re-size the contingent CFM framework to about 104, sized to our own needs only.

Joint Venture: NGSA's engines were fitted at EIS in 2037. On a plain reading we keep two sources either way. Whether Rolls-Royce then counts as a third maker is for the GM to rule. We stay neutral.

A350 Re-engine: passes engineering capacity (no overlap, no strain), absorption, supply crunch and the ramp shield. I hold no veto. The gap is the engine: nothing on record can be proven by 2050. UltraFan WB, launched now, is ready in 2051; if Rolls-Royce waits for our launch, 2056. The grid does not price that slip. I lean hold. If Guillaume launches, I ask for an engine-maturity gate and a window, not a date.

- It is most likely a forgo for good. 2050 is the last decision round, a 2055 EIS is not priced, and rule 3 closes the option after a 787 Re-engine (Toepfer).

Secure our own materials and work packages

other_moves.detail: With industry associations on both sides of the Atlantic, Boeing and Embraer included as allies on trade. It stays strictly to public trade policy, with no exchange of pricing, capacity, programme or engine-selection information [AX-0088, AX-0046].

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft has been in service since 2037. Its production ramp-up continues in a disciplined and controlled way, paced by our customers' demand and the maturity of our production system, and never at the expense of safety or quality. It flies with two engine sources, CFM and Pratt & Whitney. A stable, diversified supply of parts, engines first, remains a condition of that ramp, and we are extending our long-range, rate-gated signals to our suppliers for the years ahead, sized to our own needs. How the engine makers organise themselves is their decision. On widebodies, the A350 family continues to serve our customers and we keep improving it step by step. Any further step will be taken only once its engine is mature and its durability is proven, and we will speak of it in windows, not dates. We take on one major development at a time and fund it from our own cash flow, preserving our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. With our partners across the industry, on both sides of the Atlantic, we keep working for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero trade regime in civil aerospace. And we keep recruiting and training, in Europe and across our global footprint, the people who will design and build the next generation of Airbus aircraft.
decision.rationale:
DECISION, ROUND 3 (2045): HOLD
Every field stays at its default: ngsa hold, no engine code (7 has been final since EIS), rea350 hold, delay_tactics none, a320_plan alt. That means no Board items and no override.

MY ORDER OF QUESTIONS
1. The five pillars. Both live rows pass. Every Delay Tactics row is struck.
2. The ramp. NGSA runs at 83-86% of capacity and demand sets our deliveries. Wagner reports no crunch and no event.
3. The next decades. The A350 Re-engine is the derivative path, but no widebody engine on the record can be proven by a 2050 EIS.
4. Can I take it to the Board? A hold is never vetoed. The Re-engine does not meet the Board's second condition ('Toepfer passes it').

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP

1. Deletions (red lines and the pillars, never traded for PV)
- Every Delay Tactics row is deleted.
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked and draws the $48.32B fine. One move on A scores -11.46 in S1, S6 and S8, and its best is +0.14 (S4).
  - Rule 5 fails on row A, because nothing of ours is in development.
  - Bottleneck and both also fail the pillars, and both counts as two moves.
  - The Board vetoes all three.
  - The team's stricter condition cannot be met, because NGSA has been in service since 2037. I do not set it aside.
- There is no cancel option this round.

2. Tests
- Row A (the default) survives.
  - Toepfer passes it on cash ($0), robustness (worst S8 and S9, +9.00), liquidity and Board items (none).
  - Wagner passes it on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch and the pillars.
- Row B (A350 Re-engine 2045, EIS 2050) does not survive.
  - Toepfer passes it on cash: $1.0B a year, 19% of the $5.2B line, no overlap, $0 strain.
  - He also passes it on row robustness and on the Board's $2B downside test.
  - He fails it on the $1B launch condition. The item scores +0.89 / +0.89 / +0.90 / +0.89 / +0.89 / -0.50 / -0.50 / +0.89 / +0.89, so no column reaches $1B. This is a binding soft veto.
  - Wagner holds no operating veto. He passes capacity, absorption, line readiness, safety, quality, the ramp shield and supply crunch.
  - Wagner records one exposure: Rolls-Royce has launched no UltraFan widebody, so the engine would be ready in 2051 at the earliest, or 2056 if Rolls-Royce waits. That is a slip of 1 to 6 years or more, which the grid does not price. In S6 and S7 it would leave us worse than -0.50.
- I judge Toepfer's flag sound, not mistaken.
  - He calls the clause his own reading, but profile §6 states it as a Re-engine launch condition: 'whatif shows at least $1B over Do Nothing, including strain'. My framing cited it.
  - Where the team rule and the profile differ, the profile governs.

3. Choice
- Row A is the only survivor.
- It is also the company default, within $1B of the best grid plan in my expected column. In S1 the gap is $0.89B.
- Every tie-break favours hold:
  - No early EIS: B's priced 2050 EIS is earlier than any engine on the record can be proven.
  - Less concurrency: none in A, against a widebody development during the NGSA ramp in B.
  - Later capex start: none in A, against $1.0B a year from 2045 in B.
  - Fewer Board items: 0 against 1.

4. Override
None is possible. The Re-engine's margin over the best passing option is +0.89 in S1 and +0.90 at best, below the $1B bar. The Board would also veto it on governance. The override budget stays unused.

5. Why I do not use the band the other way
The Board's horizon favours this window, and I take that seriously. In my framing I named what would move me:
- clean passes from both colleagues;
- an engine path that can be proven by 2050, or an honest re-time;
- confirmation from Thomas that returns stay fundable.
Thomas confirmed fundability and that holding is most likely a forgo for good. The other two conditions failed:
- Thomas did not pass the item.
- Lars named no engine path that can be proven by 2050.
Launching now would mean committing to a date we already know is ahead of the engine. My rule is to re-time, never accelerate, and my risk appetite on technology and EIS is Low [AX-0006, AX-0020]. On expected value alone the item would be positive: it turns negative only if S6 and S7 together carry more than 64%, and on my weights they carry 15%. So I hold on the $1B condition and on the engine, not on the downside.

6. What holding forgoes and avoids (the Board's ask)
- It forgoes +0.89 in seven columns (+0.90 in S3), which is +0.68 on my weights and +0.58 at equal weights. The plan's floor stays at +9.00 instead of +9.89.
- It avoids -0.50 in S6 and S7, the $5B bill and the unpriced slip exposure.
- It is most likely a forgo for good. 2050 is the last decision round, a 2055 EIS is not priced, and rule 3 closes the option after a 787 Re-engine.

7. Engines
- Code 7 is final, with CFM + GTF2: 2 sources and 2 makers in every cell.
- The Joint Venture: on Wagner's plain reading, NGSA keeps two sources whether or not it forms. Whether Rolls-Royce would count as a third maker is a ruling for the game master.
- The line stays neutral, with no inducement.

8. Supply
There is no crunch. On deliveries, CFM needs about 41-45 sets a month (under 51) and P&W about 54-59 (near its 2044 level). CFM's total load falls as the MAX winds down. The signals are extended to 2050 and the CFM framework is re-sized, both to our own needs only.

9. Board-gate lines
There are no Board items. For the record:
- rea350 hold: pillars pass; Toepfer passes; Wagner passes; ΔPV 0 against the default.
- The Re-engine, considered and not brought: pillars pass; Toepfer fails (soft veto on the $1B condition, passes on cash); Wagner passes, with the engine exposure recorded; grid +0.89 in seven columns and -0.50 in S6 and S7.

10. Round 2 check
I expected an fps (S2), and Boeing held (S1). This round I name S1. The choice of row does not depend on the column, because A is the only survivor in every column.
