cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's new single-aisle, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. We'll support that ramp on the signals Airbus gives us, jointly with Safran, and spares won't crowd out new engines. LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It's in every new -1A engine and going into the fleet through the shops. We'll report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say. It's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and a new engine comes when an airframer and the returns are both there.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It is the installed-base game [CX-0422], and on this board it is now the LEAP fleet's game. The board counts the narrowbody market only to 2056. Anything launched in 2045 is ready in 2051 at the earliest.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM and the rival engine fitted.
- The fps and Embraer's jet are open, and neither airframer has a case to announce.
- One Joint Venture commitment stands.
The question was whether anything on this grid earns its bill in a column the record supports. Nothing does. We win this round on safety, quality, delivery and cost [CX-0658]: LEAP time on wing, OE engines on time, spares that never crowd them out, and RISE kept whole with Safran. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

DECISION
- Hold on ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. GEnx is hold only: it has been running since 2030 and ready since 2033.
- Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board.
- Premium: $0. Game total: $0.65B of $4.0B. RISE allowance: $0.
Check file: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r3_culp_decide.py (brief numbers only).

THE GRID AGAINST HOLD (S1 / S2 / S3, $B)
- Hold: -9.47 / -10.62 / -9.97. Best plan in every column.
- Ducted: -4.29 / -4.23 / -4.38. Gross 1.71 / 1.77 / 1.62 on a $6B bill ($4B R&D plus the $2B strain next to the running GEnx).
- Ducted + Partner Embraer: -3.98 / -3.85 / -2.87. Embraer adds +0.31 / +0.38 / +1.51 on top of the Ducted, but it falls with the engine it needs.
- Open Fan alone: -23.96 / -24.18 / -23.59.
- Best Open Fan plan (with Partner Embraer and Lobby): -18.48 / -18.53 / -17.07.
- Weighted hold: -9.78 at the weights I adopt (.65 / .20 / .15), -9.72 at my framing weights, -10.02 at equal weights. Hold leads by more than $1B in every column, so the tie-break is not needed.

THE TESTS
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1.
  - Boeing: 'the business case isn't there yet' and 'I won't give you a date'.
  - Embraer: 'the numbers today do not prove the return' and 'no decision to announce'.
  - I take Ghai's weights. S2 gets a little more than S3 because Boeing says 'the technology is coming along' and is 'keeping the work going'. Leaning to the costlier column fits guiding low. The ranking cannot change.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]. Nothing is. The Ducted recovers 0.27-0.30x its bill because it counts only six years (2051-2056), on falling volumes (1,930 to 1,355 engines).
- No birthright [CX-0564]. I read S2 and S3 as hard as S1.
  - S2 costs $1.15B against S1: the rival engine shares Boeing's slot from 2055.
  - S3 costs $0.50B: Embraer's jet flies the rival engine from 2049.
  - Hold is still the best plan in both. No launch buys either back.
- H3, Ducted only as a defence. The trigger is on the record: GTF2 has been fitted next to CFM on NGSA since 2037, and a Joint Venture commitment has stood since 2035.
  - Ghai's volumes-first test passes on it.
  - Pays-for-itself fails in every column, including S2, where the rival shares the slot.
  - A trigger permits a defence; it does not pay for one. I invoke it for the record only.
  - Against hold in S1, the Ducted's $4.29B gap would also break the $2.0B round cap and the $3.35B left in the game.
- The 20% red line [CX-0217, CX-0208]. No Ducted is ordered, so the line is not engaged. For the record: a Ducted has less than half the open-fan gain [CX-0183, CX-0180] and is never the next generation. RISE is the next engine, with a design point of more than 20% that no flight test in Ali's record has yet measured.
- H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205]. A 2045 Open Fan is ready in 2055, against NGSA's 2037 entry, so the wait penalty applies in every column.
  - The RISE allowance cannot carry it. The allowance needs no wait penalty in any plausible column, and it would need at least $17.07B, above $15B.
  - The allowance stays unused because the airframer path is closed, not because of cost.
- H5: RISE is not cancelled. It stays all in as joint technology [CX-0174, CX-0398].
- Supply [CX-0613, CX-0633]. The strain reading is confirmed: the Ducted next to an Open Fan is worth +2.00 / +1.99 / +2.00 more than the Ducted alone. So the running GEnx counts, and any single launch carries the $2B. Hold adds no project.
- Safety. Ali has no open flag on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX, or on GEnx. No cross-functional answer is pending. Any finding goes to a cross-functional team first [CX-0012].

THE THREAT WE CAN'T PRICE
A formed P&W-RR Joint Venture is in no column. Ghai sizes it at -$1.7B to -$3.9B, depending on when it counts. With it, the 2050 share is about 49.9-50.1% in S1 and S2, a coin toss on the line, and about 49.2% in S3.
No lever on the grid acts before 2050:
- the Ducted counts from 2051;
- Partner Embraer counts from 2052;
- the Open Fan's one early effect, the wait penalty, cuts the wrong way.
A 2050 Ducted would count one year (about $0.2B gross), and Embraer from 2057, outside the window. So the engine-lever door on this board is closed (inference from the board's years). We answer the threat with LEAP durability, time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran. We never name it [CX-0580] and never cut price [CX-0609].

BIASES IN PLAY
- Installed-base lens, 'the price of admission' [CX-0557]. It could rationalise a Ducted. The grid says no, and I won't pay $4B for a feeling.
- Deference to airframers [CX-0452]. Here the board's calendar, not deference, closes the door.
- Money guided low [CX-0270, CX-0324]. I book -11.0, not the S1 row of -9.47.

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
No CFM narrowbody order is placed, so consent is not engaged.
- Ducted: the trigger is on the record, so consent would be assumed, but it fails on money.
- Open Fan: a RISE product launch with no airframer path is outside joint practice. I state no reason for Safran to agree, and I do not order it.
- Partner Embraer and Lobby: both fall with their engines.
- Every NGSA, fps and Embraer supply or engine move states that price and capacity are joint with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166, CX-0160].

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
- Partner Embraer and Lobby follow the profile.md §6 playbook. My record does not address either.
- The Joint Venture response follows the reaction function in profile.md §5 and §7.

PUBLIC LINE
I dropped two lines from 2035:
- 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer'. In S2, Boeing would be that airframer and a new CFM engine is -4.23. When the facts change, we change the line [CX-0243, CX-0434].
- 'On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in'. Ali has no fleet outcome in his record, and the line implies a result to come.
Ali's wording replaces the second line. The statement gives no dates, no price, no rival, no Joint Venture and no Airbus volumes. 'Tell you what we know, tell you what we don't' [CX-0436].

recommendations.text:
Safety and durability first.

- Airbus and Boeing now put durability first in their engine choice. LEAP time on wing is what holds CFM's NGSA position and any fps position.
- Any durability finding on the LEAP family goes to a cross-functional team before it reaches us or the public.

Hold everything, and say plainly why. Hold is the best plan in S1, S2 and S3.
- The Ducted is -4.29, -4.23 and -4.38 against hold.
- Ducted + Partner Embraer is -3.98, -3.85 and -2.87.
- The best Open Fan plan is -18.48, -18.53 and -17.07.
Choose the expected column from the record, put weights for S1-S3 in `predictions`, and book expected PV low, as Ghai advises. Holding costs nothing in any column this round.

Record that the Ducted door is closed on this board (inference from the board's years).
- A 2045 Ducted, ready in 2051, grosses only about $1.6-1.8B against a $6B bill.
- A 2050 Ducted would be ready in 2056, the last counted narrowbody year.
- The hard-rule-3 trigger on the record permits a defence; it does not pay for one.
Keep the position on record: a Ducted is a defensive derivative with less than half the open-fan gain, never the next generation, and RISE is the next engine. Give no Ducted date.

RISE. Say plainly that the Open Fan waits.
- It is ready in 2055 at the earliest, against NGSA's 2037 entry into service.
- The 'ready by 2050' objective is unmet for good, at a $0 premium.
- The RISE allowance stays unused because of the airframer path, not cost.
- RISE stays fully funded as joint technology with Safran, with no programme dividend, and is never cancelled for cost. Its technology keeps flowing into LEAP.
Nothing in pay rewards an engine in service after 2050, so the board supplies that long view from the 2050 partnership.

Joint Venture watch and the share objective.
- Rolls-Royce's commitment has stood since 2035. Pratt & Whitney leaves the door 'neither shut nor open'.
- Under rules.md, the Joint Venture forms once both commit. If GTF2 folds in, its engine could be ready early (inference). It would take about 10 pp of narrowbody share from CFM.
- Ghai should size the 2050 share in that case (his round-2 estimate was about 50.1%) and confirm that no grid lever acts before 2050.
- Answer it with LEAP durability, time on wing and delivery, on standard terms, never with a launch the grid does not pay for. Do not name it in public.

Safran and supply.
- Answer Airbus's rate-gated NGSA signals and Boeing's call for a stable, multi-source engine supply on standard terms. Airbus has said publicly that its CFM call stays at or below 51 sets a month on two sources.
- Price and capacity are joint with Safran. State that in every narrowbody supply move.
- Spares never crowd out OE engines.
- Ali should bring measured output from the 9 suppliers behind 80% of past shortages, still open since round 1, before any future stack of projects.

Capital.
- Premium $0 this round; the game total stays at $0.65B of $4.0B.
- No new R&D, so keep at least 70% of free cash flow returned and the A-range rating whole.
- Declare every premium in dollars against the best plan in the expected column, with the RISE allowance stated separately as $0.

Public statement.
- Name no rival or Joint Venture, and blame no one.
- Give no Ducted, Open Fan or RISE date.
- No CFM price or capacity talk without Safran, and no NGSA volumes Airbus has not stated.
- Keep 'We don't have a birthright on that next order.'
- Reconsider 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer.' If Boeing launches the fps with CFM in its code (S2), a new CFM engine is -4.23 on the grid. The line should not read as a promise of one. Our suggested wording: a LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and a new engine comes when an airframer and the returns are both there.

frame.question:
What game are we playing in 2045, and how do we win? [CX-0467]

It is still the installed-base game [CX-0422]. On this board it is now the LEAP fleet's game. The board counts the narrowbody market only to 2056, and anything we launch today is ready in 2051 at the earliest.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM and the rival engine fitted. That split is on the record.
- The fps and Embraer's jet are still open. Neither airframer has a launch to announce.
- One Joint Venture commitment stands. The other side has left the door neither shut nor open.

So the question is plain. Does anything on this grid earn its bill in a column the record supports? My read is no: hold is the best plan in all three columns. If that survives your tests, we win this round on safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order [CX-0658]: LEAP time on wing, OE engines on time, spares that never crowd them out, and RISE kept whole as technology with Safran. We don't buy a launch the grid doesn't pay for. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

We don't have a birthright on the next order [CX-0564]. So I read S2 and S3 as hard as S1:
- S2: an fps on all three codes, where the rival engine shares a Boeing slot that is all CFM today.
- S3: an Embraer jet on the rival's engine.
Both cost us money. A launch buys neither back.

I also want to fix one public line. 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer' reads as a promise. In S2, Boeing would be that committed airframer, and a new CFM engine is -4.23 there. When the facts change, we change the line [CX-0243, CX-0434].

- Book low: about -10.6 (hold in S2), below the weighted -9.72, and lower if Ghai's Joint Venture sizing says so [CX-0536].

WHY HOLD, ON MY TESTS
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]: nothing is.
  - The Ducted loses $4.23-4.38B in every column. It grosses $1.6-1.8B on a $6B bill because it is ready only in 2051.
  - Ducted + Partner Embraer loses $2.87-3.98B.
  - The best Open Fan plan loses at least $17.07B.
- No birthright [CX-0564]: S2 and S3 each take something from us ($1.15B and $0.50B against S1), and hold is still the best plan in both. A launch doesn't buy it back.
- H3: the trigger is on the record. It permits a defence; it does not pay for one. I invoke it for the record only.
- Tie-break: not needed. Hold leads by more than $1B everywhere.
- Deference to airframers can make us late to a threat [CX-0452]. Here the board's calendar, not deference, closes the door. The installed-base lens, 'the price of admission' [CX-0557], could rationalise a Ducted. The grid says no, and I won't pay $4B for a feeling.

THE THREAT WE CAN'T PRICE
- A formed P&W-RR Joint Venture takes the 2050 share to about the 50% line (Ghai's round-2 estimate, to re-check). No lever acts before 2050.
- We answer it with LEAP time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran. We never name it [CX-0580] and never cut price [CX-0609]. That's the scoreboard: win rates [CX-0218].

OPEN FAN: it waits, and we say so plainly.
- It would be ready in 2055 against NGSA's 2037 entry. 'Ready by 2050' is unmet for good, at a $0 premium.
- The allowance stays unused because of the airframer path, not cost.
- RISE stays all in as joint technology, with no programme dividend and no cancel for cost [CX-0214, CX-0174, CX-0398].

SAFRAN
- The lean places no CFM narrowbody order, so consent is not engaged.
- Had a Ducted come in, the trigger is on the record, so consent would be assumed, but it fails on money.
- An Open Fan with no airframer path would be outside joint practice.
- Every supply move says price and capacity are joint [CX-0184].

PUBLIC LINE: tell you what we know, tell you what we don't [CX-0436].
- LEAP durability facts only. On the -1B, only what Ali can back.
- Drop the promise of a new engine. Say instead: 'A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and a new engine comes when an airframer and the returns are both there.'
- Keep 'We don't have a birthright on that next order.'
- No dates, no price, no rival named. It's that simple, ain't that hard.

WHAT WOULD MOVE ME: an open safety or durability flag from Ali (it changes the LEAP moves, not the launch call), or an error in my grid reading from Ghai. Short of that, we hold.

cfo.memo:
Larry, the money in dollars. Your grid reads right to the cent. Hold is the best plan in all three columns: -9.47, -10.62, -9.97. The Ducted grosses $1.6-1.8B on a $6B bill and loses $4.23-4.38B everywhere. With Embraer it still loses $2.87-3.98B. The strain is confirmed at $2.00B, so the GEnx still counts. Volumes first passes on hard rule 3, but pays-for-itself fails in every column, and the premium would break both caps. The best Open Fan plan needs $17.07-18.53B, above the $15B allowance. So hold passes every binding test: $0 premium, $0.65B of $4.0B for the game, $0 of new R&D, payout and rating whole.

What the case leaves out is a P&W-RR Joint Venture. If GTF2 folds in and it counts from 2046, it costs about $3.5B; from 2051, about $1.7B. It takes the 2050 share to 49.9-50.1%, a coin toss on the line, and about 49% in S3. Nothing on this board lifts that before 2050. The Ducted counts from 2051 and Embraer from 2052. The one early lever, the Open Fan's wait penalty, cuts the wrong way. And 2050 shuts the door: a Ducted would count for one year, about $0.2B.

But the good news is the LEAP load is falling, so supply should carry Airbus's signals without spares crowding out OE. Ali to confirm.

Book low: about -11.0, my weighted -9.78 less a one-in-three Joint Venture. Your line passes my terms test. We've been proven wrong on volumes before.

Partner Embraer: counts at launch + 7. GEnx: launch + 3, and not before the first re-engined 787 or A350 (2042 if none). This is my test standard applied to the board's development times (inference).
tests.numbers: Launch year 2045. Ducted ready 2051 (2045+6). Open Fan ready 2055 (2045+10, above the 2045 floor). Partner Embraer counts from 2052 (2045+7). GEnx is already running: launched 2030, ready 2033 (+3), counting from 2042 because no 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record. Lobby is immediate. The recommended orders (hold on every field) rest on no ready year at all. Culp's grid rows (round3.md section 3) rest on the board's years and nothing earlier. I checked them against the brief, and all are correct. Against hold (S1 / S2 / S3): Ducted -4.29 / -4.23 / -4.38 (-13.76 / -14.85 / -14.35 less -9.47 / -10.62 / -9.97); Ducted + Partner Embraer -3.98 / -3.85 / -2.87; Open Fan -23.96 / -24.18 / -23.59; Open Fan + Partner Embraer + Lobby -18.48 / -18.53 / -17.07. The 2050 round (board years, inference): a Ducted would be ready in 2056, the last counted NB year; an Open Fan in 2060; Embraer would count from 2057, outside the window. Said plainly, as in round 2: 2051 is the board's year, not a test result. Nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off in my record. The test basis I have is hot-section technology: LEAP-1A HPT hardware certified December 2024, more than 350 RISE tests, and compact-core HPT dust testing from October 2025. That backs the technology, not a product date. My own pattern: I met the test-backed fixes and missed the demonstration dates (the RISE demo went from 'by the middle of this decade' to 'this decade'; the 1B went from 2025 to 1H 2026). On this board the development times are floors, so my test can hold a date or move it later, never earlier. Check file: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r3_ali_tests.py.

tests.numbers: Ducted ready 2051. NGSA has been in service since 2037 (on the record, every column), so the Ducted is 14 years behind it. CFM NB volumes over those years fall from 1,930 (2051) to 1,355 (2056). The late date fails nothing on my test. The short window is why the Ducted grosses only 1.71 / 1.77 / 1.62 on a $6B bill. That is Ghai's money ground, not mine.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan (advice; H2 from the readiness side)
tests.threshold: An Open Fan that is ready after the first new NB's entry into service takes the board's 35 pp loss (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap.
tests.numbers: Open Fan ready 2055. NGSA entered service in 2037, so the Open Fan is 18 years late. It is 6 years behind the S3 Embraer jet (2049). It is level with the S2 fps (2055), but NGSA came first. The wait penalty therefore applies in every column. Against hold: -23.96 / -24.18 / -23.59, which is 13.96 / 14.18 / 13.59 beyond its $10B bill. Lobby on the Open Fan adds +4.98 / +5.07 / +4.83: it caps the loss at 20 pp but does not close it. H2 is confirmed. 'Ready by 2050' is unmet for good, since a 2045 launch is ready in 2055. The physics is ours; the calendar is the airframer's.

tests.name: Physics (wording check; Culp's 20% line)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine gets 'less than half' the gain and is never called the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is company doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words.
tests.numbers: The brief has no fuel-burn data, so this is a wording check. Confirmed: 20% is 'practically impossible ... without the open fan. And the reason is physics' [CX-0180]. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the open-fan gain [CX-0183]. RISE's design point is 'more than 20%' [CX-0001], against the customers' 'at least 20%' [CX-0217]. Durability and fuel burn are not traded [CX-0208]. Culp's frame calls the Ducted a defensive derivative, never the next generation, so it passes. Caution for the Board: 'more than 20%' is a design point. No ground or flight test in my record measures it.

tests.name: Durability first, and the LEAP report against my promise (Culp's asks 3 and 4)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. Every durability claim in public must be backed by test or field data (inference; Culp's line applied to my seat).
tests.numbers: Hold trades nothing. The statement makes LEAP durability claims, so I check what can be backed. LEAP-1A, which I can state on test evidence: the HPT durability hardware was certified by the FAA and EASA in December 2024 [CX-0225]; it is in all LEAP-1A deliveries and shop visits [CX-0209]; and new -1A engines perform at CFM56 levels (Ghai's words) [CX-0996]. Not stateable as achieved: the 8,000 harsh and 17,000 neutral cycles, which are Culp's targets ('we think') [CX-0655], and 'more than twofold', which is a forecast [CX-0209]. LEAP-1B, reported against my promise: I said the 1B 'will follow in 2025' [CX-0008]; it became certification in 1H 2026 [CX-0210, CX-0656], and the 1B has flown fewer cycles than the 1A [CX-0988]. The fleet outcome of the kit is NOT in my record, and the game gives none. I claim nothing either way. Public wording I can back: 'LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified and is in every new -1A engine and in the fleet through the shops. We report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it.' I advise dropping 'On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in.' It cannot run forever, and it implies a result to come. Retrofits go in at shop visits, 'years, not months' [CX-0649]. FLAG: none. No test or field data in my record shows a failure on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX. My record has no test of the NGSA LEAP derivative itself. The record shows it in service since 2037 under Airbus's rule that each engine enters only once its durability is proven. That is the airframer's acceptance, not my test.

tests.name: Supply load: hold (seat doctrine, advice)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain on the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. My supply role is in Culp's words only (inference).
tests.numbers: The strain reading is confirmed from the grid: the Ducted next to an Open Fan, less the Ducted alone, is +2.00 / +1.99 / +2.00. So the running GEnx counts as one project. Hold adds no project and triggers no strain, so $0 of new strain.

tests.name: Supply load: any single launch next to the running GEnx (seat doctrine, advice)
tests.threshold: As above: the grid must pay more than the $2B strain.
tests.numbers: Ducted alone, against hold: -4.29 / -4.23 / -4.38. Its gross of 1.71 / 1.77 / 1.62 does not cover the $2B strain on its own, before the $4B R&D. Ducted + Partner Embraer: -3.98 / -3.85 / -2.87. Its gross of 2.02 / 2.15 / 3.13 just covers the strain but not the R&D. Lobby alone: $1B plus the $2B strain for nothing on the board (about -3.00, Culp's inference; there is no grid row). Every Open Fan plan fails on the wait penalty first. No launch passes. No evidence in my record sizes the strain: following doctrine, $2B is a floor, not a ceiling.

tests.name: Supply: NGSA rate-gated signals plus shop-visit spares, OE first (Culp's ask 5; seat doctrine, advice)
tests.threshold: The load must sit inside output the system has delivered, and spares never crowd out OE engines [CX-0529]. Supplier-level output is to be measured, not estimated (inference; my supply role is in Culp's words only).
tests.numbers: This passes on the assembled total only. Delivered CFM NB engines (bulletin): 2,553 in 2034 (1,684 aircraft x 2 x 75.8%) and 2,429 in 2044 (1,895 x 2 x 64.1%). The 2044 split was 1,368 on the 737 MAX (684 x 2) and 1,061 on Airbus, about 44 sets a month. That is inside Airbus's stated ceiling of 51, on the inference that a set is a pair. The board's load falls: 2,191 in 2045 (-9.8% on 2044, -14.2% on the 2034 peak), 1,926 in 2050 (-20.7% / -24.6%) and 1,355 in 2056. The upper bound is Airbus's 51-set ceiling (1,224 engines a year) plus the full 2044 MAX rate (1,368), which gives 2,592, +1.5% on the 2034 peak. The MAX phases down from 2045, so that bound is not reached on the board. Not measured: shop-visit spares volumes (none in the brief) and output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages [CX-0613]. I cannot bring that measurement; it is not in my record or my brief, open since round 1. Following Culp: OE engines first, spares never crowd them out [CX-0529], and price and capacity are joint with Safran (Culp and Ghai's ground). I would add no NGSA volume Airbus has not stated.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign (advice)
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures. This is no argument against the Open Fan as the next generation (inference).
tests.numbers: GEnx: hold only. It is running on a proven architecture, ready since 2033, counting from 2042, with WB share at 44.8% from 2042. LEAP: the derivative stays on offer on NGSA, the fps and Embraer's jet. CFM is never dropped from a new airframe, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. The hot-section cycles remain the moat [CX-0169].

tests.name: Safety call (advice)
tests.threshold: A problem or order that touches safety or durability needs a cross-functional team, not one person.
tests.numbers: The brief raises no safety issue, and no test or field result in my record raises one on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX, or on GEnx. No flag is open, so Culp has nothing to answer this round. Any finding goes first to the cross-functional team, with enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make shops and in MRO [CX-0010, CX-0012]. Culp answers it on evidence before anything reaches the Board or the public.

tests.name: RISE progress, as far as my record goes (Culp's ask 2; report)
tests.threshold: Report only what testing shows. Give no RISE date.
tests.numbers: I have no evidence after October 2025, and the game gives none. My record ends at: more than 350 RISE tests with an early focus on durability [CX-0216]; dust testing on next-generation HPT blades for the compact core from October 2025, the earliest we have ever started it [CX-0222]; a Chief Mechanic and Architect for the Open Fan, with durability a top priority [CX-0223]; noise tests with Airbus, lower than today's LEAP [CX-0013]; and ground and flight test 'this decade' [CX-0211], slipped from 'by the middle of this decade' [CX-0151]. I cannot report a flight-test result, a measured 'more than 20%', or open-fan blade and core durability in dust. RISE stays whole as technology with Safran. No cancel: 'We failed twice. We got it done' [CX-0002].

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch, in any combination (alone, with Lobby, with Partner Embraer, or with the Ducted)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not my binding date ground. The grid values rest on the board's 2055 ready year (2045+10, above the 2045 floor), so the order passes my date test. It fails the airframe test: 18 years after NGSA's 2037 entry and 6 after the S3 Embraer jet (2049). Against hold the wait penalty gives -23.96 / -24.18 / -23.59; the best Open Fan plan gives -18.48 / -18.53 / -17.07. This is H2 from the readiness side. It would become a binding date veto only if the case for it, or the statement, rested on an Open Fan or RISE entry earlier than 2055 for a 2045 launch. Inference note: my veto right over programme dates is an inference from my 2024 'turn on and turn off' and 'real testing' words as VP of Engineering, applied to my current role. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence. Here it is not engaged.

vetoes.plan: ducted: launch alone, or with partner_embraer
vetoes.ground: Advice only (supply load, seat doctrine; my supply role is in Culp's words only). The dates pass: Ducted ready 2051 = 2045+6, and Embraer counts from 2052 = 2045+7. But 2051 is the board's year, not a test result: nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off. The grid never pays the $2B strain from the running GEnx. Ducted alone: -4.29 / -4.23 / -4.38, gross 1.71 / 1.77 / 1.62, below the strain alone. Ducted + Partner Embraer: -3.98 / -3.85 / -2.87. It has only 6 counted years (2051-2056), so it cannot act on the 2050 share. Condition carried forward: any Ducted is gated by test before entry into service, and durability is never traded for 2051. Inference note: my date veto is an inference from my 2024 words as VP of Engineering. No date ground is engaged, so nothing binds.

vetoes.plan: Public statement and other moves (watch list for the step-4 veto check)
vetoes.ground: Not a veto now: Culp plans no date, and the revised line carries none. At the veto check, binding ground 2 applies to any of these: a Ducted ready date (2051 is an untested board year); any Open Fan or RISE entry date; any RISE ground-test or flight-test date; a CFM engine on Embraer's jet before 2052; any line implying that a new CFM engine acts on the 2050 share or on a Joint Venture before 2051; any LEAP-1B time-on-wing result, or a date for one. Wording advice, not a date ground: drop 'On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in'. Use instead: 'We report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it.' Inference note: my veto right over dates in public is an inference from my 2024 'turn on and turn off' and 'real testing' words as VP of Engineering, read in my current role. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence.

ops.would_change_mind_if: Only test and field data, never analysis. (1) LEAP-1B fleet data in cycles, harsh and neutral, against the 8,000 / 17,000 targets. That closes the item open since round 1 and changes the statement, not the orders. (2) A durability or safety finding from test or the field on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX. It goes to the cross-functional team first. It would change the LEAP moves (inspection, shop-visit priority, spares against OE), and it would put a flag on any launch until Culp answers it on evidence. (3) Measured output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages, carrying shop-visit spares beside OE. That would let me read the $2B strain as enough rather than a floor. It does not change hold. (4) A Ducted core turned on and turned off in hot-and-harsh test. That would make 2051 a tested date. It cannot make the date earlier, because the board's years are floors, so it buys back no counted years. (5) A RISE ground and flight test measuring 'more than 20%', with open-fan blade and compact-core durability in dust. That confirms the physics but does not move the calendar: NGSA has been in service since 2037. (6) An airframer launch on the record with CFM in its code, where the grid pays. The column is Culp's call. I would test only its dates.
ops.memo:
I report against what I said.

Dates. A 2045 launch gives a Ducted in 2051, launch plus six; an Open Fan in 2055; Embraer counting from 2052. These are the board's years. No test backs 2051: nothing ducted has been turned on and turned off. Hold rests on no ready year. No binding veto.

Against the airframes. NGSA entered service in 2037: the Ducted is fourteen years behind it, the Open Fan eighteen. Embraer's S3 jet, 2049: Ducted two years late, partnership three. The S2 fps, 2055: Ducted four years ahead, with six counted years left. The Open Fan waits in every column.

Physics. A ducted engine has less than half the open-fan gain. Never the next generation. RISE is designed for more than 20%. No flight test in my record measures it.

Durability. LEAP-1A: hardware certified, in every new engine and every shop visit, at CFM56 levels. LEAP-1B: I said 2025; it moved to 2026. The fleet outcome is not in my record. I claim nothing either way. Drop 'when the fleet data is in'; report cycles once the fleet proves them. No safety or durability flag is open.

Supply. We delivered 2,553 LEAP engines in 2034 and 2,429 in 2044. The load falls: 2,191 now, 1,926 in 2050. Airbus's 51-set ceiling plus today's MAX rate is about 2,592, near our 2034 peak. That is the assembled total. Output at the nine suppliers is not measured.

Orders: hold everything. The revised line gives no date: it passes.

other_moves.move: RISE kept whole as technology with Safran
other_moves.detail: RISE stays fully funded as a joint CFM technology programme. There is no product launch and no 'program dividend' [CX-0174, CX-0214], and it is never cancelled for cost [CX-0398]. Testing continues with our partners, and RISE technology keeps flowing into LEAP upgrades [CX-0162]. No entry date, and no ground-test or flight-test date [CX-0205, CX-0009]. This fits joint practice: Safran is a full partner in RISE.

other_moves.move: LEAP durability and delivery first
other_moves.detail: LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It is in every new -1A engine and goes into the fleet at shop visits [CX-0225, CX-0209]. We report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it, and we claim nothing before then (Ali's wording; the -1B fleet outcome is not in his record) [CX-0210, CX-0009]. OE engines come first, and spares never crowd them out [CX-0529]. This is joint practice with Safran. Facts only, no promise dates [CX-0436].

other_moves.move: Support NGSA with the LEAP family on Airbus's rate-gated signals, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: CFM is fitted on NGSA on the record. We answer Airbus's long-range, rate-gated supply signals on standard terms, with no launch-era pricing, concession or free upgrade. We quote no volume or rate that Airbus has not stated, and we do not repeat Airbus's own ceiling in our statement (Ghai's advice). Narrowbody price and capacity are a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166, CX-0160]. The LEAP load falls from 2,191 engines (2045) to 1,926 (2050). OE comes first and spares never crowd it out [CX-0529]. Platform talks stay private [CX-0586].

other_moves.move: Engine talks with Boeing and Embraer, jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: We refuse no one and lock no one out (H1) [CX-0587, CX-0185]. A LEAP derivative is on offer for the fps and for Embraer's next jet, on standard terms. Narrowbody price and capacity are joint with Safran [CX-0184]. Boeing wants more than one engine source with durability first, so we come with time-on-wing facts we can back on test or field data, and no price. A new CFM engine comes only when an airframer and the returns are both there. Talks stay private. No comment on US-Brazil trade.

other_moves.move: Answer the market with win rates, not reactions
other_moves.detail: We make no public comment on any rival or any Joint Venture, and no price cut in response [CX-0580, CX-0609, CX-0625]. We compete on LEAP durability, time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran. That's the scoreboard [CX-0218]. Ghai keeps his Joint Venture sizing (-$1.7B to -$3.9B; 2050 share about 49.9-50.1%) on the internal watch list and re-books if a commitment from the other partner appears on the record. No board effect.

other_moves.move: Measure supplier output before any future stack (lean before capital)
other_moves.detail: Ali reports that output at the 9 suppliers and 15 sites behind 80% of past shortages is not measured in his record [CX-0613]. We measure it, at supplier level, against OE plus shop-visit spares, before any future programme stack. We fix flow before we add capital [CX-0540, CX-0633]. No capital commitment and no board effect.

other_moves.move: Hot-and-harsh core testing inside the RISE envelope
other_moves.detail: Compact-core HPT durability testing in dust continues inside the existing joint RISE budget, and its results feed LEAP upgrades [CX-0222, CX-0216]. It builds the turn-on, turn-off test basis Ali says we lack [CX-0009]. No Ducted launch, no date and no new bill.

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Here's what we know. CFM, with our partners at Safran, is on Airbus's new single-aisle, and we'll earn our place on it every day, on time on wing. We'll support that ramp on the signals Airbus gives us, jointly with Safran, and spares won't crowd out new engines. LEAP-1A durability hardware is certified. It's in every new -1A engine and going into the fleet through the shops. We'll report LEAP time on wing in cycles once the fleet has proven it. The GEnx upgrade is ready for our 787 customers.

Here's what we don't know: when the next new narrowbodies will be launched, by whom, and on which engines. That's really not for us to say. It's the airframers' call. We don't have a birthright on that next order. We intend to earn it. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer, and a new engine comes when an airframer and the returns are both there.

RISE stays all in as technology, together with Safran. When that architecture enters service is really not for us to say. We'll tell you about dates when the testing tells us.

We get paid in dollars, not in percentages. It's that simple, ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN [CX-0467]
It is the installed-base game [CX-0422], and on this board it is now the LEAP fleet's game. The board counts the narrowbody market only to 2056. Anything launched in 2045 is ready in 2051 at the earliest.
- NGSA has been in service since 2037 with CFM and the rival engine fitted.
- The fps and Embraer's jet are open, and neither airframer has a case to announce.
- One Joint Venture commitment stands.
The question was whether anything on this grid earns its bill in a column the record supports. Nothing does. We win this round on safety, quality, delivery and cost [CX-0658]: LEAP time on wing, OE engines on time, spares that never crowd them out, and RISE kept whole with Safran. We are not going for share [CX-0493].

DECISION
- Hold on ducted, open_fan, partner_embraer and lobby_emissions. GEnx is hold only: it has been running since 2030 and ready since 2033.
- Every field is at its default, so no item goes to the Board.
- Premium: $0. Game total: $0.65B of $4.0B. RISE allowance: $0.
Check file: /tmp/wargame-cfm/dash-2050-emb/work/r3_culp_decide.py (brief numbers only).

THE GRID AGAINST HOLD (S1 / S2 / S3, $B)
- Hold: -9.47 / -10.62 / -9.97. Best plan in every column.
- Ducted: -4.29 / -4.23 / -4.38. Gross 1.71 / 1.77 / 1.62 on a $6B bill ($4B R&D plus the $2B strain next to the running GEnx).
- Ducted + Partner Embraer: -3.98 / -3.85 / -2.87. Embraer adds +0.31 / +0.38 / +1.51 on top of the Ducted, but it falls with the engine it needs.
- Open Fan alone: -23.96 / -24.18 / -23.59.
- Best Open Fan plan (with Partner Embraer and Lobby): -18.48 / -18.53 / -17.07.
- Weighted hold: -9.78 at the weights I adopt (.65 / .20 / .15), -9.72 at my framing weights, -10.02 at equal weights. Hold leads by more than $1B in every column, so the tie-break is not needed.

THE TESTS
- Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. The expected column is S1.
  - Boeing: 'the business case isn't there yet' and 'I won't give you a date'.
  - Embraer: 'the numbers today do not prove the return' and 'no decision to announce'.
  - I take Ghai's weights. S2 gets a little more than S3 because Boeing says 'the technology is coming along' and is 'keeping the work going'. Leaning to the costlier column fits guiding low. The ranking cannot change.
- Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301, CX-0355]. Nothing is. The Ducted recovers 0.27-0.30x its bill because it counts only six years (2051-2056), on falling volumes (1,930 to 1,355 engines).
- No birthright [CX-0564]. I read S2 and S3 as hard as S1.
  - S2 costs $1.15B against S1: the rival engine shares Boeing's slot from 2055.
  - S3 costs $0.50B: Embraer's jet flies the rival engine from 2049.
  - Hold is still the best plan in both. No launch buys either back.
- H3, Ducted only as a defence. The trigger is on the record: GTF2 has been fitted next to CFM on NGSA since 2037, and a Joint Venture commitment has stood since 2035.
  - Ghai's volumes-first test passes on it.
  - Pays-for-itself fails in every column, including S2, where the rival shares the slot.
  - A trigger permits a defence; it does not pay for one. I invoke it for the record only.
  - Against hold in S1, the Ducted's $4.29B gap would also break the $2.0B round cap and the $3.35B left in the game.
- The 20% red line [CX-0217, CX-0208]. No Ducted is ordered, so the line is not engaged. For the record: a Ducted has less than half the open-fan gain [CX-0183, CX-0180] and is never the next generation. RISE is the next engine, with a design point of more than 20% that no flight test in Ali's record has yet measured.
- H2, the airframer sets the date [CX-0205]. A 2045 Open Fan is ready in 2055, against NGSA's 2037 entry, so the wait penalty applies in every column.
  - The RISE allowance cannot carry it. The allowance needs no wait penalty in any plausible column, and it would need at least $17.07B, above $15B.
  - The allowance stays unused because the airframer path is closed, not because of cost.
- H5: RISE is not cancelled. It stays all in as joint technology [CX-0174, CX-0398].
- Supply [CX-0613, CX-0633]. The strain reading is confirmed: the Ducted next to an Open Fan is worth +2.00 / +1.99 / +2.00 more than the Ducted alone. So the running GEnx counts, and any single launch carries the $2B. Hold adds no project.
- Safety. Ali has no open flag on the LEAP family on NGSA or the MAX, or on GEnx. No cross-functional answer is pending. Any finding goes to a cross-functional team first [CX-0012].

THE THREAT WE CAN'T PRICE
A formed P&W-RR Joint Venture is in no column. Ghai sizes it at -$1.7B to -$3.9B, depending on when it counts. With it, the 2050 share is about 49.9-50.1% in S1 and S2, a coin toss on the line, and about 49.2% in S3.
No lever on the grid acts before 2050:
- the Ducted counts from 2051;
- Partner Embraer counts from 2052;
- the Open Fan's one early effect, the wait penalty, cuts the wrong way.
A 2050 Ducted would count one year (about $0.2B gross), and Embraer from 2057, outside the window. So the engine-lever door on this board is closed (inference from the board's years). We answer the threat with LEAP durability, time on wing, delivery and standard terms, jointly with Safran. We never name it [CX-0580] and never cut price [CX-0609].

BIASES IN PLAY
- Installed-base lens, 'the price of admission' [CX-0557]. It could rationalise a Ducted. The grid says no, and I won't pay $4B for a feeling.
- Deference to airframers [CX-0452]. Here the board's calendar, not deference, closes the door.
- Money guided low [CX-0270, CX-0324]. I book -11.0, not the S1 row of -9.47.

SAFRAN GATE (H7)
No CFM narrowbody order is placed, so consent is not engaged.
- Ducted: the trigger is on the record, so consent would be assumed, but it fails on money.
- Open Fan: a RISE product launch with no airframer path is outside joint practice. I state no reason for Safran to agree, and I do not order it.
- Partner Embraer and Lobby: both fall with their engines.
- Every NGSA, fps and Embraer supply or engine move states that price and capacity are joint with Safran [CX-0184, CX-0166, CX-0160].

DOCTRINE, NOT MY RECORD
- Partner Embraer and Lobby follow the profile.md §6 playbook. My record does not address either.
- The Joint Venture response follows the reaction function in profile.md §5 and §7.

PUBLIC LINE
I dropped two lines from 2035:
- 'CFM will commit a new engine with a committed airframer'. In S2, Boeing would be that airframer and a new CFM engine is -4.23. When the facts change, we change the line [CX-0243, CX-0434].
- 'On the -1B, we'll tell you the results when the fleet data is in'. Ali has no fleet outcome in his record, and the line implies a result to come.
Ali's wording replaces the second line. The statement gives no dates, no price, no rival, no Joint Venture and no Airbus volumes. 'Tell you what we know, tell you what we don't' [CX-0436].

memo_weighing.cfo:
Ghai's memo is weighed fully. His tests carry the decision. His record on profit calls is strong; his volume dates slip [CX-0910, CX-0987]. Here he dates no volumes.
- His binding tests: hold passes all of them. Every launch fails pays-for-itself in every column.
- He checks my grid to the cent and confirms the $2.00B strain reading.
- His Joint Venture sizing (-$1.7B to -$3.9B; 2050 share 49.9-50.1% in S1 and S2, about 49.2% in S3) is an estimate calibrated on the grid's Ducted, not a grid row. I take it as the watch number, not as a column.
- I adopt his weights (.65 / .20 / .15) for guiding low, and his booking advice (about -11.0) over my -10.6: one-in-three odds of a Joint Venture counting from 2046 is a fair low case [CX-0536].
- I take his terms advice: no Airbus rate quoted in our statement, and 'jointly with Safran' on any supply line.
- His capex frame (about $2.5B a year) is advice. Hold uses $0 of it, so the 70% payout and the A-range rating stay whole [CX-0645, CX-0252].
No veto of his is engaged, because nothing launches.
memo_weighing.ops:
Ali's memo is weighed on two levels. His own record is thin: it is engineering only, and it ends in March 2024. On supply and capacity his record is my own description of his job [CX-0633], so I weigh that part against company doctrine.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
I'll start where we always start, with the fleet. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and our customers carried that. We own it, and we have not forgotten it. So we control what we can control.

GTF2 has been in service on Airbus's next-generation single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We judge it the way our customers do, on time on wing. We will report that record as the fleet measures it, and not before. Any later-block feature enters the fleet only when it is proven and instrumented. We will not compress testing to meet anyone's rate.

Supply is where we have let customers down before. So we are adding castings and forgings capacity in steps, with our suppliers, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material.

For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared, GTF2 is available today on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit, on the same terms.

Rolls-Royce has made its commitment public, and we respect it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We share risk and investment with partners, never our core technology.

We keep investing in geared technology for the next cycle. It is technology, and we have no product or date to announce.

We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
pratt_whitney.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Premium $0B. `overrides` empty. Neither field is a Board item.

THE ExCo PROCESS
1. Start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same.
2. Strike plans that fail a binding veto. Row B (hold plus `jv_with_rr: commit`) fails Mitchill's ground 4, which binds: any case for it rests on upside not on the record (a code-1 or code-4 airframe, an fps or Embraer selection of Rolls-Royce, or partner money toward a bill already paid). Eddy raises the gear flag on Row B. It is a company red line, not one of his veto grounds. I confirm the flag and strike Row B on it too. Red lines are never traded for PV.
3. Set the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035]. GTF2 has been ready since 2036, so it beats every EIS now possible: Embraer 2049 (+13 years), an fps in 2052 or 2055 (+16, +19). Nothing is compressed. The deferred CMC block stays out until it is proven and instrumented. Eddy's ground-1 standing condition binds on the statement: no durability figure that is not measured fleet data.
4. Optimise inside the constraint. Hold/hold is +6.10 / +5.86 / +6.50 (S1-S3), the best row in every column. On my predictions (S1 0.50, S2 0.35, S3 0.15) its expected PV is +6.08, and its worst column is S2 at +5.86. Row B is -0.59 / -0.60 / -0.02, an item value of -6.69 / -6.46 / -6.52. That is -6.58 weighted (-6.60 on my framing weights, -6.56 on equal weights), and 3.23-3.35x its own $2B bill in every column. Hold dominates on any weights.

MY TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass, as above. The fleet record is now the test, and Eddy has no measured GTF2 data in evidence. So I cite no figure, and the record goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee.
- Visible demand: met on NGSA code 7, on the public record since 2030.
- Miss a cycle: does not apply this round. No column has a new narrowbody entering service without P&W. S2's -0.24 is timing, per Mitchill's reading: the fps enters service in 2055 and the board stops counting in 2056. It is not a lost position, since we are fitted on code 7. The cycle after GTF2 is answered by technology-only geared funding inside the envelope. 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is RTX-wide, applied to engines here by inference.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine order, the best-PV order and the objective order are the same, so no premium is needed. The shared-source relief on code 7 is declared at $0B [PX-0058, P-1292].
- Dividend safe: Mitchill confirms $0 of new R&D, the dividend and pre-ASR debt path untouched, the envelope fitted and the stretch unused. He has no 2045 debt figure in his files and says so; it is a dated follow-up.
- Value, not share: every other move is on standard terms. No discount, concession, free upgrade, take-or-pay or volume promise. Mitchill's ground 3 is clean.
- Objective status: credibility and Capitalise are both met in all three columns under hold. A commit would turn Capitalise to missed in all three.

THE JOINT VENTURE
With Rolls-Royce committed since 2035, our `commit` would form the Joint Venture this round. It is not an option. The cost is all share, none of it cash: the fold-in write-off is $0 and new spend is $0. It gives Rolls-Royce an equal narrowbody share on NGSA through our engine, and that is the -6.69 if nobody new selects it. It folds GTF2's gear and core into a shared programme [P-1233]. It hands back all of GTF2's remaining +5.72 gain over Do Nothing, and about $1B more. My record on a Joint Venture is Low, so this follows doctrine plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, and the grid says no on its own terms. I name my architecture-loyalty bias [PX-0014]; it is not the reason. The partner relationship stays respectful [PX-0038], and the 2050 revisit conditions are written down.

TIE-BREAKS
None was needed. The fleet beats a new engine, so the capacity plan gives the installed fleet first call. No rival's discount entered.

BIASES NAMED
- Optimism on operating dates [PX-0017, PX-0098]: no ramp, peak or recovery date of ours goes into the statement.
- Incrementalism [PX-0093]: I under-called an airframer launch in 2030. So I take Mitchill's higher S2 weight (0.35 against my 0.30). The MAX phases out from 2044, and 2045 is the last round an fps can enter service inside the count.
- Supply-first caution [PX-0085]: shown in the tranche plan with no fixed plant. It fits the 40% post-peak decline and does not cost a selection.

CONTINUITY
This is round 3 of a plan that has held. The 2030 `launch_if_selected` fired on NGSA code 7, and in 2035 we held through the cancel round and kept the Joint Venture off. GTF2 is now in service, and both objectives are met.

frame.question:
Control what you can control [PX-0020]. Round 3, decision year 2045.

The engine work of the last two rounds is done:
- The 2030 conditional order fired on NGSA's code 7.
- GTF2 was ready in 2036 and has flown on NGSA since 2037, fitted alongside CFM.
- NGSA is in service, so its code is fixed. Last round's big loss column (Airbus moving to code 5) is gone for good.

Only one of our order fields is live. `gtf2_solo` has one legal value, `hold`: GTF2 is ready, so it cannot be cancelled and there is nothing to launch. The real question is `jv_with_rr`.

Rolls-Royce's commitment has stood since 2035, so a P&W `commit` is no longer an option we can keep open. It forms the Joint Venture this round:
- our ready GTF2, gear and core included, folds into a shared programme;
- Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce then hold equal narrowbody shares.

So I am asking three things:
1. Does anything on the grid, or anything we can prove, justify forming the Joint Venture? The grid says it costs -6.69 / -6.46 / -6.52 against `hold`.
2. If not, what do we do with the moves that matter more now: the GTF2 fleet record, capacity up to the 2052 peak and down from it, GTF2 on offer for any fps or Embraer narrowbody, and the cycle after GTF2?
3. How do we say it in public without claiming durability the fleet has not shown, or speaking for an airframer?

The job is unchanged: set the safety and durability constraint, take the best PV inside it, and keep the gear ours.
frame.situation:

- Airbus: NGSA launched 2030, in service since 2037. Code 7 (CFM, P&W, Rolls-Royce). Fitted: CFM and P&W; Rolls-Royce dropped, not ready by EIS. The code is now fixed. MY LEAN
Row A: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Premium $0B. `overrides` empty. Not a Board item, but the full case goes into the notes because the Board asked for it: all the data, with all the thinking [PG-0016].

WHY
- Hold is the brief's best plan in every column: +6.10 / +5.86 / +6.50.
- It meets credibility and Capitalise in all three.
- GTF2 stays on NGSA and stays ready for any fps or Embraer narrowbody that selects us.

WHY NO JOINT VENTURE
- With Rolls-Royce committed, our commit is the formation, not an option.
- It costs 3.2-3.35x its own bill in every column.
- It hands half our narrowbody share and our gear and core to a partner whose only route onto NGSA is our engine.
- It turns Capitalise from met to missed.
- My record here is Low, so this follows doctrine plus Neil's and Shane's tests. The grid says no on its own terms.
- I name my architecture-loyalty bias [PX-0014]; it is not the reason.
- We keep the partner relationship respectful. The GTF risk-sharing model is critical [PX-0038], but we never share core technology.

TESTS
- Safety and durability: the fleet record is now the test, and I want Shane's data.
- Visible demand: met on NGSA.
- Miss a cycle: no grid column has a new narrowbody without P&W, and the ready GTF2 covers every possible EIS. The next cycle is answered by technology funding inside the envelope, not a launch.
- Responsible bet: the doctrine order, the best-PV order and the objective order are the same.
- Dividend: no new R&D.
- Value, not share: standard terms throughout.

OTHER MOVES
Public:
1. GTF2 on offer on standard terms to any fps or new narrowbody that selects P&W, sole or shared. For Embraer, GTF2 or the GTF family at the Advantage standard, Embraer's choice. No selection claimed, and no dates.
2. NGSA rate-gated supply agreements continue on standard terms.
3. A respectful answer to Rolls-Royce: no Joint Venture to announce, no terms opened.
4. The Hot Section kit continues at shop visit, upgrades sold, not given.
Internal:
1. Shane's castings and forgings tranches for the 2051-52 step, ordered by about 2049, using partner capacity over fixed plant.
2. The GTF2 fleet record and the CMC block status, to the Governance and Public Policy Committee.
3. The annual NPV review, with the commit's item value recorded.
4. Technology-only next-generation geared funding inside the envelope, if Neil and Shane clear it.
5. The 2050 Joint Venture revisit conditions (weighted value ≥ 0, no column below -$2B, trigger met, ready by EIS, gear and core out).

PROPOSED DISCLOSURE, IN MY VOICE
"I'll start where we always start, with the fleet. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and our customers carried that. We own it, and we have not forgotten it. So we control what we can control. GTF2 has been in service on Airbus's next-generation single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We judge it the way our customers do, on time on wing, and we will report that record as the fleet measures it, not before. Any later-block feature enters the fleet only when it is proven. We will not compress testing to meet anyone's rate. Supply is where we have let customers down before, so we are adding castings and forgings capacity in steps, with our suppliers, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material. For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared, GTF2 is available today on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit. Rolls-Royce has made its commitment public, and we respect it. We have no Joint Venture to announce: we share risk and investment with partners, never our core technology. We keep investing in geared technology for the next cycle, as technology, with no product or date to announce. We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks."

The next-cycle sentence stays only if Neil clears ground 4 and the envelope. A time-on-wing figure goes in only if Shane brings measured fleet data.

cfo.memo:
Low end first. Hold/hold is +5.86 in our worst column, a Boeing fps on the 10-year ramp, and +6.10 if rivals hold. On my weights (S1 0.50, S2 0.35, S3 0.15) it's +6.08 expected. I weight Boeing above Chris: the MAX phases out from 2044, and this is the last round an fps can enter service before the board stops counting. Hold is best in every column, whatever the weights.

S2 is timing, not position. The fps enters service in 2055 and ramps from zero; the board counts our engines only to 2056. The same move launched in 2035 was worth +0.15 to us.

The Joint Venture costs 6.69 if nobody new selects it, and at least 6.46 in every column: 3.2 to 3.35 times its own $2B bill. It's all share: our $2B is spent and exactly fills our share, so no write-off and no new cash. It gives back all of GTF2's remaining gain over Do Nothing, 5.72 from 2045, and about $1B more. In 2035 I put a 2045 formation at $3B to $4.4B. I was wrong: too low. Any case for it rests on upside nobody has recorded: ground 4, binding.

Cash: no new R&D, no cancel round, nothing at risk. The dividend and the debt path don't move. Technology funding passes inside the envelope, with no number until the scope is known.

We've earned 2.32 of the 8.05. I want a few more reps before I call the rest.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ENGINE ORDERS (round 3, decision year 2045): gtf2_solo: hold; jv_with_rr: hold. Neither order is a Board item.

WHY gtf2_solo: hold
- It is the only legal value. GTF2 launched in 2030, has been ready since 2036, and has flown on NGSA since 2037 (code 7, fitted with CFM and P&W).
- Hold keeps GTF2 on NGSA and ready for every EIS now possible.
- Grid row 'GTF2: hold': +6.10 / +5.86 / +6.50. It is the best row in every column.
- Cancel is not legal, so there is no cancel test to flag.

WHY jv_with_rr: hold
- Rolls-Royce's commitment has stood since 2035, so a P&W commit forms the Joint Venture this round. It is not an option we can keep open.
- NGSA is in service, so no live airframe not yet in service carries code 1, 4, 5 or 7.
- Readiness passes: 2045 with GTF2 folded in (my reading of 'further along'), or 2051 if an already-ready engine does not count.
- The gear condition fails. Formation folds GTF2's gear and core into the shared programme [P-1233].
- Item value -6.69 / -6.46 / -6.52 (row 'hold + commit' minus row 'hold').
- My technical conditions fail on the gear. The call is Calio's. I propose hold.

ANSWERS TO CALIO

(2) READINESS. GTF2 has been ready since 2036.
- Embraer narrowbody launched in 2045: EIS 2049, +13 years. GTF2 would have 12 years on NGSA by then.
- fps launched in 2045: 2052 on the 7-year ramp (+16). 2055 on the 10-year ramp or via Embraer (+19).
- Joint Venture formed now: ready 2045 with the fold-in, or 2051 without it. At 2051 it would miss an Embraer 2049 EIS. The board fits only ready engines, so no order puts it on an airframe early.
- What the Joint Venture brings that GTF2 does not: nothing any EIS needs.
  - UltraFan is technology inside Rolls-Royce's base R&D, and Rolls-Royce has 'no solo narrowbody programme'.
  - GTF2's development is done, so there is no development risk left to share.
  - Partner shops we already use [PX-0118].
- Embraer engine choice (inference; Embraer decides). Both options are installations, not developments, on standard terms.
  - I lean to the GTF family at the Advantage standard. It runs on GTF tooling that the A320neo tail frees around 2045 (the Alt plan's roughly eight years from 2037), rather than stacking on the GTF2 lines in the run to the 2052 peak.
  - Offer GTF2 if Embraer wants it, once the measured GTF2 record has cleared the Governance and Public Policy Committee.

(3) FLEET RECORD. It is not in my evidence or the brief, and the board does not model durability. I have none of the following:
- time on wing;
- unscheduled removals;
- life-limited parts against full life;
- severe-environment subfleet data;
- the Hot Section kit's measured time on wing. My evidence stops at the 2025 target of 90-95% of the Advantage gains [PX-0088][PX-0106].
What the brief does show:
- GTF2 in service since 2037.
- P&W's narrowbody share up from 24.2% to 35.9% (2044).
- 4,880 P&W narrowbody engines delivered in 2041-44. The brief does not split GTF2 from the A320neo GTF tail.
- No AOG, escape or removal figure in the bulletin. That means no problem has been reported. It is not proof of durability [PX-0112].
At these volumes the fleet is far past the 1M-hour benchmark [P-0847] (inference). So the record exists inside the company; it just is not here.
- CMC block: its status is not in evidence. I treat it as still waiting, out of the fleet. It enters only as a later block, instrumented and proven at no less than the Advantage endurance multiple [P-1214][P-0779].
- Statement: no figure.

(4) CASTINGS, FORGINGS AND SHOPS. Numbers from the hold row; my arithmetic.
- Curve:
  - 1,299 (2045), 1,449 (2049), 1,548 (2051) and the 1,597 peak (2052). That is +23% on 2045 and +236 on the 1,361 delivered in 2044.
  - Then 1,462 (2053) and down 40% to 951 by 2060.
  - Years above 1,361: 2048-55 only.
- Tranche 1, ordered now: the 2049 level. That is +88 over 2044.
- Tranche 2, ordered by about 2049 (before the 2050 round, at 2 to 2.5 years of lead [P-0079]): the 2051-52 step, +148 over 2049. It runs above 1,449 only in 2051-53.
- No new fixed plant. The 2044 capacity of 1,361 covers every year from 2056. Everything above it is bought from suppliers and partners, in tranches against Airbus's rate signals, through Mitchill.
- Embraer (S3), contingent:
  - Line ramping straight from EIS 2049 to 8 a month by 2055: about 96 gross engines in 2052 and 192 by 2055. Net is lower, because it takes customers from Boeing and Airbus.
  - Pre-qualify suppliers now. No capital until a launch is on the record.
- fps (S2), EIS 2055: it ramps into the decline. Do not shed suppliers after 2052 until S2 is resolved. A 7-year ramp (2052) would land on our peak; that is the stretch case.
- Shops: shop visits for the installed GTF and GTF2 fleet rise as OE falls (inference; the board does not model MRO). Post-peak castings swing to spares.
- Use the 2045-47 plateau (1,299 to 1,355) for fleet lift.
- Allocation is daily, reported weekly to the ExCo and balanced with Airbus [PX-0123][PX-0131][PX-0099][PX-0110]. The fleet keeps first call.

(5) ENGINEERING LOAD (no strain charge on this board; my judgement). None of these is a new engine development:
- CMC block: a block change, run to test results, not a date.
- Hot Section embodiment: sustaining work.
- Embraer: an installation in 2045-49.
- fps: an installation in about 2050-55.
- Next-generation geared work: technology only, inside the envelope.
We can carry it all if fleet engineering is ring-fenced with first call. When work collides, the order is: fleet, then an installation with a date on the record, then the CMC block, then technology. The stretch case is Embraer 2049 plus an fps on the 7-year ramp to 2052. I have no headcount data. I support the technology-only geared work: it keeps the gear and core ours for the next cycle [PX-0129].

(6) JOINT VENTURE, TECHNICAL
- Yes, formation puts the gear and core into a shared programme. I raise the gear flag.
- Terms that would ever keep them out:
  - P&W designs, builds and owns the gear and core modules and their data.
  - P&W holds the type certificate, design authority, integration and continued airworthiness for the in-service fleet.
  - Rolls-Royce shares risk only on modules it owns.
  - IP is licensed for the Joint Venture product only.
- Even on those terms the board gives Rolls-Royce an equal narrowbody share.

(7) VETO CHECKS
- Row A passes both of my grounds.
- Row B: no binding veto. Readiness passes and no launch is involved. The gear flag stands as a company red line.
- The draft statement passes. It cites no figure, durability is a record to report, and it gives no dates. Advice: keep 'not in the early entry phase', which is a pricing line [PX-0055], next to 'standard terms' so it is not read as a maturity claim.
- The parts view is my own record. The Joint Venture, Embraer, load and MRO views are the seat's doctrine or inference.

ops.memo:
The bad number first: I can't give you the GTF2 fleet record. Eight years on NGSA, and neither the brief nor my evidence carries a time-on-wing figure, a removal rate, an LLP count, severe-environment data, the Hot Section kit's measured time on wing or a CMC test result. So no figure goes in the statement, and I won't fill the gap with "no surprise coming". The measured record goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee.

My proposal: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. GTF2 has been ready since 2036 and covers every EIS on the table: Embraer 2049 (+13 years), an fps 2052 or 2055 (+16, +19). Hold is the best row in every column: +6.10 / +5.86 / +6.50.

The Joint Venture brings nothing GTF2 needs. Formation folds our gear and core into a shared programme, so I raise the gear flag. That's the company's red line, not one of my veto grounds.

Capacity: 1,299 engines this year, 1,597 at the 2052 peak, +23%, then down 40% to 951 by 2060. Forgings take 2 to 2.5 years, so the 2051-52 tranche is ordered by 2049, before the next round. Everything above the 1,361 we built in 2044 comes from suppliers and partners, not fixed plant. The fleet keeps first call.

The CMCs stay out until they're proven and instrumented.

Both my checks pass on Row A. My record is thin: one investor day, June 2023. The Joint Venture, Embraer and load views are the seat's doctrine.

decision.public_statement:
I'll start where we always start, with the fleet. For years the GTF fleet was not where it needed to be, and our customers carried that. We own it, and we have not forgotten it. So we control what we can control.

GTF2 has been in service on Airbus's next-generation single-aisle since 2037, alongside CFM. We judge it the way our customers do, on time on wing. We will report that record as the fleet measures it, and not before. Any later-block feature enters the fleet only when it is proven and instrumented. We will not compress testing to meet anyone's rate.

Supply is where we have let customers down before. So we are adding castings and forgings capacity in steps, with our suppliers, and the fleet flying today keeps first call on material.

For any airframer that selects Pratt & Whitney, sole or shared, GTF2 is available today on standard terms. We're not in the early entry phase, the launch phase. The GTF Hot Section kit remains available at shop visit, on the same terms.

Rolls-Royce has made its commitment public, and we respect it. We have no Joint Venture to announce. We share risk and investment with partners, never our core technology.

We keep investing in geared technology for the next cycle. It is technology, and we have no product or date to announce.

We speak for our engines, not for any airframer's dates or rates. We have learned our lesson from the prior iterations of the GTF. These are responsible bets with responsible paybacks.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: hold`. Premium $0B. `overrides` empty. Neither field is a Board item.

THE ExCo PROCESS
1. Start from Eddy's proposal: hold/hold. Mitchill recommends the same.
2. Strike plans that fail a binding veto. Row B (hold plus `jv_with_rr: commit`) fails Mitchill's ground 4, which binds: any case for it rests on upside not on the record (a code-1 or code-4 airframe, an fps or Embraer selection of Rolls-Royce, or partner money toward a bill already paid). Eddy raises the gear flag on Row B. It is a company red line, not one of his veto grounds. I confirm the flag and strike Row B on it too. Red lines are never traded for PV.
3. Set the safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035]. GTF2 has been ready since 2036, so it beats every EIS now possible: Embraer 2049 (+13 years), an fps in 2052 or 2055 (+16, +19). Nothing is compressed. The deferred CMC block stays out until it is proven and instrumented. Eddy's ground-1 standing condition binds on the statement: no durability figure that is not measured fleet data.
4. Optimise inside the constraint. Hold/hold is +6.10 / +5.86 / +6.50 (S1-S3), the best row in every column. On my predictions (S1 0.50, S2 0.35, S3 0.15) its expected PV is +6.08, and its worst column is S2 at +5.86. Row B is -0.59 / -0.60 / -0.02, an item value of -6.69 / -6.46 / -6.52. That is -6.58 weighted (-6.60 on my framing weights, -6.56 on equal weights), and 3.23-3.35x its own $2B bill in every column. Hold dominates on any weights.

MY TESTS
- Safety and durability: pass, as above. The fleet record is now the test, and Eddy has no measured GTF2 data in evidence. So I cite no figure, and the record goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee.
- Visible demand: met on NGSA code 7, on the public record since 2030.
- Miss a cycle: does not apply this round. No column has a new narrowbody entering service without P&W. S2's -0.24 is timing, per Mitchill's reading: the fps enters service in 2055 and the board stops counting in 2056. It is not a lost position, since we are fitted on code 7. The cycle after GTF2 is answered by technology-only geared funding inside the envelope. 'Miss a cycle' [PX-0071] is RTX-wide, applied to engines here by inference.
- Responsible bet [PX-0010]: the doctrine order, the best-PV order and the objective order are the same, so no premium is needed. The shared-source relief on code 7 is declared at $0B [PX-0058, P-1292].
- Dividend safe: Mitchill confirms $0 of new R&D, the dividend and pre-ASR debt path untouched, the envelope fitted and the stretch unused. He has no 2045 debt figure in his files and says so; it is a dated follow-up.
- Value, not share: every other move is on standard terms. No discount, concession, free upgrade, take-or-pay or volume promise. Mitchill's ground 3 is clean.
- Objective status: credibility and Capitalise are both met in all three columns under hold. A commit would turn Capitalise to missed in all three.

THE JOINT VENTURE
With Rolls-Royce committed since 2035, our `commit` would form the Joint Venture this round. It is not an option. The cost is all share, none of it cash: the fold-in write-off is $0 and new spend is $0. It gives Rolls-Royce an equal narrowbody share on NGSA through our engine, and that is the -6.69 if nobody new selects it. It folds GTF2's gear and core into a shared programme [P-1233]. It hands back all of GTF2's remaining +5.72 gain over Do Nothing, and about $1B more. My record on a Joint Venture is Low, so this follows doctrine plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test, and the grid says no on its own terms. I name my architecture-loyalty bias [PX-0014]; it is not the reason. The partner relationship stays respectful [PX-0038], and the 2050 revisit conditions are written down.

TIE-BREAKS
None was needed. The fleet beats a new engine, so the capacity plan gives the installed fleet first call. No rival's discount entered.

BIASES NAMED
- Optimism on operating dates [PX-0017, PX-0098]: no ramp, peak or recovery date of ours goes into the statement.
- Incrementalism [PX-0093]: I under-called an airframer launch in 2030. So I take Mitchill's higher S2 weight (0.35 against my 0.30). The MAX phases out from 2044, and 2045 is the last round an fps can enter service inside the count.
- Supply-first caution [PX-0085]: shown in the tranche plan with no fixed plant. It fits the 40% post-peak decline and does not cost a selection.

CONTINUITY
This is round 3 of a plan that has held. The 2030 `launch_if_selected` fired on NGSA code 7, and in 2035 we held through the cancel round and kept the Joint Venture off. GTF2 is now in service, and both objectives are met.

On my record versus doctrine: the safety, capital-order, pricing and durability-first views are my record (High). The Joint Venture, Embraer engine choice and capacity split rest on doctrine and on my colleagues' tests.
