rolls_royce.public_statement: So. Our commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney stands, as we said it would. When we commit something, we honor it. It is on standard terms, terms that credit the technology we bring. No payment, no concession. No solo narrowbody programme. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through our partners will be in place before we take any share of the fleet. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION: all four orders at hold. `jv_with_pw: hold` keeps the 2035 commitment standing. None of the orders differs from the default, so there is no Board item, and no order needs McCabe's co-signature. Both memos and the Board's guidance recommend this plan.

1. Weights (my expected scenario and predictions)
- S1 0.55, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05, S6 0.10. These are the Board's illustrative weights, and McCabe uses the same set.
- Nothing on the record names UltraFan or commits a partner. Each non-hold column is at most a weak signal, about P 0.10, and S5 is a joint event.
- The bulletin rules out no column.
- The decision does not depend on the weights: the hold row is the best plan in every column, as the brief itself says.

2. Grid rows, S1-S6 ($B ΔPV; items measured against 'UltraFan NB: hold')
Submitted row, 'UltraFan NB: hold':
- -0.56, -0.56, +6.01, -0.56, -0.31, -0.56.
- Weighted +0.11 (0.1095). Worst column -0.56 (S1, S2, S4, S6).
Rows tested and rejected, as item values:
- Withdraw the Joint Venture commitment: 0, 0, -6.57, 0, 0, 0. Weighted -0.66, worst -6.57.
- Trent 1000 upgrade beside the standing commitment: -1.48, -1.48, -6.48, -1.48, -1.46, -1.48. Weighted -1.98. Worst -6.48, beyond its $2B bill, with $5B of strain in S3.
- Withdraw + upgrade: -1.48, -1.48, -8.05, -1.48, -1.46, -1.48. Weighted -2.14. Against the withdraw row alone it is -1.48 flat.
- UltraFan WB: -4.00, -4.00, -9.00, -3.28, -3.02, -4.00. Weighted -4.38. Worst -9.00, beyond its $4B bill. It loses even in S4 and S5: ready in 2051 against a Re-engine EIS of 2050.
- `launch_if_selected`: 0, -7.01, 0, 0, 0, 0. Weighted -0.70. Worst -7.01.
- Unconditional Solo: -7.03, -7.01, 0, -7.03, -7.02, -7.09. Weighted -6.33. Worst -7.09.
- Solo + withdraw: -13.60 in S3.
Every alternative is below 0 on any weights.

3. The 2045 review, read openly
- Our recorded round-2 default was 'withdraw unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS'. It was McCabe's condition and the Board's 2035 recommendation 5.
- Read literally, it says withdraw. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and no fps is on the record.
- Its premise was an inference: a late formation would be ready about formation + 6 (2051), and would be an orphan worth about -4.00 that locks the widebody slot.
- The 2045 grid contradicts that premise. If P&W commits (S3), GTF2 folds in. It has been ready since 2036, and NGSA flies it. Our share is 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050 for $4.0B, with no strain: +6.01 against -0.56, or +6.57 for keeping the commitment.
- A withdraw gains nothing in any column.

McCabe's reading:
- Her 2035 words were 'withdraw unless a live airframe can use it'. NGSA is live and uses the Joint Venture engine through the fold, so her words are met.
- The literal default is not met, but its inference was wrong. She rebases on the data, and her 2035 co-signature covers a 2045 formation on Watson's ruling.

Watson finds no Civil ground for a withdraw. The Board has revised its own recommendation 5 and would veto a withdraw on the present record.

So I do not take the default. Frankly, the condition was written to stop $4B going into an engine no airframe flies, and holding meets that purpose. This is not options management. I close what no airframe can use [RX-0051, R-1573], and here an airframe can. The choice was made in public in 2035, and it costs nothing unless P&W comes to the table. 'When we commit something, we honor it' [RX-0124]. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098].

4. Watson's ruling on a 2045 formation (S3), carried into this decision
- The ready year the board prices is the formation year. GTF2 was launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2036, on a six-year, durability-first programme. It has been in service on NGSA since 2037, so it has eight years of fleet time.
- Nothing is compressed. The fold starts no new clock. Our share is counted by 2050 (26.1%); the brief does not show 2045 for S3.
- UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme. Nothing changes the core definition before it is proven, and our case counts on none of it.
- Support is in place before our share starts, because support already exists. The plan:
  (1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA is the base from day one, written into the agreement at formation.
  (2) Partner shops on the Singapore model, named at formation, take work as each qualifies.
  (3) Spares, repair technology and field service sit inside our $4B.
  (4) Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
  (5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators.
  (6) Our V2500 operator relationships.
  We review GTF2 time on wing and size the spares pool before our share starts. Watson reports through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. We accept no terms that leave us carrying support alone.
- Readiness against an fps launched this round: UltraFan NB launched now would be ready in 2052. That is three years of margin against an fps 10-year EIS of 2055, and zero margin against a 7-year EIS of 2052. We launch neither form, so this is not tested.
- Widebody: UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2051, against a 2050 Re-engine EIS (S4, S5). That fails as advice.

5. Cash: McCabe's numbers, taken as my evidence
- No `launch`, `launch_if_selected` or `commit` value is submitted, so no co-signature is needed.
- Spend is £0 in five columns. In S3 our $4B share is £2.94bn at 1.36 $/£: about £0.49bn a year over six years, or £2.94bn if booked at formation, about a third of GS 2036E sustainable FCF of £9.3bn. The 2026 models end in 2030-31, so this is inference.
- Her flag: £2.94bn in a single year would not fit a flat envelope. Accepted as advice. The money is redeployed from base UltraFan maturation.
- Off-grid worst case: no plausible case loses more than the $4B bill. NGSA's code 7 is final and cannot change in service. GTF2's write-off at a fold falls on P&W.
- The widebody slot closes for 2050 if the Joint Venture forms. That is an option given up. Every widebody item loses in every column on this grid, so she prices it at about 0.
- Her crude IRR, about 120%, rests on board numbers. I take the direction, not the figure.
- No equity, no borrowing, and the capital order is unchanged.

6. ExCo veto checks
McCabe:
- Her binding co-signature refusals cover the Solo (-6.33), `launch_if_selected` (-0.70), UltraFan WB (-4.38), the upgrade beside the commitment (-1.98, worst -6.48), and the upgrade beside a withdraw without a declared premium.
- All are respected; none is submitted. None of her balance-sheet vetoes applies.
Watson:
- His Civil veto is not invoked. I meet each of its three conditions:
  (a) The statement and the public other moves carry no EIS, ready, NGSA or airframer date, and nothing on when our share joins NGSA's fleet. 'Formation plus six' is not revived. The support line uses his no-date form.
  (b) Nothing counts on UltraFan content entering before it is tested.
  (c) The support plan is in this rationale.
Red-line flags:
- McCabe and Watson both flagged 'never both' for the upgrade or UltraFan WB beside the standing commitment. Struck: both are held.
- No flag stands on the submitted plan.
- `overrides` is empty.

7. Red lines, checked against the final orders
- Airframers first: no unconditional launch. Pass.
- No narrowbody item with a weighted value below 0. Pass.
- No item that can lose more than its own bill. Pass.
- Never both. Pass.
- Control's $4B bound: $4.0B in S3 only. Pass.
- No early date. Pass.
- No cancel: nothing of ours is live. Pass.
- No concession. Pass.
- Widebody at 50% or more. Pass.

8. Premium
- $0. The hold row is the best plan in every column, so no held field gives up PV.
- There is no widebody shortfall: 55.2% clears the line without the upgrade.
- What I decline: the upgrade's 60.0% would cost -1.98 and break 'never both'. A withdraw would cost -0.66 and buy nothing.

9. Control's mission metrics on the submitted plan
Own narrowbody money / strain / widebody share 2050 / narrowbody share 2050:
- S1, S2, S4, S5, S6: $0.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 0.0%.
- S3: $4.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 26.1%.
Met in every column. Airbus widebody airframe share is 41.2% (40.2% in S4).

10. Where this is doctrine, not my record
My record has no narrowbody launch decision and no Joint Venture terms. The partner-first rule, the weights, the item test and the 2050 test are team and company doctrine (teams.md, profile.md §9, dashboard_game.md §5), and McCabe's test.

recommendations.text:
Keep the standing Joint Venture commitment: `jv_with_pw: hold`. We revise our round-2 guidance recommendation 5 and our review's first recommendation. Both rested on the inference that a Joint Venture formed after 2035 would be an orphan, worth about -4.00, that locks the widebody slot. The 2045 grid prices it otherwise:
- If P&W commits, the row 'UltraFan NB: hold' is +6.01, against -0.56 for the withdraw row.
- That gives us 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050 for our $4.0B, with no strain.
- A withdraw gains nothing in any column.
Read the ExCo's private 2045 default openly in `rationale` against these figures, and ask McCabe how she now reads her 2035 condition ('withdraw unless a live airframe can use it'). This is not options management. The choice was made in public in 2035 and costs nothing unless P&W commits: 'when we commit something, we honor it'.

Hold UltraFan NB Solo in both forms.
- No live airframe that is not yet in service carries an RR code, so the unconditional launch has no airframe and loses about $7B in five columns.
- `launch_if_selected` fires only in S2. There an fps launched in 2045 enters service in 2055, too late for an $8B engine to pay back on a market the board counts only to 2056: -7.01, and $8.0B against Control's bound.
Airframers go first, and we won't do anything not profitable. Our narrowbody entry is the Joint Venture.

No widebody programme this round.
- Widebody share is 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, above the 50% line, and no Re-engine is on the record.
- Beside the standing commitment the upgrade costs -6.48 in S3 and UltraFan WB -9.00. Both are worse than their own bills, and both would break 'never both'.
Protect the widebody core through Trent time on wing and durability inside base R&D, which is not a programme and carries no strain. Re-test the upgrade only if the commitment is withdrawn on our tests. Re-test UltraFan WB only against a Re-engine on the record, priced with the $5B strain if the Joint Venture has formed.

Disclosure and terms.
- The public statement gives no entry or ready date, says nothing on NGSA's or any airframer's dates, and says nothing on when our engine would join NGSA's fleet. 'Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing' is the right register.
- Restate the standing commitment on standard terms, respectfully. Make no payment or concession to induce P&W or Airbus. 'Terms that credit the technology we bring' asks for value; it is not a concession.
- Any change of terms comes back with joint CEO-CFO sign-off.

Capital.
- Show our Joint Venture share against a broadly flat R&D envelope: $4B, about £0.49bn a year over six years at 1.36 $/£, or about £2.94bn if the board books it at formation, because the folded engine is ready at once.
- The 2026 analyst models end in 2030-31. Any 2045 cash comparison is therefore inference. GS's sustainable free cash flow of £9.3bn in 2036E is the nearest guide, and £2.94bn is about a third of it.
- The capital order stands: balance sheet, then the dividend, then investment. No equity, no new borrowing, no borrowing for buybacks.

The 2050 review. 2050 is the last round. If the Joint Venture has not formed by then, re-test the standing commitment on the 2050 grid. Withdraw it then only if the withdraw's weighted value is at least 0, or if no live airframe can use the engine in time. Cancel what no airframe can use, and keep what pays.

frame.question:
So. 2045, put in cash and quality of earnings. Every new programme on this grid loses money in every column. The live question is the Joint Venture commitment we made in public in 2035.
- Keep it standing (`jv_with_pw: hold`). It costs nothing unless P&W commits. If P&W commits, it is worth +6.57 against a withdraw.
- Or withdraw it, as our recorded 2045 default says. That default rested on a premise the 2045 grid no longer supports.
Second question: is any widebody or Solo money worth spending when hold is the best plan in every column? I say no. I want both of you to test it.
frame.situation:
Airframes
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, in service since 2037. Its selection is code 7 (RR, P&W, CFM), and Airbus restated it as final. Fitted: CFM + P&W. RR was dropped, not ready by EIS. NGSA is in service, so its code cannot change any more.
- fps (Boeing): not launched. "The business case isn't there yet." No date. More than one engine source, durability first. Charleston is 787 production capacity, not a Re-engine.
- Embraer: no launch, "no decision to announce". It talks to all engine makers. On this board it flies P&W or CFM.
- No live airframe that is not yet in service carries an RR code.

Engines
- P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready since 2036, on NGSA since 2037.
- CFM/GE: GEnx upgrade ready since 2033. It took our widebody share from 58.0% to 55.2% from 2042. A LEAP derivative is on offer to every airframer. CFM commits a new engine only with a committed airframer. RISE stays technology.

Joint Venture
- Our commitment has stood since 2035.
- P&W's words: "no Joint Venture to announce", no terms opened this round, "we share risk and investment with partners, not our core technology". The door is "neither shut nor open".
- If P&W commits this round (S3), the Joint Venture forms with GTF2 folded in. Grid: +6.01 against -0.56. That is 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050 for our $4.0B, with no strain.

Widebody Re-engines: none on the record, A350 or 787.

Our position
- ΔPV -0.56 if nobody moves (yield 99.49%).
- The board counts the narrowbody market to 2056 and the widebody to 2061.

Objectives
- Enter narrowbody: not met (0.0% in 2045 and 2050). The only route left on this grid is the Joint Venture in S3: 26.1% in 2050. The brief does not show 2045 for S3.
- Widebody dominance: met. 55.2% in the worst year, in every column.
- Control's mission: met. $0.0B of our own narrowbody money, $0 strain.

The 2045 review
- Our recorded default (round 2: McCabe's condition and the Board's 2035 recommendation 5): "withdraw unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS".
- Its premise: a late formation would be ready about formation + 6 (2051) and would be an orphan worth about -4.00.
- The 2045 grid prices it otherwise: withdraw is 0, 0, -6.57, 0, 0, 0 against hold.
- The Board has revised its own recommendation and now leans to hold. It would veto a withdraw on the present record.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
I would recommend a withdraw, and my 2035 signature on a 2045 formation would go, if Watson rules with reasons either of two things:
- a 2045 formation cannot put the folded engine on NGSA without compressed maturity;
- support (P&W's GTF2 network, partner shops, spares inside the $4B) cannot be in place before our share starts.

- At exactly 0 everywhere, the commitment stands, as we said it would.

I re-test `launch_if_selected` only if an airframer publicly names RR on an airframe whose EIS our engine can meet, with enough market left to pay back $8B. I re-test UltraFan WB only against an A350 Re-engine (or a 787 Re-engine naming UltraFan) on the record, priced with the $5B strain if the Joint Venture has formed.

Delivered numbers and announced customers move me. Projections do not.
cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet. All four at hold passes both.

The question is the 2045 review. In 2035 I wrote "withdraw unless a live airframe can use it"; the recorded default added "not yet in service, by its EIS". Read literally, it says withdraw. It rested on my inference that a late formation would be ready about 2051, an orphan worth about -4.00. That was wrong. GTF2 has been ready since 2036, it folds in, and NGSA flies it. Against hold the withdraw is 0, 0, -6.57, 0, 0, 0: -0.66 on the Board's weights, below zero on any weight for S3. The condition was there to stop $4B going into an engine no airframe flies. Holding meets that purpose. My 2035 co-signature covers a 2045 formation, on Rob's ruling that nothing is compressed and support is in place before our share starts. If he cannot confirm it, my signature goes.

Downside: zero in five columns. In S3 we spend $4B: £0.49bn a year over six years, or £2.94bn if booked at once, about a third of GS's 2036E sustainable free cash flow. No plausible case loses more than the bill. No equity, no borrowing; the capital order stands.

I will not sign a Solo in either form (-6.33, -0.70), UltraFan WB (-4.38) or the upgrade beside the commitment (-6.48).

My record on launch economics is thin; these are board numbers. Hold the commitment as free unless P&W comes. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: An engine must be ready by the EIS of the airframe it serves. For the Joint Venture that means formation + 6, or the earlier ready year of a folded Solo that is further along. For UltraFan NB it means launch + 7, and for UltraFan WB launch + 6, counting only once a Re-engine is in service. Zero margin passes, with a note. A fail is advice, not a veto: the engine is simply not fitted, and McCabe prices the downside (inference).
tests.numbers:
Plan tested: all four fields at hold, with the 2035 commitment standing.

NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, EIS 2037, in service. Code 7 is final, and CFM and P&W are fitted. We can reach it only through the Joint Venture.

S3 (P&W commits this round): the Joint Venture forms in 2045 with GTF2 folded in.
- GTF2 was launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2036 (bulletin), on P&W's six-year, durability-first programme. It has been in service on NGSA since 2037, so it has eight years of fleet time by 2045.
- The ready year the board prices is the formation year, because the folded engine is already ready. The rules allow an earlier ready year when a partner folds in a Solo that is further along. Without the fold it would be formation + 6, or 2051.
- The engine was ready one year before NGSA's 2037 EIS. A 2045 formation changes who holds the share, not the engine's ready year.
- Grid: 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050, for $4.0B of our money.
- Ruling: nothing is compressed.
- Condition: UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, on their own test programme. Nothing changes the core definition before it is proven. This matches P&W's own line: 'Any feature that is not proven in time waits for a later block.'

fps (Boeing): not launched. Against an fps launched this round, UltraFan NB launched in 2045 is ready in 2052.
- fps 10-year or via Embraer: EIS 2055, three years of margin. Pass.
- fps 7-year: EIS 2052, zero margin. Pass, with a note; no column shows this case.
- `launch_if_selected` passes by construction.
- An unconditional Solo is ready in 2052 for no airframe on the record. Fail (advice).

Embraer (S6): it flies P&W or CFM, not us. Not applicable.

Widebody:
- UltraFan WB launched in 2045 is ready in 2051, against a 787 or A350 Re-engine EIS of 2050 (S4, S5). That is one year late. Fail (advice).
- The Trent 1000 upgrade counts from 2048, which is after 2035. No readiness issue.

tests.name: No early date
tests.numbers:
The CEO's draft ('...No solo narrowbody programme. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing...') gives no date and nothing on NGSA. Pass.

The draft public other moves give no dates either: the restated standing commitment on standard terms, and UltraFan maturation inside base R&D. I recheck the final text at step 4.

Notes, not veto grounds:
(1) Say nothing on when our share of NGSA would start. If S3 forms, the bulletin publishes the ready date; do not restate it.
(2) Do not revive 'formation plus six' (2051). It is now wrong in the late direction, which is not a veto ground, but it contradicts the fold.
(3) The draft drops our 2035 line 'Support through partner shops will be in place before entry into service'. If you want a support line, use a form with no date, for example 'Support through our partners will be in place before we take any share of the fleet.' Advice only.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale. A support plan through partner shops must exist before any narrowbody EIS; for a fold, before our share starts (inference). A standing commitment that can form this round counts as a commit for this test.
tests.numbers:
Lead time: zero years from formation until our share starts, on the board's pricing. The folded engine is ready at formation, so our share can start in 2045. The brief shows S3 only for 2050 (26.1%), so 2045-49 is inference.

The plan must therefore be in place at formation. It can be, only because support already exists. The plan:
(1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA, which has supported the fleet since 2037, is the base from day one. This is written into the Joint Venture agreement at formation.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model, named at formation, take work only once each one is qualified.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, inside our $4B.
(4) Castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines. P&W already plans castings and forgings ahead of the ramp.
(5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators, named at formation. There is no new EIS, because the engine is already in service.
(6) Our V2500 operator relationships.

Before our share starts, we review GTF2's fleet time on wing and size the spares pool to it. Watson reports the plan through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

Pass, on condition that the plan goes into the rationale. If the Joint Venture terms left us carrying support alone from day one, support would not be in place. That would be a Civil veto ground.

Only cancelling one before it is ready removes it. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an UltraFan NB Solo unless both are selected, and no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (inference).
tests.numbers:
All-hold: $0 strain in every column. In S3 our own narrowbody money is $4.0B, with $0 strain.

Confirmed: any widebody item beside the standing commitment costs $5B in S3.

- UltraFan WB row in S3: $4.0B / $5B. Its item value is -9.00, worse than its $4B bill.

Confirmed: once the Joint Venture forms, its engine is ready at formation and cannot be cancelled before it is ready. Any widebody programme in 2050 would then carry $5B, so the widebody slot stays shut for 2050.

Withdraw plus upgrade: $0 strain, -1.48 against the withdraw row.

No red line is touched on all-hold.

Hold year table: 197 widebody engines a year to 2041 and 188 a year from 2042 to 2060, with 0 narrowbody. The brief reports no constraint.

S3: 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050. On 2050 demand of 1,933 aircraft at two engines each, that is about 1,009 engines a year credited to us. This is inference, because the board counts aircraft actually delivered. It is about 5.4 times the Trent rate, with P&W on an equal share.

Advice:
- P&W's network leads overhaul at first.
- We add partner-shop capacity on the Singapore model, and high-performing supplier capacity.
- Trent time on wing, the Trent XWB and the Trent 7000 keep first call on engineers, shops and castings.
- My shop-visit baseline is my midterm figure of 1,100-1,200 a year, not the 1,400-1,500 Helen gave.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).

Observed: 58.0% in 2040, then 55.2% from 2042, after the GEnx upgrade (ready since 2033).
- All-hold: 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 in every column, 5.2 points above the line.
- Upgrade: 60.0% in 2050.
- UltraFan WB: 55.2% in 2050 in every column on the grid.

Risk the board does not show (S5): an A350 Re-engine launched in 2045, with EIS in 2050, puts our sole-source franchise in question.
- The board's widebody engine shares do not move with the airframe split (Airbus widebody share is 41.2% in S5 and 40.2% in S4), and the board counts the widebody market to 2061.
- UltraFan WB cannot be ready before 2051, and with the Joint Venture formed it carries $5B of strain.
- I flag this for the 2050 review. It is not a reason to act now: S5 has a weight of 0.05, and UltraFan WB loses even there (-3.02).

Time on wing inside base R&D is the lever. The Trent XWB is about 60% of our large-engine fleet in 2027.

tests.threshold: An idle or cancelled UltraFan still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively; grid values are never adjusted (inference).
tests.numbers: UltraFan maturation inside base R&D feeds Trent time on wing. In S3 we could also gain a two-way flow of geared-architecture durability learning between GTF2, UltraFan and the Trent (inference). No grid adjustment.

vetoes.plan: Row A, 'UltraFan NB: hold' with the commitment standing (the CEO's lean)
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked. I check the Civil veto at step 4, on its grounds only, and under the team rule it binds if any of these holds:
(a) The final statement or a public other move gives any EIS or ready date, any NGSA date, or when our engine or share joins NGSA's fleet. In particular, nothing may be earlier than the bulletin's folded-GTF2 ready year (2036) or formation + 6 (2051).
(b) The statement, an other move or the rationale counts on UltraFan content entering service inside the Joint Venture engine before it is tested. That would reopen the test programme.
(c) The rationale carries no partner-shop support plan in place before our share starts, for a commitment that can form this round.
These grounds rest on attributed transcript turns [RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283].

vetoes.plan: Rows B and D, any withdraw of the Joint Venture commitment
vetoes.ground: No Civil ground. I do not rule that a 2045 formation compresses maturity: GTF2 has been ready since 2036 and in service since 2037. I do not rule that support cannot be in place before our share starts: P&W's network is the base. A withdraw therefore cannot rest on my ground. Whether to withdraw is the CEO's and the CFO's call, on the partner test.

vetoes.plan: Row C, the Trent 1000 upgrade beside the standing commitment; row E, UltraFan WB
vetoes.ground: These are red-line and strain concerns, not Civil vetoes. Each breaks 'never both' in S3, at $5B of strain: -6.48 for the upgrade and -9.00 for UltraFan WB. UltraFan WB also fails Ready by EIS as advice: ready in 2051 against a Re-engine EIS of 2050. The CEO strikes the breach. The upgrade is my time-on-wing tool. Defer it to a plan with no narrowbody programme on record.

vetoes.plan: Rows F and G, UltraFan NB `launch_if_selected` and the unconditional Solo
vetoes.ground:
Not invoked, and conditional.
- G fails Ready by EIS as advice: ready in 2052, with no airframe on the record.
- F passes readiness by construction: ready in 2052, against an EIS of 2055 (three years of margin) or 2052 (zero margin).
- Both would be an all-RR narrowbody with no P&W network behind it. Either one, submitted without a partner-shop support plan in place before EIS, binds on ground (c) at step 4.
- The $8B against Control's $4B bound is Tufan's and Helen's call.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
I would invoke the Civil veto, or change my advice, in seven cases.

Cases where the veto binds:
(1) The Joint Venture terms put UltraFan content into the core definition before it is tested, reopening the test programme. That is compressed maturity. The veto binds unless the content moves to a later insertion.
(2) The rationale leaves out the support plan, or the terms leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one. The veto binds on ground (c).
(3) The statement or a public other move gives any date: an EIS, a ready date, an NGSA date, or when our engine or share joins the NGSA fleet. The veto binds.

Cases where my advice changes:
(4) Public fleet evidence shows GTF2 failing on durability or time on wing on NGSA. The folded engine would no longer be a mature base, and I would re-rule on maturity before our share starts.
(5) The bulletin rules out S3, or the commitment is withdrawn on the 2050 test, so no narrowbody programme is on record. I would then back the Trent 1000 upgrade as my time-on-wing tool, priced at -1.48 as a declared premium.
(6) A 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record names UltraFan, and the Joint Venture has not formed. I would re-test UltraFan WB.
(7) An fps is launched naming RR. `launch_if_selected` passes readiness (ready 2052, against EIS 2052 or 2055), and I would test its support plan. The money and the $4B bound are Tufan's and Helen's call.
ops.memo:
Tufan, Helen: one Rolls-Royce, one programme: the commitment we already made.

My ruling on a 2045 formation (S3): nothing is compressed. GTF2 was launched in 2030, was ready in 2036 on P&W's six-year, durability-first programme, and has flown on NGSA since 2037. The fold brings in a proven engine and starts no new clock. Without it, formation plus six would be 2051. UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions on their own test programme, never into the core definition before it is proven.

Support. The board can start our share in the formation year, so there is no lead time. That works only because support already exists: P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA is the base from day one. On top of it: partner shops on the Singapore model, taking work as they qualify; spares and field service inside our $4B; castings and forgings with high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines; a fleet team with Airbus. Put it in the rationale, or I veto at step 4. I report it through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

Load. Strain is $0 on all-hold. Any widebody item beside the commitment costs $5B in S3; once formed, the widebody slot stays shut for 2050.

Capacity. S3 means about 1,000 narrowbody engines a year by 2050, against 188 Trent. Trent keeps first call.

Widebody: 55.2% in 2045 and 2050, every column.

No ground for a withdraw. All four at hold, no veto. We're pacing that programme properly.

other_moves.move: Standing Joint Venture commitment with Pratt & Whitney, restated on standard terms
other_moves.detail: The 2035 `jv_with_pw: commit` stands. It is for an airframe that has chosen both makers. The terms credit the technology Rolls-Royce brings. That asks for value; it is not a concession. There is no payment to P&W or to any airframer, no launch-style pricing and no free upgrades. The terms are unchanged, so no new joint CEO-CFO sign-off is needed. No dates, and nothing on any airframer's fleet or on when our share would start.

other_moves.move: Continue UltraFan technology maturation inside the existing R&D envelope
other_moves.detail: Demonstrator and geared-architecture work continues inside base R&D and feeds Trent time on wing and durability. No new programme, no new bill, no dates.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan, named at formation and in place before our share starts (Watson)
other_moves.detail:
If P&W commits this round, the plan goes into the Joint Venture agreement at formation:
(1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA, which has supported the fleet since 2037, is the base from day one.
(2) Partner shops on the Singapore Joint Venture model are named at formation and take work only once each is qualified.
(3) A spares pool, repair technology and field service, funded inside our $4B share.
(4) Narrowbody castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
(5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators is named at formation.
(6) Our V2500 operator relationships.
Before our share starts, we review GTF2's fleet time on wing and size the spares pool to it. We will not accept terms that leave us carrying narrowbody support alone from day one. Watson reports the plan through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. Milestones stay private.

other_moves.move: UltraFan insertion rule for the Joint Venture engine
other_moves.detail: The core definition is the folded GTF2, a proven engine. UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme. Nothing that would reopen the folded engine's test programme goes in, and nothing changes the core definition before it is proven. The business case counts on none of it. This is Watson's condition.

other_moves.move: 2050 review of the standing commitment (last round)
other_moves.detail:

- Keep the commitment if the formation column is at least 0 against the withdraw and its off-grid worst case is no worse than the $4B bill.

decision.public_statement: So. Our commitment to a Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney stands, as we said it would. When we commit something, we honor it. It is on standard terms, terms that credit the technology we bring. No payment, no concession. No solo narrowbody programme. Maturity sets the date, and we compress nothing. Support through our partners will be in place before we take any share of the fleet. Widebody is our core, and we will protect it. We are not after market share. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: all four orders at hold. `jv_with_pw: hold` keeps the 2035 commitment standing. None of the orders differs from the default, so there is no Board item, and no order needs McCabe's co-signature. Both memos and the Board's guidance recommend this plan.

1. Weights (my expected scenario and predictions)
- S1 0.55, S2 0.10, S3 0.10, S4 0.10, S5 0.05, S6 0.10. These are the Board's illustrative weights, and McCabe uses the same set.
- Nothing on the record names UltraFan or commits a partner. Each non-hold column is at most a weak signal, about P 0.10, and S5 is a joint event.
- The bulletin rules out no column.
- The decision does not depend on the weights: the hold row is the best plan in every column, as the brief itself says.

2. Grid rows, S1-S6 ($B ΔPV; items measured against 'UltraFan NB: hold')
Submitted row, 'UltraFan NB: hold':
- -0.56, -0.56, +6.01, -0.56, -0.31, -0.56.
- Weighted +0.11 (0.1095). Worst column -0.56 (S1, S2, S4, S6).
Rows tested and rejected, as item values:
- Withdraw the Joint Venture commitment: 0, 0, -6.57, 0, 0, 0. Weighted -0.66, worst -6.57.
- Trent 1000 upgrade beside the standing commitment: -1.48, -1.48, -6.48, -1.48, -1.46, -1.48. Weighted -1.98. Worst -6.48, beyond its $2B bill, with $5B of strain in S3.
- Withdraw + upgrade: -1.48, -1.48, -8.05, -1.48, -1.46, -1.48. Weighted -2.14. Against the withdraw row alone it is -1.48 flat.
- UltraFan WB: -4.00, -4.00, -9.00, -3.28, -3.02, -4.00. Weighted -4.38. Worst -9.00, beyond its $4B bill. It loses even in S4 and S5: ready in 2051 against a Re-engine EIS of 2050.
- `launch_if_selected`: 0, -7.01, 0, 0, 0, 0. Weighted -0.70. Worst -7.01.
- Unconditional Solo: -7.03, -7.01, 0, -7.03, -7.02, -7.09. Weighted -6.33. Worst -7.09.
- Solo + withdraw: -13.60 in S3.
Every alternative is below 0 on any weights.

3. The 2045 review, read openly
- Our recorded round-2 default was 'withdraw unless a live airframe not yet in service can use the engine by its EIS'. It was McCabe's condition and the Board's 2035 recommendation 5.
- Read literally, it says withdraw. NGSA has been in service since 2037, and no fps is on the record.
- Its premise was an inference: a late formation would be ready about formation + 6 (2051), and would be an orphan worth about -4.00 that locks the widebody slot.
- The 2045 grid contradicts that premise. If P&W commits (S3), GTF2 folds in. It has been ready since 2036, and NGSA flies it. Our share is 26.1% of narrowbody engines in 2050 for $4.0B, with no strain: +6.01 against -0.56, or +6.57 for keeping the commitment.
- A withdraw gains nothing in any column.

McCabe's reading:
- Her 2035 words were 'withdraw unless a live airframe can use it'. NGSA is live and uses the Joint Venture engine through the fold, so her words are met.
- The literal default is not met, but its inference was wrong. She rebases on the data, and her 2035 co-signature covers a 2045 formation on Watson's ruling.

Watson finds no Civil ground for a withdraw. The Board has revised its own recommendation 5 and would veto a withdraw on the present record.

So I do not take the default. Frankly, the condition was written to stop $4B going into an engine no airframe flies, and holding meets that purpose. This is not options management. I close what no airframe can use [RX-0051, R-1573], and here an airframe can. The choice was made in public in 2035, and it costs nothing unless P&W comes to the table. 'When we commit something, we honor it' [RX-0124]. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098].

4. Watson's ruling on a 2045 formation (S3), carried into this decision
- The ready year the board prices is the formation year. GTF2 was launched in 2030 and has been ready since 2036, on a six-year, durability-first programme. It has been in service on NGSA since 2037, so it has eight years of fleet time.
- Nothing is compressed. The fold starts no new clock. Our share is counted by 2050 (26.1%); the brief does not show 2045 for S3.
- UltraFan content goes in only as later insertions, each on its own test programme. Nothing changes the core definition before it is proven, and our case counts on none of it.
- Support is in place before our share starts, because support already exists. The plan:
  (1) P&W's GTF2 network on NGSA is the base from day one, written into the agreement at formation.
  (2) Partner shops on the Singapore model, named at formation, take work as each qualifies.
  (3) Spares, repair technology and field service sit inside our $4B.
  (4) Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers, off the Trent lines.
  (5) A fleet-transition team with Airbus and the NGSA operators.
  (6) Our V2500 operator relationships.
  We review GTF2 time on wing and size the spares pool before our share starts. Watson reports through the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. We accept no terms that leave us carrying support alone.
- Readiness against an fps launched this round: UltraFan NB launched now would be ready in 2052. That is three years of margin against an fps 10-year EIS of 2055, and zero margin against a 7-year EIS of 2052. We launch neither form, so this is not tested.
- Widebody: UltraFan WB launched now would be ready in 2051, against a 2050 Re-engine EIS (S4, S5). That fails as advice.

5. Cash: McCabe's numbers, taken as my evidence
- No `launch`, `launch_if_selected` or `commit` value is submitted, so no co-signature is needed.
- Spend is £0 in five columns. In S3 our $4B share is £2.94bn at 1.36 $/£: about £0.49bn a year over six years, or £2.94bn if booked at formation, about a third of GS 2036E sustainable FCF of £9.3bn. The 2026 models end in 2030-31, so this is inference.
- Her flag: £2.94bn in a single year would not fit a flat envelope. Accepted as advice. The money is redeployed from base UltraFan maturation.
- Off-grid worst case: no plausible case loses more than the $4B bill. NGSA's code 7 is final and cannot change in service. GTF2's write-off at a fold falls on P&W.
- The widebody slot closes for 2050 if the Joint Venture forms. That is an option given up. Every widebody item loses in every column on this grid, so she prices it at about 0.
- Her crude IRR, about 120%, rests on board numbers. I take the direction, not the figure.
- No equity, no borrowing, and the capital order is unchanged.

6. ExCo veto checks
McCabe:
- Her binding co-signature refusals cover the Solo (-6.33), `launch_if_selected` (-0.70), UltraFan WB (-4.38), the upgrade beside the commitment (-1.98, worst -6.48), and the upgrade beside a withdraw without a declared premium.
- All are respected; none is submitted. None of her balance-sheet vetoes applies.
Watson:
- His Civil veto is not invoked. I meet each of its three conditions:
  (a) The statement and the public other moves carry no EIS, ready, NGSA or airframer date, and nothing on when our share joins NGSA's fleet. 'Formation plus six' is not revived. The support line uses his no-date form.
  (b) Nothing counts on UltraFan content entering before it is tested.
  (c) The support plan is in this rationale.
Red-line flags:
- McCabe and Watson both flagged 'never both' for the upgrade or UltraFan WB beside the standing commitment. Struck: both are held.
- No flag stands on the submitted plan.
- `overrides` is empty.

7. Red lines, checked against the final orders
- Airframers first: no unconditional launch. Pass.
- No narrowbody item with a weighted value below 0. Pass.
- No item that can lose more than its own bill. Pass.
- Never both. Pass.
- Control's $4B bound: $4.0B in S3 only. Pass.
- No early date. Pass.
- No cancel: nothing of ours is live. Pass.
- No concession. Pass.
- Widebody at 50% or more. Pass.

8. Premium
- $0. The hold row is the best plan in every column, so no held field gives up PV.
- There is no widebody shortfall: 55.2% clears the line without the upgrade.
- What I decline: the upgrade's 60.0% would cost -1.98 and break 'never both'. A withdraw would cost -0.66 and buy nothing.

9. Control's mission metrics on the submitted plan
Own narrowbody money / strain / widebody share 2050 / narrowbody share 2050:
- S1, S2, S4, S5, S6: $0.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 0.0%.
- S3: $4.0B / $0B / 55.2% / 26.1%.
Met in every column. Airbus widebody airframe share is 41.2% (40.2% in S4).

10. Where this is doctrine, not my record
My record has no narrowbody launch decision and no Joint Venture terms. The partner-first rule, the weights, the item test and the 2050 test are team and company doctrine (teams.md, profile.md §9, dashboard_game.md §5), and McCabe's test.

I also took her capex in £ at 1.36 $/£ and her 2050 test. Her binding co-signature refusals (Solo, `launch_if_selected`, UltraFan WB, and the upgrade in either form) are respected: none is submitted. Her flag that £2.94bn booked in one year would not fit a flat envelope is accepted as advice; the money is redeployed from base UltraFan maturation. His capacity advice is noted: Trent keeps first call, and P&W's network leads overhaul. His flag on the A350 franchise (S5) goes to the 2050 review, not to action now.

embraer.public_statement:
Safety first and quality always: that is the foundation of our culture. We believe we are still in our harvest season, right? We keep delivering our plan with the products we have: the E2 family, our executive jets, defence and services. And we keep a healthy balance sheet to support a potential next move.

On a new airplane I will give you the same answer I always give. We are investing in new technologies so that we are prepared to make that decision when the time comes. A launch needs a strong product with a strong value proposition and a robust, I mean, funding strategy, because we don't want to put in risk the financial health of the company. We have done the work again this year, and the numbers do not prove the return. The investment has to prove its return. So today we have no decision to announce, and we will not discuss a segment or a date. We continue to talk to our partners, including in Korea, and to all the engine makers. Any large investment will be made with partners, with the funding defined at the time of approval. I will not say conservative, but I would say, realistic.

On the decisions of other manufacturers: those are their decisions. We have our own strategy, and I can only speak for Embraer.

On trade, Embraer is about engineering. We focus on data and things that are under our control. More than 40% of our aircraft is US content, so tariffs mean fewer US parts bought and fewer US jobs. We continue to work with both governments for zero tariffs in aerospace, and we are cautiously optimistic.

We compete hard in every campaign, but we don't sell our aircraft below cost. As we proudly say in Embraer, We Live for the Challenge.
embraer.rationale:
Decision: Hold (`enb: hold`). Hold is the default, so it is not a Board item and needs no override. The grid decides this, not the tie-break.

1. The grid (brief §3: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea against Do Nothing, debt penalty included)
- S1, Rivals hold: -0.28 $B (97.5%, -2.5 yp).
- S2, Boeing launches fps 10-yr: -0.31 $B (97.2%, -2.8 yp).
- S3, Boeing launches fps 7-yr: -0.35 $B (96.9%, -3.1 yp).
Do Nothing is +0.00 $B (100.0%) in every column, and the brief names it the best plan in all three.

My expected column is S1. The bulletin shows no fps launched, and I do not speculate on Boeing's sealed order. S1 is also the most favourable column for a launch, so the answer does not turn on which column I name. The risk column is S3, the worst plausible one, because the brief labels no risk case.

Four rebuilds agree: mine, Santana's, Meijer's and the Board's.
- $0.27B of operating profit in PV;
- less $0.50B for our $5.50B share, booked at 2049 (discount factor 0.0907);
- less $0.05B, the PV of a $0.59B debt-penalty rise as net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B (56% of EV).
- Result: -0.28. The grid already nets the penalty, so I do not subtract it again (work/r3_decide_calc.py).

2. My four questions
- (1) Strong product, strong value proposition? Weak. It would enter service in 2049, twelve years after NGSA (in service since 2037). It is only slightly better than the A320neo and 737 MAX, and those types are leaving production by then. It wins 6.3% of new customers, and 3.6% once fps is in service. Its later years meet falling demand: 1,701 a year in 2055, 1,106 in 2060. The row improved from -0.58 (2035) to -0.28 only because the bill is booked ten years later. The product is not stronger. It is later.
- (2) Robust funding, without risk to financial health? No. Team Korea's 30% ($3.0B) and partners' 45% ($4.5B) are in the brief. But our $5.50B takes net debt to $6.2B, 56% of EV and about 7.5x against the inherited 2x. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2045-48, 69% of the ~$2B floor each year. The row is below zero in S1.
- (3) Technology available? Yes. P&W is fitted, GTF2 has been ready since 2036 on standard terms, and the brief reports no engine or supply problem. But the window is narrow in every column.
- (4) Will the investment prove its return? No. It is below Do Nothing in every column, and the gap is outside the 2-yp tie band ($0.22B) on the wrong side. Even at 96 a year sold right to 2068 it is -0.21.

3. The team rule, applied as written
- Santana's funding test:
  - leg 1 passes (Team Korea's 30% is in the brief);
  - leg 2 fails (-0.28 $B in S1, below zero);
  - leg 3 passes (S3 at -3.1 yp, inside 5).
  The veto binds, with no override, so Launch is out on this ground alone.
- Meijer's soft veto, leg (a), stands. NGSA is in service at our 2049 entry into service in every column. An override needs a plan more than +5 yp (+$0.55B) above Hold in S1. The launch is 2.5 yp below Hold, and even a zero own share gives only about +$0.27B. No override is possible, and I record none.
- Company hard rules:
  - H2 would be breached by a launch (below zero in the expected column).
  - H3 is not engaged: fps would come in 2052 (S3) or 2055 (S2), more than 2 years after us.
  - H6 is not live.
  - H1 passes.
  - H4 does not apply, since nothing is launched.
- A 2045 launch would also be a one-way door. It enters service in 2049, before the 2050 round, so no cancel could answer a slip.

4. What did not decide this
I did not weigh 'last chance' arguments, a place in the market for its own sake, pre-empting Boeing's fps via Embraer (by rule Boeing's order would stand anyway), or Boeing's or Airbus's statements. Those are their decisions [EX-0093, EX-0069]. This is not 'not yet': every test is resolved, and on these terms the answer is no.

5. Premium and objective
- Premium logged: $0.00B (0 yp). The 2040 in-service objective has been out of reach since the 2035 Hold, so there is nothing to buy.
- 'ΔPV at or above zero, debt penalty included' stays met under Hold and would be broken by a launch.
- No premium cures a failed H2 or a failed leg 2.

6. Forward look to 2050
The rough readings of a 2050 Launch row (entry into service 2054) are all below zero: -0.17 to -0.23 $B in S1. Any fps launched this round would shut that window under H3. I expect Do Nothing to stay right unless a brief shows partners carrying about 71% or more of the bill. The 2050 grid decides.

Where this came from: my record drove the four questions and the red lines. Company doctrine (profile H1 to H6) and the team rule drove the thresholds.

In S3, lifting it (3.6% back to 4%) recovers only about $0.01B on my estimate.

tests.name: Full cost of a cancel (rule)
tests.threshold: Write-off = our share x years elapsed / 4. Cancel only before entry into service, and only when writing off beats continuing by more than 2 yp (H4). Sunk money is no reason either way.
tests.numbers: Nothing is launched, so there is no Cancel row this round. CEO ask (7) confirmed: a 2045 launch enters service in 2049, and the only later round is 2050. The rules allow a cancel only until entry into service, so no round could cancel it. It is a one-way door with no write-off option. At entry into service the spend to date would be the whole $5.50B (4/4) anyway.

tests.name: Premium in dollars (rule)
tests.threshold: Report any value given up for the objective in $B and yp, inside the 5 yp cap ($0.55B) of H5. The objective never overrides a failed leg.
tests.numbers: CEO ask (9) confirmed. The objective 'in service by 2040' has been out of reach since the 2035 Hold, and a 2049 entry into service cannot meet it, so a Launch would buy nothing on it. It would also break the objective's other half, 'ΔPV at or above zero, debt penalty included', which Hold keeps met. The Launch's 2.5-3.1 yp ($0.28-0.35B) sits inside the 5 yp cap, but no premium can be logged against a failed leg 2 or a failed H2. Logged premium under Do Nothing: $0.00B (0 yp). The condition that breaks this number is a brief showing more partner money (see the gap test).

tests.name: Hard-rule watch (H1, H2, H4, H5, H6)
tests.threshold: Flag any breach as a red line for the CEO to strike.
tests.numbers: For the Launch row: H1 passes (Team Korea's 30% is in the brief). A Launch breaches H2, since the grid is below zero in the expected column and the funding test fails. H4 does not apply. H5: the gap is outside the band, and the cap cannot cure a failed leg. H6: Boeing's fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing ordered it this round, Boeing's order would stand and ours would be refused, so it is no reason to launch. H3 is Meijer's count: on the bulletin it is not engaged at 2049 (fps no earlier than 2052). Do Nothing breaches nothing.

tests.name: What closes the gap on the brief's terms (advice; CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: Using only money and terms the brief shows, Launch must be at or above zero with the debt penalty included in S1, and no worse than -5 yp in S3.
tests.numbers: My rebuild, anchored to the grid's S1 and S3 figures, confirms the CEO's numbers. Leg 2 (S1 at zero) needs our own share at 28.9%, with partners at 71.1%. That is $2.61B more than the $4.5B shown, and net debt at entry into service would be 33% of EV. S2 at zero needs 25.8%. Leg 3 (S3 at -5 yp) already passes at 55%. The Board's -2 yp in S3 needs 43.4%, $1.16B more. The +5 yp override bar cannot be reached even at a zero own share, which gives +$0.27B. The leverage line needs <= 9.5%. I see no other route in the brief. Price, margin and line rate are the game master's terms, and no order moves them. The tail after 2060 is worth about $0.01B in the grid, and even 96 a year to 2068 gives -0.21. Tariffs add nothing in S1 and about $0.01B in S3. The penalty moves only with our share. No credit for money a brief does not show.

tests.name: Forward flag for 2050 (advice; CEO ask 10)
tests.threshold: A 2050 Launch (entry into service 2054) must pass the same three legs on the 2050 brief's own grid.
tests.numbers: Rough readings of S1: a pure five-year discount of -0.28 gives -0.17 $B (-1.5 yp). The line to 2060 only gives -0.23 (operating profit $0.09B, bill $0.30B, penalty $0.03B). Full 96 a year to 2073 gives -0.12. All are below zero, and the pure-discount figure is likely optimistic: last round's flag (-0.20) understated this round's actual -0.28 because demand falls. It is a one-way door again, since no round follows 2050. Meijer's H3 count: any fps launched this round shuts a 2054 window. The 2050 grid decides.

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea (2045 launch, entry into service 2049)
vetoes.ground: The funding test fails on leg 2. In S1, the CEO's expected column, Launch against Do Nothing is -0.28 $B (97.5%, -2.5 yp), below zero with the debt penalty included. S1 is the best column, and S2 (-0.31) and S3 (-0.35) are lower still, so the result does not depend on which column is named. Leg 1 passes: Team Korea's 30% and the partners' 45% ($4.5B) are in the brief. Leg 3 passes: S3 is -3.1 yp, inside the 5-point limit. A pass on legs 1 and 3 does not cure leg 2. Under the team rule this veto binds, with no override. Neither 'last chance', a place in the market for its own sake, pre-empting fps via Embraer nor a rival's statement cures a failed leg. The verdict on the CEO's question: yes, the binding veto stands.

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea (2045 launch, entry into service 2049)
vetoes.ground: Advice, not binding (inherited from Garcia). Net debt goes from $0.7B to $6.2B, 56% of EV, about 7.5x against the 'below 2x' comfort, and in my reading investment grade does not survive that. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2045-48: 3.4x the capex run rate, 6.9x the free-cash-flow guide and 69% of the ~$2B cash floor each year. Cash conversion is suspended for four years. There is no cancel round before entry into service in 2049, so it is a one-way door. No objective is left to buy, so the premium is zero.

cfo.would_change_mind_if: I would change my mind on a brief whose grid shows 'Launch the new narrowbody with Korea' at or above zero, debt penalty included, in the expected column Gomes Neto names, and no worse than -5 yp (-$0.55B) against Do Nothing in the risk column. On this brief's terms that needs our share of the $10.0B bill at or below about 29%: partners near 71%, about $2.6B more than the $4.5B shown. The money has to appear in the brief's economics, not in a promise. To pass the advice lines as well (2x leverage, investment grade), our own share would have to fall to about $0.95B. For 2050 I carry these numbers forward: $0.27B of operating profit against $0.50B of bill and $0.05B of penalty in PV at a 2049 entry into service, and net debt to $6.2B (56% of EV). The 2050 grid then decides, with no credit for money it does not show. As soon as we have more visibility, then we can make any change.
cfo.memo:
Felipe here. Brief's numbers only. Expected column S1, as Gomes Neto named it; risk column S3, worst plausible, since none is labelled. Thresholds inherited from Garcia, unchanged; the 5-point limit is the team rule.

Leg 1, partners: pass. Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), suppliers 10%, Brazilian research 5%, all in the brief. Our 55%, $5.50B, is booked at entry into service in 2049.

Leg 2, cost of capital: fail. Launch against Do Nothing in S1 is -0.28 $B, -2.5 yield points, debt penalty netted once ($0.59B rise, $0.05B in present value). My rebuild reconciles: $0.27B operating profit, less $0.50B bill, less $0.05B. S1 is the best column, so it fails everywhere. Even 96 a year to 2068 gives -0.21.

Leg 3, bad case: pass. S3 is -0.35 $B, -3.1 points, inside 5. It does not cure leg 2.

I veto a 2045 launch, and the team rule makes it binding.

Advice, inherited from Garcia: net debt goes to $6.2B, 56% of enterprise value, about 7.5x against "below 2x". In my reading investment grade does not survive that. The cash call is $1.375B a year in 2045-48, 3.4x our capex run rate, 69% of the $2B floor each year. No cancel round before 2049: a one-way door.

The better row is timing, not product: a trend, not a one-off. Zero needs our share near 29%, $2.6B more partner money. No credit until a brief shows it, right?

No objective left to buy: premium zero. Do Nothing. A conservative approach.

tests.name: Market window against fps and NGSA (veto leg a; CEO ask 1)
tests.threshold: From the bulletin, find any launched fps or NGSA and its EIS. Window = the first new-generation EIS minus ours. Pass if none is launched or the window covers our ~6-year ramp. Flag (advice) if it is shorter than the ramp. Fail (soft veto, leg a) if a new-generation type is in service or due at or before our EIS. Basis: my E2 record applied to a narrowbody by inference, plus company record (no head-to-head entry while Boeing and Airbus hold that segment).
tests.numbers: Bulletin: NGSA launched 2030, in service since 2037. fps not launched. Our EIS is 2049 (2045 + 4). Window = 2037 - 2049 = -12 years, so the narrowbody enters service twelve years behind a new-generation type in S1, S2 and S3. The CEO's reading is confirmed: narrow in every column, not shut (H3), and H6 not live. An fps launched this round would enter service in 2052 (S3, 7-yr, 3 years after ours) or 2055 (S2, 10-yr, 6 years after). Neither is within 2 years, so H3 is not engaged. How much value depends on the rivals: no column on this grid has neither type in service. NGSA is a fact, not a sealed order. The second type costs $0.03B (S2: -0.31 against -0.28) and $0.07B (S3: -0.35). Leg (a) fails on the public record (record, by inference; company record).

tests.name: Share path through the ramp, by column: who sets deliveries (CEO ask 2)
tests.threshold: Read our share at EIS and at full rate from the brief, and say whether the line or customer demand sets deliveries. Uses the rules' demand curve, shown both on total demand and with COMAC taken off the top (inference).
tests.numbers: Shares after the US cut: S1 6.3% from 2049. S3 6.3% to 2051, then 3.6% from 2052. S2 6.3% to 2054, then 3.6% from 2055. Line 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96 (2049-2054), then 96 a year to 2068 (20 market years). Wanted at 6.3% (with COMAC off the top in brackets): 121 (106) in 2049, 122 (106) in 2050, 110 (94) in 2054, 107 (91) in 2055, 100 (84) in 2056, 85 (69) in 2058, 70 (54) in 2060. In S1 the line sets deliveries to about 2055-56. After that, demand would set them, but the brief shows 96 a year to 2060 (8.7% of market deliveries), so overflow fills the line. That is inference from the rules: the MAX phases out to none by 2060 and there is no fps in S1. At 3.6%, about 66 (57) are wanted in 2052 and 61 (52) in 2055, so the share binds from fps EIS: 2052-53 in S3 and 2055 in S2. My share-bound shortfall with no overflow, to 2060: $0.08-0.10B (S3) and $0.06-0.07B (S2). The grid shows $0.07B and $0.03B, because overflow refills some slots. Tail after 2060: count about $0.01B, what the grid implies (operating profit PV of $0.272B against $0.262B with the line to 2060). At 96 a year to 2068 it would be $0.347B and the row -0.21, still below zero. Work: work/r3_meijer_test_calc.py.

tests.name: Product edge over the A320neo and 737 MAX
tests.threshold: State the edge in the brief's numbers and whether it is compelling (company record: no head-to-head entry without a compelling advantage). Inference: my E2 case does not carry over to a 150-180 seater. Advice only, not a veto leg.
tests.numbers: Rules: the narrowbody is 'slightly better for airlines than the 737 MAX and A320neo and worse than a new-generation airplane'. By 2049 the types it beats are leaving production (rules, by inference): the A320 Alt-plan tail runs about eight years from 2037, and the MAX falls from 2044 to none by 2060. So its real rival is NGSA, which has twelve years in service at our EIS. The share it wins falls from 12% to 7% with one type in service, and to 6.3% after the US cut. $50M at 12% gives $6.0M a jet, $0.576B a year at 96. That edge is slight, not compelling. My E2 case (trip cost, complementing the big jets) does not carry over to a 150-180 seater that fights them head-on, and the first E-Jet 'struggled to get to the right cost level' against them. I name my E2 anchoring here. This is advice, not a veto ground (CEO ask 1).

tests.name: Customers and campaigns
tests.threshold: Back a launch only where Embraer's share is positive at EIS and at full rate in the expected case, and Hold's E2 business is not reduced (inference from record).
tests.numbers: Expected column S1, share of market deliveries (brief): about 0.8% in 2049 (16 jets), 1.7% in 2050 (32), 4.4% in 2053 (80), 5.7% in 2055 (96) and 8.7% in 2060 (96). It is positive. The brief says the E-Jets and business jets are the same in every plan, so Hold's E2 business is not reduced. Buyers (inference): E-Jet operators moving up, multi-OEM buyers, lessors and low-cost carriers, won with local sales and support. I note my campaign optimism; only the brief's share is in these numbers.

tests.name: Price discipline
tests.threshold: Report the price effect from the brief and whether it reaches Embraer's own margin, as a number (inference).
tests.numbers: Rules: from 2048, one year before our EIS, the price of every new single-aisle jet Boeing and Airbus deliver falls in a straight line over 7 years: 0.57% in 2049, 1.43% in 2052, 2.0% from 2054. On Boeing it is up to 2.6% in years with no new Boeing narrowbody in service: every year in S1, to 2051 in S3, to 2054 in S2. The cut falls on their margins, not ours, because the brief fixes ours at $50M and 12%. Advice (inference against company record): 12% is 4.6 times the 2.6% Commercial Aviation earned in 2025. Each 1 pp of our margin is worth about $0.023B in PV on this row. Zero in S1 would need about 24% at $50M, and the override bar about 49%. The brief shows 12%, so no credit. Pricing to win against NGSA would push the margin down, not up.

tests.name: Supply chain and ramp (veto leg b; CEO asks 4 and 5)
tests.threshold: Take the brief's ramp as given, never a faster one. Fail (soft veto) if the brief reports a supply-chain problem that would hold the line. Flag a lesser risk as advice. Mostly company record.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no supply-chain problem, so leg (b) passes on supply. The ramp is taken as given: 16 in 2049 rising to 96 a year from 2054, six years. Advice, not veto grounds (CEO ask 4). (1) Company record: the E-Jet line climbs toward about 120 commercial jets a year, 'if the investments justify the return', with bottlenecks that move from one supplier to another. Adding 96 makes about 216 a year by 2054, 1.8 times that target. (2) Rules and bulletin: NGSA has been at rate 100 a month since about 2045, and Airbus adds lines from 2045 (+5 a month each year, up to +20). Airbus is securing its own titanium, additive and Spirit work packages, and Korean industry builds structures for Boeing and Airbus. So a second line competes for the same supply base (inference). (3) Our hit has been 'a lot less than on the competitors' because core work stays in-house (record).

tests.name: Engines and system supply (veto leg b; CEO ask 3)
tests.threshold: Pass if the brief shows an engine on offer by EIS with no live delivery or durability problem. Fail (soft veto) if no engine is on offer or a live engine problem would hold the line. Record plus company record.
tests.numbers: Rules: the narrowbody flies P&W engines (the E2's maker). CFM's Embraer partnership is not live, since no such order is on the bulletin. Bulletin: GTF2 has been ready since 2036, thirteen years before our 2049 EIS, and P&W offers it 'on standard terms' to any new narrowbody that selects P&W. CFM offers a LEAP derivative to every airframer. The brief reports no engine problem, so nothing holds the line or the four-year development. Advice, not a veto ground: (1) at full rate the line needs 192 P&W engines a year before spares; (2) P&W says 'the fleet flying today keeps first call on material' and is signing Airbus's rate-gated agreements; (3) P&W says the GTF fleet 'was not where it needed to be' for years and reports no Hot Section kit time on wing yet. Engines were 'part of the supply chain challenges' in our guidance (record). Korea has no airliner engine (research, unverified).

tests.name: Clean-sheet schedule and certification (CEO ask 5)
tests.threshold: Advice only: set the board's 4-year development against our own record. A slip is a veto ground only if the brief reports one (inference).
tests.numbers: The brief reports no development or certification problem, so there is no veto ground. Company record: the E2, a re-wing and re-engine of an existing family, took about 4 years 10 months from launch (June 2013) to first delivery (April 2018), with a clean entry into service. The board gives a clean-sheet 150-180 seater, a step Embraer has never taken, four years (2045-2049), then a six-year ramp. One-way door: EIS in 2049 comes before the 2050 round, so no cancel could answer a slip (the board prices none). Embraer integrates and certifies; the partner cannot fill that gap (research, unverified).

tests.name: Partner fit (Team Korea)
tests.threshold: Report the partner's share of the bill from the brief. Flag a plan that relies on the partner for integration or certification (inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: Team Korea 30% ($3.0B), risk-sharing suppliers 10% ($1.0B), Brazilian state research money 5% ($0.5B). Partners carry $4.5B in all. Embraer carries 55% ($5.50B), booked at EIS 2049 (PV $0.50B at 1/11.03). Embraer leads the airframe (inference from the 2011 lead-airframer stance), and the brief does not rely on the partner for integration or certification. On this row, zero in S1 needs our own share near 29% (my rebuild). The funding verdict is Santana's.

tests.name: Customer politics and the high-volume market (CEO ask 6)
tests.threshold: Advice only: report the tariff effect from the brief and discount US campaigns by a number (company record plus inference).
tests.numbers: Brief: the US climate cuts our share of new customers by 10% (7% to 6.3%, 4% to 3.6%). In S1 the line binds to about 2055, so the cut costs about $0.01B in PV. In S2 and S3, 4.0% against 3.6% is about 5-7 jets a year, about $0.01B. So the discount on US campaigns is 10% of share, worth about $0.01B on this grid. Can it sell its line into the big markets, the US included? In S1, yes to about 2055: 107-122 wanted against 96. But the big market shrinks, from 1,701 a year in 2055 to 1,106 in 2060. By share it is not a small-market product (5.7% of deliveries in 2055, 8.7% in 2060). It is a late one, and in S2 and S3 the 3.6% fills about two-thirds of the line. Not priced: BNDES credit, the golden share, any US response to a Brazil-Korea airliner. Over 40% US content cuts both ways (company record).

tests.name: Override of my soft veto (team rule; CEO ask 7)
tests.threshold: An override needs a plan more than 5 yp (+$0.55B) better than Hold in the expected column, recorded by the CEO as a Board item.
tests.numbers: Expected column S1: Launch -0.28 $B (97.5%, -2.5 yp) against Hold at +0.00. The bar is +0.55 $B, so the launch falls $0.83B (7.5 yp) short. At a zero own share the row is about +0.27 $B, the operating profit alone, still $0.28B short. Only a margin near 49% at $50M would reach the bar, and the brief shows 12%. No valid override exists on this brief, and none is possible on these terms.

tests.name: Hard-rule check (H1 partner, H3 shut window, H6 fps via Embraer)
tests.threshold: Flag an order the rules or the profile's hard rules forbid. This is not my veto.
tests.numbers: H1: Team Korea's 30% is in the brief. H3: at EIS 2049 only NGSA is in service (since 2037). fps would be due in 2052 (S3) or 2055 (S2), not within 2 years, so H3 is not engaged in any column. H6: Boeing's fps via Embraer is not live. If Boeing orders it this round, its order stands and our launch is refused. H2 and the funding legs are Santana's. I state only the grid: -0.28 (S1), -0.31 (S2), -0.35 (S3), and my rebuild: bill PV $0.499B, debt-penalty rise $0.590B (net debt $0.7B to $6.2B, 56% of EV), PV $0.054B, counted once. That gives -0.29 with the line to 2060 only.

tests.name: Forward flag: a 2050 launch, EIS 2054 (CEO ask 8)
tests.threshold: The same window rule applied forward: narrow (soft veto) if one type is in service at 2054; shut (H3) if both are in service or due within 2 years. Not this round's order.
tests.numbers: Confirmed: any fps launched this round shuts a 2054 EIS under H3. A 7-yr fps enters service in 2052, so both types are in service at 2054. A 10-yr fps enters service in 2055, so it is due within 2 years. If fps stays unlaunched this round, a 2054 EIS meets a narrow window again: NGSA has been in service for 17 years, leg (a) fails, and an fps sealed in 2050 would come in 2057 or 2060. A 2054 line reaches 96 only in 2059, when 6.3% of 1,225 is about 77 wanted (rules). So it rests on overflow from the start. The 2050 grid decides.

vetoes.plan: Launch the new narrowbody with Korea in 2045 (EIS 2049)
vetoes.ground: Narrow window, leg (a). The bulletin shows NGSA launched in 2030 and in service since 2037, twelve years before our 2049 EIS. In S1, S2 and S3 the narrowbody would enter service behind a new-generation type. Its share of new customers is already cut to 6.3% (7% less the US 10%) before its first delivery, and to 3.6% once fps follows (2052 in S3, 2055 in S2). The window is narrow, not shut: H3 is not engaged, since fps is due more than 2 years after our EIS, and H6 is not live. Leg (b) passes: P&W is fitted, GTF2 has been ready since 2036 on standard terms, and the brief reports no engine or supply-chain problem. Under the team rule this is a soft veto. It binds unless Gomes Neto records an override, as a Board item, for a plan more than 5 yp (+$0.55B) better than Hold in the expected column. In S1 the launch is -0.28 $B (-2.5 yp), $0.83B short of that bar. Even a zero own share gives about +0.27 $B, so no valid override exists on this brief. For the Board, plainly: in S1 the 96-a-year line, not the window, sets deliveries to about 2055. What sinks the row is the bill ($0.50B in PV) against $0.27B of operating profit late in a falling market.

vetoes.plan: Readiness advice on any launch (not binding)
vetoes.ground: Advice only, not a veto ground, because the brief reports none of these as a problem. (1) Supply base: about 216 commercial jets a year by 2054 (1.8 times the E-Jet target of about 120), on suppliers that also feed NGSA at 100 a month and Airbus's extra lines from 2045 (up to +20 a month). (2) Engines: 192 P&W engines a year at full rate, behind Airbus's rate-gated agreements, with the in-service fleet keeping first call on material. (3) Schedule: a clean sheet certified in four years against the E2's roughly five, with no cancel round before the 2049 EIS (a one-way door). (4) US tariffs: worth about $0.01B on this grid.

vetoes.plan: Forward flag: a launch in 2050 (EIS 2054), not this round's order
vetoes.ground: NGSA has been in service since 2037, so a 2054 EIS fails leg (a) of my soft veto whatever Boeing does. If Boeing launches fps this round, a 2054 EIS is shut under H3: a 7-yr fps enters service in 2052 (both types in service) and a 10-yr fps in 2055 (due within 2 years), so no launch is allowed at all. I will recount on the 2050 bulletin and say plainly if it is shut.

ops.would_change_mind_if: On the window, leg (a): nothing on this grid can change it. NGSA in service since 2037 is a bulletin fact, not a sealed order, and no column has it out of service. Toward a launch, two things. First, a brief showing ΔPV at or above zero in S1, debt penalty included: on these terms, our own share near 29% (partners near 71%, about $2.6B more than the $4.5B shown), or a margin near 24% at $50M. Second, to clear my veto by override, more than +0.55 $B in S1. That is out of reach even at a zero own share (+0.27 $B), and would need a margin near 49%. No credit until a brief shows any of it. Toward a harder line, either of two things. First, a brief reporting a P&W delivery or durability problem, or a supplier constraint that would hold the line (leg b). Second, fps launched this round, which shuts a 2050 launch under H3.
ops.memo:
That's a triple layer question. Three parts.

First, the window. NGSA has been in service since 2037. Our entry into service is 2049, twelve years behind it, in S1, S2 and S3. That is leg (a) of my soft veto, and it stands. Narrow, not shut: fps would come in 2052 (S3) or 2055 (S2), more than two years after us, so H3 is not engaged; fps via Embraer is not live. An override needs a plan 5 yield points better than Hold. This one is 2.5 below. Even with partners paying the whole bill, operating profit is $0.27B against a $0.55B bar. No override exists.

Second, the line. P&W is fitted, GTF2 has been ready since 2036, and the brief reports no engine or supply problem, so leg (b) passes. Advice only: 216 commercial jets a year on a supply base Airbus is loading; 192 P&W engines a year behind Airbus's agreements; a clean sheet in four years, when the E2 took nearly five, through a one-way door.

Third, the customers. At 6.3% they want 107 to 122 jets a year to 2055 against a 96 line, so the line sets deliveries in S1. Then demand falls to 1,106 by 2060, 6.3% is about 70, and the 96 leans on overflow. fps costs $0.03-0.07B, the US cut about $0.01B. The seats fill, but late, into a shrinking market.

Hold. Window and customers rest on my E2 record, by inference; supply and schedule on company record.

other_moves.move: Deliver the plan and keep building cash to support a potential next move
other_moves.detail: We keep delivering the E2 family, the business jets, defence and services to plan in the harvest season. Productivity comes before new capacity. Commercial output rises toward about 120 jets a year only where the return justifies it, and we keep supply-chain headroom [EX-0053, EX-0080, EX-0077, EX-0078, EX-0087]. We keep the cash and the low net debt ($0.7B) to support a potential next move. The board does not price this.

other_moves.move: Keep technology readiness funded for the next product cycle
Continue the Team Korea / KAI talks on a funding solution
other_moves.detail:
I follow the talks personally every two weeks [EX-0028]. The aim is a funding solution defined before any business-case approval [EX-0046, EX-0034].

On this brief's terms, a launch reaches zero in S1 only if our own share falls to about 29%. That means partners near 71%, about $2.6B more than the $4.5B the brief shows. It reaches the Board's -2 yp in S3 only at about 43%, about $1.2B more. It clears the inherited 2x leverage line only at about 9.5%. No credit until a brief shows the money.

No segment, no date, no commitment. Embraer keeps control and no military technology moves, so the state's consent is not needed (golden share; Board recommendation 8).

other_moves.move: Carry the 2045 numbers into the 2050 package
other_moves.detail:
Santana carries forward:
- $0.27B of operating profit in PV, against $0.50B for our 55% of the bill and $0.05B of debt penalty (a $0.59B rise in 2049, counted once). That gives -0.28 $B in S1.
- Net debt from $0.7B to $6.2B: 56% of EV, about 7.5x against the inherited 2x.
- The cash call of $1.375B a year against the ~$2B floor.
- The partner shares that would close the gap.
- His rough 2050 readings for S1: -0.17 by pure discount, -0.23 with the line to 2060, -0.12 at full rate to 2073. All are below zero, and the pure-discount figure is likely optimistic.
